value.text: Lucie Police Department is investigating the death of a 77-year-old man who was found in a pond, according to a press release from the PSLPD . PSLPD says that on Friday, around 1:18 p.m., officers were called to a residence on SW Mockingbird Drive in reference to a missing adult who was later identified as Michael Joseph Kramer, 77. The investigation revealed that Kramer was last seen by his wife inside of their residence at around 10:00 p.m. However, when Kramer’s wife woke up at approximately 7:00 a.m. on Friday, Kramer was nowhere to be found despite all of his personal belongings remaining in the residence. See also: Delray Beach body shop owner accused of insurance fraud stemming from 2024 claims After an extensive search of the area, PSLPD says that they located an unresponsive man that matched Kramer’s description in a pond directly across the street from the residence at around 2:00 p.m. The PSLPD Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water, and he was pronounced deceased. PSLPD says that currently, the circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear, but no indications of foul play seem apparent.

Photos show animal injury.** A Port St. Lucie man was arrested following an investigation into a social media video that shows a man abusing a small dog, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . Video from SLCSO shows Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, appearing to kick a small dog in his backyard near a pool. The video made rounds on social media, and the outrage sparked an investigation from the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. See also: Delray Beach body shop owner accused of insurance fraud stemming from 2024 claims Following the investigation, the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office’s findings gave detectives probable cause to charge Shieferstein with animal cruelty. SLCSO says that Shieferstein is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $7,500 bond. Lucie Police Department has released an update on 2 separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard.Although both incidents involve political campaign signs in the same area, police say they are being investigated as separate cases, with each evaluated independently based on their own facts, evidence, and applicable law.The first incident occurred on August 5, 2026, near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on August 7, 2026, near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. At this time, there is no indication that any campaign signs associated with this incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department."The fact that Mr. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process," the department said. "As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy."The department said that should the investigation identify any potential policy violations involving a department employee, the matter will be handled in accordance with established department procedures. Consistent with Florida law, department employees are afforded the rights and protections provided under the Florida Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. Any related administrative review will proceed following the completion of the ongoing criminal investigation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day. At approximately 1:18 p.m. today, officers responded to a residence on the 1400 block of SW Mockingbird Drive regarding a missing adult. Kramer was last seen by his wife inside their home at approximately 10 p.m. the following morning, Kramer was no longer inside the residence. Kramer’s personal belongings, including his shoes, wallet, and cellphone, were still inside the home. His wife searched for him and contacted local hospitals before reporting him missing to law enforcement at approximately 1:18 p.m. Officers began searching the neighborhood and, during the canvass, located an unresponsive person in a pond directly across the street from Kramer’s residence at approximately 2 p.m. The individual and clothing matched Kramer’s description. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water near the shoreline of the pond, where he was confirmed deceased. The circumstances surrounding Kramer’s death remain under investigation. Police said there are no known indications of foul play at this preliminary stage of the investigation. Authorities encourage the public to promptly contact law enforcement when a person is believed to be missing, emphasizing that timely reporting allows officers to begin investigative and search efforts as quickly as possible.

Lucie are investigating two separate incidents involving mayoral campaign signs being removed or tampered with, occurring two days apart and about a mile from each other. Surveillance footage shows a woman removing one of Mayor Shannon Martin’s campaign signs on SW Thanksgiving Avenue on Wednesday night. Police say the footage also shows one of Martin’s opponents, Steven Giordano, at the scene. “If I would have touched another sign, I would have been in handcuffs last night,” Giordano said. Giordano stated that the homeowner had given his volunteer permission to remove the sign. Another incident occurred early Friday morning on SW Thornhill Drive, where Giordano said he witnessed someone vandalizing his campaign sign. “I saw — I didn’t know who it was at the time — grab my sign and vandalize multiple times,” Giordano said. Police later identified the individual as Aaron Martin, the mayor’s husband and a lieutenant with the Port St. Officers said homeowners had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property, and a language barrier may have caused confusion about the signs. On Friday evening, Shannon Martin addressed the incidents on social media, stating that she was aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of her campaign signs over several days. She said some of her signs had been taken down without permission and replaced with Mr. “At no time did my husband steal Mr. Giordano's sign nor did he damage or vandalize it. The sign remained at the location. Giordano contacted law enforcement and has characterized these actions as burglary and vandalism. His allegations are completely false,” Martin said in a post. Police emphasized that the fact that the mayor’s husband is a lieutenant will not affect the investigation. Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore — one that washed up dead and another of fishermen struggling with a hooked one. Both incidents occurred Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident and avid beach walker Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the deadly beast and released it back into the water. Shark expert and conservationist Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark by looking at the video. Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County, which also includes Hutchinson Island, to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

Thomas Todd, and his wife, have a neighbor they're worried about — not because of anything they can see, but because of what they can hear and smell. WATCH BELOW: 'She really has legally walled us off from investigating,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek tells Chief Investigative Reporter Jamie Ostroff The couple sent video of dogs barking from behind a fence next door at their Martin County home. Todd said he believes there are between 15 and 20 dogs on the property. I visited the Todds' home on a calm, July afternoon. But when the wind picks up, Todd said the smell coming from next door is overwhelming. "It's a combination of garbage and animal feces and urine," Todd said. "I mean, I don't know how somebody could live in that." Todd first raised his concerns at a WPTV Let's Hear It event in Jensen Beach in May. When asked what a solution would look like, his answer was simple: "Save those dogs. Get them out of there." Public records obtained by WPTV show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. The owner is not being named because she has never been charged with a crime. One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. Records show the owner did clean up after initial visits and told animal control she had re-homed some of the dogs, but she eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside. Multiple reports note that deputies were not allowed to see the dogs when they visited the home. A code enforcement officer took photos through the glass front door in 2023, noting "a dog with feces on it." After that visit, the owner put up a fence. Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. For Todd, what's out of sight is not out of mind — let alone out of sound or smell. And there's nothing anybody can do or will do," Todd said. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation. "You can't even see into the property anymore," Budensiek said. "So, she really has legally walled us off from investigating exactly what's going on inside." When asked whether deputies have a lawful way to enter the property and look for themselves, Budensiek said they do not — unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that -- you know -- dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of — we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there," Budensiek said. Florida statutes require that confined animals be provided "a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water." Budensiek said that standard appears to be met based on what deputies can observe. "We saw recently — as recently as last week — that there's food boxes that are out there, empty food boxes, so we know the animals from the outside look to be being taken care of," Budensiek said. I attempted to reach the owner by phone and left three voicemails. In the most recent incident report — from July 2025 — the owner told deputies she had 7 dogs, then "redacted and said that she only had five dogs," according to the report. Todd said he does not believe that statement. "Seems like from everything I've been told, the law's on her side," Todd said. Since I visited the Todds last month, they say they continue to hear the dogs and have continued to follow up with the sheriff's office. They have also seen animal control in front of the owner's house a few times since this story began — but deputies have not gone in. Budensiek acknowledged the neighbors' frustration but said there is little more his office can do. "I know the neighbors are worried and, and we'll still respond out there for complaints. But again, it's not illegal to be a bad neighbor," Budensiek said. We want to be your voice and help you find solutions. Lucie Mets celebrate their game 2 win against the Daytona Tortugas on August 5. This was the second game of a doubleheader to make up for a rainout on June 20. Lucie Mets split a doubleheader with the Daytona Tortugas on Wednesday at Clover Park, falling 8-4 in the opener before rallying for an 11-10 victory in 10 innings in the nightcap. The twin bill made up a June 20 rainout. Lucie avoided a doubleheader sweep, while Daytona’s seven-game winning streak came to an end. The Mets won the second game when John Smith III delivered a two-run single in the bottom of the 10th inning, scoring Wyatt Vincent and Vladi Gomez after Daytona had taken a 10-9 lead in the top of the inning. Lucie forced extra innings after erasing a three-run deficit in the seventh. Gomez’s two-strike, bases-loaded double tied the game 6-6 with two outs. Both teams scored in the eighth before trading two-run homers in the ninth. Daytona’s Dylan King put the Tortugas ahead 9-7, but Julio Zayas answered with a game-tying two-run homer for the Mets. Gomez finished 4 for 5 with three doubles, two RBIs and two runs. Smith III went 2 for 5 with three RBIs, while Zayas was 3 for 4 with a home run, two RBIs and two runs scored. 5 prospect Aaron Watson earned the win in his Single-A debut, limiting the Mets to two runs over five innings despite allowing eight hits. The Tortugas took control early, capitalizing on two Mets throwing errors in the first inning before scoring four runs in the fourth, highlighted by Adolfo Sanchez’s solo home run. Lucie collected 10 hits in the loss. Elian Peña went 2 for 4 with a double and two RBIs, while Aiden Robbins and Bohan Adderley each had two hits. Kuhio Aloy recorded the first hit of his professional career with a fifth-inning single. The Mets (14-22, 47-55) and Tortugas (23-13, 44-58) continue their series Thursday, August 6 at Clover Park with first pitch scheduled for 6:10 p.m. It’s $2 Night, featuring select $2 beer, hot dogs, fountain drinks and popcorn. Daniel Eugene Holmes, 42, is in the St. Lucie County Jail on a $31,000 bond for two counts of burglary of a conveyance and one count of loitering and prowling, according to the jail web site. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office investigators say he is linked to a recent series of burglaries in St. LUCIE COUNTY – A man allegedly linked to several burglaries in the St. Lucie Village community was arrested by St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office deputies on Aug. 5, according to a sheriff’s office Facebook posting. Daniel Eugene Holmes, 42, was charged with two counts of burglary of a conveyance and one count of loitering and prowling after officers found him going through trash near the road at 2900 block of North Indian River Drive, according to the Facebook posting. During their investigation, deputies determined Holmes matched the description of a person of interest developed during an ongoing burglary investigation in St. Through additional investigative efforts, deputies established probable cause linking Holmes to other reported crimes in the area, according to the Facebook posting. Holmes also had a bicycle with fishing equipment attached, according to the Facebook posting. Holmes was taken to the St. Lucie County Jail, where he remained as of Aug. “This case highlights the value of proactive patrol and the attention to detail our deputies demonstrate every day,” said Sheriff Richard Del Toro in the Facebook posting. “What began as a call about suspicious activity quickly developed into an investigation that solved multiple crimes and removed a repeat offender from our community. We remain committed to aggressively investigating property crimes and holding those responsible accountable.” The investigation remains active and additional information will be provided as appropriate. A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say they responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident. "These two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, and this is based off the dash camera and witness statements that we've collected," said Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. See also: Miami man faces prison after pleading guilty to online threats against Rubio, Noem Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center , per PSLPD. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition.\ Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The investigative findings indicate that the pickup truck was actively pursuing that motorcyclist just moments prior to that crash, said McNally. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m. This case does, though, serve as hopefully a powerful reminder that allowing your anger to dictate your actions behind the wheel can put multiple innocent lives at risk, McNally said.

Ricky Lee Schieferstein, 68, of Port St. Lucie County Jail as of Aug. 7 on a $7,500 bond on a charge of cruelty to animals, according to the jail web site. The investigation began after numerous members of the community shared the video and tagged the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office across its social media platforms, according to the sheriff’s office Facebook posting. A 76-year-old woman was arrested after police said she used barcode stickers and tags she brought into the store with her to pay deeply reduced prices for merchandise at a Target store in Port St. Officers responded Tuesday, August 4 to the Target at Tradition store, 10720 SW Village Parkway after store loss-prevention employees detained Joan McKeon, according to the Port St. Investigators said McKeon entered the store carrying barcode stickers and barcode tags for lower-priced products. She allegedly placed or scanned those barcodes at self-checkout instead of using the barcodes attached to the merchandise she selected. During the most recent incident, police said an item priced at $32.99 was scanned as a $1.29 purchase. Officers searching McKeon’s purse found 28 barcode stickers, some bearing the names of other retailers, including TJ Maxx, Publix and Burlington, police said. Investigators planned to contact those businesses as part of the continuing investigation. "Listen, times clearly are hard for people in America. Healthcare is high, food is high so people are doing anything that they can to make ends meet," said Noesha Jennings, a shopper from Port St. "Me personally I think it's pretty clever but we are a growing city and we can't be having those things going on around here, man," said Stephon Jennings, a shopper from Port St. See also: No Powerball jackpot winner; prize climbs to estimated $856 Million Target loss-prevention employees told officers the incident was not isolated. According to the arrest report, a Target Loss Prevention Manager at that store told police this was the twelfth retail theft McKeon committed at that store, dating back to September 2025. McKeon is charged with fraud-swindle-obtain property under $20,000. "You don't rip anybody off like that. I'm very shocked how the world's turning out. So it's very disappointing to hear," said Kimise Volpe, a shopper from Palm Beach Gardens. We reached McKeon by phone Friday. She said she did commit the crime and she did not know why she did it. She also said she was not thinking clearly and she said I know I was wrong. Target's media relations office did not respond to an e-mail seeking comment.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for donations, foster homes, adopters, and help from rescue organizations after taking in more than 100 animals from what the Martin County sheriff described as the worst animal hoarding case in the county’s history. "We need adopters and fosters. Anyone that's willing to adopt and has been thinking about getting a pet, the time is now," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Employees and volunteers have been working around the clock to care for the animals while the Palm City shelter continues its regular operations. A total of 108 animals were brought to the humane society for medical treatment and care after 77-year-old Gail Giustino was arrested July 20. Since then, 10 cats and 17 dogs from the case have been adopted, while five microchipped cats have been reunited with their owners. "I think she thought she was doing a good thing. She thought she was rescuing cats from the outdoors and unfortunately, she was way in over her head, couldn't care for it and ended up in a terrible situation," Fisher said. The shelter’s workload has continued to grow. Following the initial case, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reportedly received an influx of requests for animal welfare checks. Last week, the humane society took in 26 cats from another situation and five dogs from a separate case. We expect more animals in the coming weeks due to the calls that have come in requesting animal welfare checks and the initial information we are receiving from Animal Services, which is following up on these calls, Humane Society Director of Operations Lori Tucker said. Many calls have been cleared, but there are cases that are requiring further follow-up. The organization said monetary donations are its greatest immediate need because of the continuing costs of medical care, food and housing while the animals await placement. Donations may be made through the shelter’s emergency medical fund. The humane society is also urging residents to adopt or foster animals already in its care. Officials said the influx doubled the shelter’s animal population even as normal admissions and services continued. Adopting or fostering a dog, cat, rabbit or guinea pig would free space for rescued animals still receiving treatment and preparing for adoption. See also: Road rage ends in violent 4-vehicle crash on U.S. Lucie man arrested We are still in need of people to adopt working cats, that is, cats that are suitable for safe outdoor living, Tucker said. We also are in desperate need of adopters and rescue groups willing to help take some of our animals. The shelter is offering a Name Your Price adoption special until further notice. Short- and long-term foster opportunities are also available. Information about adoptable animals is available at hstc1.org/Adopt , and foster information is available at hstc1.org/foster . Prospective adopters may call 772-223-8822 . Foster inquiries may be sent to catfoster@hstc1.org or dogfoster@hstc1.org , or made by calling 772-600-3220 . The Humane Society will also offer public microchipping services from 10 a.m. Registration is available at hstc1.org/Clinic . The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is a private, locally operated nonprofit at 4100 SW Leighton Farm Ave. The no-kill animal welfare organization has served the Martin County area since 1955 and relies on donations to support its programs and services.

After a unanimous vote, the redevelopment of the old Sears space at Gardens Mall is moving forward, with a second vote expected in September.WATCH: Gardens Mall shoppers hear about the possible changesA new Dick's House of Sports and outdoor athletic field are one step closer to replacing the old Sears at the Palm Beach Gardens Mall, following a unanimous vote by local officials.The redevelopment has been years in the making, with plans dating back to 2011. Progress stalled multiple times along the way, including in 2017 when controversy over whether the retailer would sell guns brought negotiations to a halt. Dick's Sporting Goods has since stopped selling guns in its stores, clearing a major point of contention and helping move the project forward.Dick's House of Sports is a larger, experience-focused concept that goes beyond traditional retail. The location would feature rock-climbing walls, HitTrax batting cages, VR sports, and more, alongside an outdoor field for community events, recreational leagues, camps, and other programming. The development would also bring more retail space to the mall.Shoppers in Palm Beach Gardens said the project sounds like an exciting addition to one of the most popular shopping destinations in the city.Suzanne Schoen said:"It's a welcome change."John Schoen said:"I think that's an interesting concept."Amy Smith said:"I think it's a good idea. I mean, I want to try start playing pickleball. That'd probably be a good way to try it."Susan Sands said:"It's convenient, and then it's one-stop shopping. You roam the mall, and it sounds wonderful. So when will they begin it?"The project still requires a second vote in September before receiving final approval. But that vote seems like all but a formality at this point.

As the August election approaches, tensions are rising between the two political camps as incumbent Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steve Giordano in the race for mayor. So far, tensions have escalated beyond the polls, with campaign signs being removed or moved. The incidents prompted the Port St. Lucie Police Department to launch investigations into two separate cases involving campaign signs, one of which led to a confrontation. The first incident occurred Wednesday, Aug. 5, near the intersection of Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thanksgiving Avenue. PSLPD said one of its sergeants noticed mayoral candidate Steve Giordano and an unidentified woman near political campaign signs. An investigation was launched after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard. Investigators reviewed surveillance footage that showed Giordano and the woman approaching campaign signs displayed in the yard. PSLPD said the video then showed the woman removing a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before another sign was placed in the yard. PSLPD said officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement and authorization of the campaign signs. The August 7th Incident During the overnight hours Friday, Aug. 7, Giordano told CBS12 News that he and his campaign manager were putting up signs near Southwest Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thornhill Drive. Giordano said he saw a man remove a sign from the ground and throw it. Giordano then grabbed his cellphone and began recording the encounter. The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant with the Port St. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Martin. The two can be heard shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission. See also: South Florida Wendy's worker's lunch break sparks viral friendship PSLPD said investigators learned that one homeowner had given permission for one campaign sign to be placed on the property, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, told members of the opposing campaign they could also place a sign there. Investigators said the language barrier contributed to the confrontation over the campaign signs and whether the previously placed sign could be moved or removed. PSLPD said investigators are reviewing the video. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged. Lucie Police Department acknowledges that Aaron Martin is employed by the department. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process. As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy," PSLPD said in a news release. Following the incident, Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement: My campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of my campaign signs at different locations over several days. Signs were taken down without permission and replaced with Mr. In response, my husband simply restored the signs that had been removed. At no time were my opponent's signs stolen or damaged, one small sign was temporarily moved and put back in the ground. Lucie Police Department is investigating reports related to political campaign signs that occurred this week. We fully support a thorough, impartial review of the facts. I remain focused on the issues that matter to the city and will continue running a positive, transparent campaign. According to police, officers responded to the reported incidents, documented the scenes, collected available evidence and began interviewing those involved. Detectives are reviewing physical evidence, speaking with witnesses and verifying statements provided to investigators. The investigations remain active. Police said all available facts and evidence will be reviewed before any determination is made. Lucie Police Department said it remains committed to conducting a fair, impartial and fact-based investigation.

The location and aerial maps of the 33.23-acre parcel that G.L. Homes wants to rezone in order to build a 135,000-square-foot indoor and outdoor recreation area known as the Riverland-West Sports Recreation complex. Because so many residents both emailed the city and spoke out in protest during the July 27 quasi-judicial rezoning hearing, the City Council voted unanimously that day to table the request until Aug. 24 to give the applicant time to hold a neighborhood meeting. LUCIE – City Council members found themselves defending their actions to frustrated Tradition-area residents July 27, prompting them to table a quasi-judicial rezoning request from the developer of the Riverland/Kennedy Development of Regional Impact. The delay will give the developer’s representatives time to meet with area homeowners and address their concerns. Planner Francis Forman introduced the controversial agenda item that evening to a packed Chambers. “The item before you is the Riverland-West Sports Recreation Master Planned Unit Development rezoning,” he said. “The applicant is Azlina Goldstein with Riverland/Kennedy II LLC. This site is located south of Southwest Discovery Way and east of Southwest Sundance Vista Boulevard. The request is to rezone approximately 33.23 acres from St. Lucie County Agricultural to Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD.” Forman proceeded to provide more details on the GL Homes request to develop the site in a manner that many Riverland homeowners claim is different than what was planned when they purchased their properties years ago. “This site is designated Neighborhood Village Commercial, which allows a mixture of residential and non-residential uses such as commercial and offices, personal and household services, institutional, public facilities, parks, playgrounds and similar services,” he explained. “Any Neighborhood Village Commercial area must contain at least two of those uses. Currently the Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD is proposing to provide about 135,000 square feet of indoor recreation with some commercial as well as some outdoor RV/boat storage areas.” Because the city had received numerous emails from nearby residents in opposition, Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo immediately asked City Attorney Richard Berrios to describe the formalities of the quasi-judicial process. “This is a rezoning, which is limited to what Mr. Forman presented,” Berrios said. “Not part of it are things like landscaping, indoor and outdoor features and specifics of what it will ultimately be. Those things are better suited for the site-plan process. As far as the process here, the legislators take off their legislative hats and put on their judge robes, and it’s limited to taking sworn testimony and the facts presented and applying them to a specific problem.” Councilman Anthony Bonna, however, believed more information was needed for the area residents. “Can you go into more detail about what evidence is allowed to be weighed [and] is a rezoning discretionary?” he asked. While Berrios admitted the Council’s hands were tied as far as any pre-existing DRI entitlements, he deferred Councilman Bonna’s question to Planning Zoning Director Mary Savage-Dunham. The latter emphasized the legal framework of controlling agreements and city codes. A pre-existing Development of Regional Impact (DRI) is a large-scale project approved under older Florida growth laws that retains vested development rights despite later changes to local plans or the elimination of the state’s formal DRI program. “The DRI document talks about what’s going to be built there,” Savage-Dunam said. “We also have the comprehensive plan. As staff testified, this rezoning was found to be consistent with the comprehensive plan, [which] follows the DRI. Those are the road maps that guide development in that section of the city. So, you would be looking at the totality of what the applicant submitted showing their intended uses there and how that aligns with the comp plan and the DRI.” Vice-Mayor Caraballo then chimed back in with her own perspective. “If you’re confused, I understand,” she said. “It’s not our process – it’s the way it’s legally required by the state. It’s definitely not the simplest thing for anybody to understand.” After the applicant’s contracted Land Use Attorney Goldstein provided her own presentation, 10 nearby homeowners aired their complaints, beginning with Southwest River Rock Road resident Jim Riordan. “My property is located at the southern end of the proposed Riverland-West Sports Recreation Center,” he said. “I spoke at the July 7 Planning Board meeting, and the chairman encouraged me to meet with Ms. At that time, I gave her our primary concerns with the project. On Friday, she did contact me, but none of those concerns were addressed. What she did say was exactly what she said right now: This is not the time – the time is later – but we feel this is the time before we move forward.” Riordan pointed out that GL Homes had “1,300 other acres where they could build this complex.” “GL has already sold parcels in the new section advertising the fitness center,” he continued. “So, I guess it’s a done deal based on this picture and what they’re advertising. We purchased our property, as well as every citizen here, from The Grove with the understanding that this parcel will be a city park. Now they’re basically trying to make this something different.” Both Harriet Gallas and her husband Lawrence agreed. “We chose to move here for quality of life,” the former said. “When we bought our house, we were told there was going to be a park over the berm next to us. They’re [now] talking 72 pickleball courts, bocci courts, tennis courts, a dog park and RV park, and that’s going to destroy my quality of life. Noise pollution’s a real thing: It causes stress, and pickleball is loud, stabbing and sharp. I respectfully beg you to not pass this rezoning.” The other residents echoed similar fears, resulting in more staff explanations and Council debate until Mayor Shannon Martin asked Goldstein a pivotal question. “Has their been a public meeting with the neighbors with regard to this issue?” she asked. Riordan regarding the issue of the buffer,” Goldstein responded. That response gave Mayor Martin the impetus she needed. “Being that there are so many concerns from the residents, is GL willing to have a meeting with the residents in order to address the issues?” she prodded. Goldstein, however, resisted the delay at first. “This is a straight-forward rezoning,” she insisted. “We don’t have all those details yet for the site plan because that’s not this process. When we’re ready to get there and we have those details, we’d be more than happy to meet with everybody to discuss what’s planned.” That response brought a loud uproar of protest from the audience and a plea from the vice-mayor. “I would really appreciate very much if you’d be willing to just table this,” Caraballo said. “I’m sorry to slow it down, but even this part of the process I don’t think they comprehend.” The City Council then voted unanimously to table the request until the Aug. Dana Trabulsy (R-Fort Pierce) FORT PIERCE–State Rep. Dana Trabulsy (R-Fort Pierce) says Fort Pierce needs the tax base generated by new development, but not at the size of a massive, mixed-use project proposed for Causeway Cove on Seaway Drive. Trabulsy told the Fort Pierce City Commission this week that the hotel, condominium, retail and dining development spread over five proposed high-rise buildings is fraught with map errors, environmental and traffic questions and may conflict with the city’s comprehensive land use plan. According to Trabulsy, 62 percent of local residents disapprove of the Causeway Cove plan in its current form. Causeway Cove includes a complex of five buildings, ranging from 14-17 stories tall. The largest proposes 180 condos, a 204-room hotel, a convention center, bar/restaurant, retail and club space. A second building proposes 365 residential condos, ranging from studios, 1- and 2-bedrooms, while a third building shows 40 condos ranging from 1- to 3-bedrooms and a 203-room hotel. Two other buildings each feature 164 condominium units, and nearly 14,000 square feet of retail space. Causeway Cove is set on an $8 million land parcel at 601 Seaway Dr., currently occupied by a 50-year-old, 1,500-square-foot building with adjacent deck and dock. FLASH General Partners Inc., West Palm Beach. Both Trabulsy and city commissioners also questioned so-called “affordable housing” factors – part of Florida’s Live Local Act – that limit local officials’ say over how the plan is developed if it guarantees that 40 percent of the housing units will qualify as “affordable” for the next 30 years. This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience.WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy.I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader."It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good.The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America."And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members.But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride.After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next.But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication.As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades.As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

Early voting for Florida's August primary begins Aug. 8 in Palm Beach County and across the Treasure Coast, with dates and hours varying by location. In Palm Beach County, early voting runs through Aug. Voters can cast their ballots at any of the 28 designated early voting sites in the county from 7 a.m. This differs from Election Day, when voters must go to their assigned polling place. Wendy Sartory Link, Palm Beach County supervisor of elections, shared advice for voters preparing for the primary. "Make sure they have a plan. The vote-by-mail deadline to request that we send you a ballot has already passed. If you need to come to our office to pick up a vote by mail ballot, you can do that," Link said. "And if you are waiting until Election Day, just make sure that you know where you're supposed to go." Voters should bring a current, valid photo ID with a signature. If the photo ID does not include a signature, a second form of identification may be required. Election officials recommend checking voter information and reviewing sample ballots before heading to the polls. The county's website also allows voters to check wait times and schedule optional early voting appointments. Early voting in Treasure Coast and Okeechobee counties runs from Aug. 15, with the following hours: Martin County: 8 a.m. Indian River County: 8 a.m. Okeechobee County: 8:30 a.m. Hours and locations vary, so voters should check with their county supervisor of elections before heading to the polls. Florida has closed primaries, meaning party registration determines which primary ballot voters receive. The deadline to change party affiliation has passed. However, all registered voters may still be eligible to vote in nonpartisan or universal-primary contests, depending on their location. Election Day is Tuesday, Aug. Lucie Police Department has released an update on 2 separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard.Although both incidents involve political campaign signs in the same area, police say they are being investigated as separate cases, with each evaluated independently based on their own facts, evidence, and applicable law.The first incident occurred on August 5, 2026, near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on August 7, 2026, near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. At this time, there is no indication that any campaign signs associated with this incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department."The fact that Mr. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process," the department said. "As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy."The department said that should the investigation identify any potential policy violations involving a department employee, the matter will be handled in accordance with established department procedures. Consistent with Florida law, department employees are afforded the rights and protections provided under the Florida Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. Any related administrative review will proceed following the completion of the ongoing criminal investigation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie Police Department is investigating the death of a 77-year-old man who was found in a pond, according to a press release from the PSLPD . PSLPD says that on Friday, around 1:18 p.m., officers were called to a residence on SW Mockingbird Drive in reference to a missing adult who was later identified as Michael Joseph Kramer, 77. The investigation revealed that Kramer was last seen by his wife inside of their residence at around 10:00 p.m. However, when Kramer’s wife woke up at approximately 7:00 a.m. on Friday, Kramer was nowhere to be found despite all of his personal belongings remaining in the residence. See also: Delray Beach body shop owner accused of insurance fraud stemming from 2024 claims After an extensive search of the area, PSLPD says that they located an unresponsive man that matched Kramer’s description in a pond directly across the street from the residence at around 2:00 p.m. The PSLPD Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water, and he was pronounced deceased. A Martin County community is restoring a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroyed.Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club spent two years cultivating 6,000 mangroves in an on-site nursery. Now, they are planting them in the waterway to bring the island back to life.WATCH BELOW:"The mangroves were so thick and lush and we've watched them deteriorate and in some areas the island is dead now," Lisa Standing, a resident at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club, said.Standing rallied her neighbors to take action. The community built 10 planter pools to grow red and white mangroves."We were able to collect just white and red seeds from our mangrove island," Standing said.The effort required extensive research and permitting before a single plant could go into the water. They say it was an elaborate operation that turned into a labor of love"We tried to match the habitat of all of our plants to the river habitat," Standing said. "We were here almost every day in the nursery and we inspected the plants, watered them if needed, monitored their health, matched salinity to the river."With the nursery phase complete, residents brought in Keith Rossin, CEO of Mang Consulting Services, to do the planting."These are dredge filled little management areas and so they take that dredge fill and they actually bring it up to the right level for the elevation for the mangroves and that allows for us to plant these mangroves in here so this very unique way I've never actually seen this done before of how we can actually create mangrove habitat," Rossin said.What are now thousands of small trees are expected to grow into the foundation of a new ecosystem."We will be able to go down to the mangrove island and enjoy beautiful lush island," Standing said. "It's just wonderful."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. LUCIE – The Daytona Tortugas scored 11 unanswered runs over the final three innings on Thursday to pull away for a 17-3 win over the St. Lucie Mets at Clover Park. The Mets hit three doubles in the fifth inning, including back-to-back RBI doubles by John Smith III and Julio Zayas to cut the Daytona lead to 6-3. But the Tortugas took advantage of six walks issued by Mets relievers Jean Brito and Luis Sotillo in the seventh inning. They scored six runs in the frame to go up 12-3 and break the game open. The Mets relied the DH Zayas to finish the game on the mound for the final two innings. The Tortugas scored five runs off Zayas in the eighth inning to stretch the lead to 17-3, but Zayas pitched a scoreless ninth. He induced a double play in the inning. The Mets scored first in the game on a RBI single by Reed Stallman in the second inning. Then with the bases loaded and one out, Tortugas started Mason Morris started a 1-2-3 double play off the broken bat of Kooper Schulte to escape further damage. The Tortugas used that momentum in the top of the third. They scored five runs on five hits off Mets starter Jose Lopez to go up 5-1. Bernard Moon hit a two-run double in the inning which was his FSL-leading 28th double. Lopez pitched well outside of the third inning. Overall he pitched 5.1 innings and gave up six runs on seven hits. He walked one and struck out six. It was the longest outing by a Mets pitcher since the first game of the second half on June 19th. Elian Peña went 2 for 5 with a double. It was the third straight two-hit game for Peña. Smith III was 2 for 4 with a double and RBI. He allowed three runs over 5.0 innings. The Mets (14-23, 47-56) and Tortugas (24-13, 45-58) continue their series at Clover Park on Friday. All veterans and active duty military receive free admission courtesy of LYNQ Real Estate. The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce is facing another delay.WATCH BELOW: 'It's taking so long,' Funky Cuda owner Jon Nolli tells WPTV's St. Lucie County reporter Tyler HatfieldLive Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners they’re short said they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project — and city commissioners are divided on what to do next.Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told commissioners the $15 million shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs.“We have seen construction costs continue to balloon, “ said CEO Paul Bertozzi. “We've had those challenges across multiple industries but that is a portion of the cause of the delta that is being created."City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant.Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied."Unfortunately, the city does not have $15 million. Nor would I advocate the city investing $15 million into a private enterprise,” said Broderick.Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun."We're already in the process of reaching out to participating parties,” said Bertozzi. "We're looking at friends and families and investment and private equity verses institutional investors."But commissioners are debating about the city reclaiming the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming."Clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money,” said Broderick.He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for."What are we going to lose by 180 days? That's the question I would ask,” said Broderick. “What are we going to lose? It's just time."Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait."I think it's time to as they say, cut bait and move on," he said.Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished."It's been taking some time,” said Nolli.Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area. He said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing — but the delays are wearing on him."I've got a couple deposits on the commercial side. I was looking to a beer garden, and a deli, and I mean it's taking so long that I don't even know the trends have changed,” said NolliWPTV reached out to Live Oak Development and still working on a response. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to open its doors on Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county’s fastest-growing communities. Crews have worked throughout the summer to prepare the campus for its first group of students. Principal Latanya Greene said the school’s motto, "Traditions begin here," reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. Your neighborhood: Local coverage from WPBF 25 News "Throughout this process, we have talked a lot about traditions and accomplishments and the achievements that we want to build and grow at this school. Hence, our motto for the school year is that tradition leads K through eight. Traditions begin here," Greene said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Greene emphasized that months of planning have gone into creating an environment where students can grow academically and socially. "It's about being in an environment that you can grow and continue with great levels. But bigger than that, you begin to set the tone of creating those strong academics that move with you from year to year to year. You develop friendships," Greene said. The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school’s convenient location. "We are busting at the seams in the south and the west. And this school is so conveniently located to families that we're going to have a tremendous number of students that are walking or even other parents dropping the kids off in a golf cart," said John R. Prince, superintendent of St. Lucie County Public Schools. As the first day approaches, Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school’s inaugural year. "The academics component is going to be there, but it is going to be walking through this inaugural year and looking back on all the traditions that we have created as a team, as a family, and the strength of our culture, and how we just grow throughout the first year will be beyond the definition of success for us," Greene said. Tradition Lakes K-8 will officially open on August 10, marking the beginning of a new chapter for students and families in the Tradition area.

Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day. At approximately 1:18 p.m. today, officers responded to a residence on the 1400 block of SW Mockingbird Drive regarding a missing adult. Kramer was last seen by his wife inside their home at approximately 10 p.m. the following morning, Kramer was no longer inside the residence. Kramer’s personal belongings, including his shoes, wallet, and cellphone, were still inside the home. His wife searched for him and contacted local hospitals before reporting him missing to law enforcement at approximately 1:18 p.m. Officers began searching the neighborhood and, during the canvass, located an unresponsive person in a pond directly across the street from Kramer’s residence at approximately 2 p.m. The individual and clothing matched Kramer’s description. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water near the shoreline of the pond, where he was confirmed deceased. The circumstances surrounding Kramer’s death remain under investigation. Police said there are no known indications of foul play at this preliminary stage of the investigation. Lucie Police Department has released an update on 2 separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard.Although both incidents involve political campaign signs in the same area, police say they are being investigated as separate cases, with each evaluated independently based on their own facts, evidence, and applicable law.The first incident occurred on August 5, 2026, near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on August 7, 2026, near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. At this time, there is no indication that any campaign signs associated with this incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department."The fact that Mr. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process," the department said. "As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy."The department said that should the investigation identify any potential policy violations involving a department employee, the matter will be handled in accordance with established department procedures. Consistent with Florida law, department employees are afforded the rights and protections provided under the Florida Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. Any related administrative review will proceed following the completion of the ongoing criminal investigation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

A Martin County community is restoring a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroyed.Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club spent two years cultivating 6,000 mangroves in an on-site nursery. Now, they are planting them in the waterway to bring the island back to life.WATCH BELOW:"The mangroves were so thick and lush and we've watched them deteriorate and in some areas the island is dead now," Lisa Standing, a resident at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club, said.Standing rallied her neighbors to take action. Thomas Todd, and his wife, have a neighbor they're worried about — not because of anything they can see, but because of what they can hear and smell. WATCH BELOW: 'She really has legally walled us off from investigating,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek tells Chief Investigative Reporter Jamie Ostroff The couple sent video of dogs barking from behind a fence next door at their Martin County home. Todd said he believes there are between 15 and 20 dogs on the property. I visited the Todds' home on a calm, July afternoon. But when the wind picks up, Todd said the smell coming from next door is overwhelming. "It's a combination of garbage and animal feces and urine," Todd said. "I mean, I don't know how somebody could live in that." Todd first raised his concerns at a WPTV Let's Hear It event in Jensen Beach in May. When asked what a solution would look like, his answer was simple: "Save those dogs. Get them out of there." Public records obtained by WPTV show Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies have visited the home at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about the dogs and their owner. The owner is not being named because she has never been charged with a crime. One incident report from 2020 describes accounts of as many as 25 dogs inside the home. On multiple occasions, authorities noted feces on the floor and furniture. Records show the owner did clean up after initial visits and told animal control she had re-homed some of the dogs, but she eventually stopped allowing law enforcement inside. Multiple reports note that deputies were not allowed to see the dogs when they visited the home. A code enforcement officer took photos through the glass front door in 2023, noting "a dog with feces on it." After that visit, the owner put up a fence. Todd said she also stopped letting the dogs outside, but he can still hear them barking in the house. For Todd, what's out of sight is not out of mind — let alone out of sound or smell. And there's nothing anybody can do or will do," Todd said. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the fence has created a legal barrier to further investigation. "You can't even see into the property anymore," Budensiek said. "So, she really has legally walled us off from investigating exactly what's going on inside." When asked whether deputies have a lawful way to enter the property and look for themselves, Budensiek said they do not — unless there is visible evidence of mistreatment. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that -- you know -- dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of — we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there," Budensiek said. Florida statutes require that confined animals be provided "a sufficient quantity of good and wholesome food and water." Budensiek said that standard appears to be met based on what deputies can observe. "We saw recently — as recently as last week — that there's food boxes that are out there, empty food boxes, so we know the animals from the outside look to be being taken care of," Budensiek said. I attempted to reach the owner by phone and left three voicemails. In the most recent incident report — from July 2025 — the owner told deputies she had 7 dogs, then "redacted and said that she only had five dogs," according to the report. Todd said he does not believe that statement. "Seems like from everything I've been told, the law's on her side," Todd said. Since I visited the Todds last month, they say they continue to hear the dogs and have continued to follow up with the sheriff's office. They have also seen animal control in front of the owner's house a few times since this story began — but deputies have not gone in. Budensiek acknowledged the neighbors' frustration but said there is little more his office can do. "I know the neighbors are worried and, and we'll still respond out there for complaints. But again, it's not illegal to be a bad neighbor," Budensiek said. We want to be your voice and help you find solutions. Jacob Craig will perform MacDowell s Piano Concerto No. 2 with the Space Coast Symphony Orchestra during Landscapes Legends. For tickets,visit SpaceCoastSymphony.org or call toll-free (855) 252-7276. VERO BEACH – The Space Coast Symphony Orchestra explores magic and myth during Landscapes Legends on Sunday, Aug. The concert at the Community Church of Vero Beach, 1901 23rd Street, opens with Dukas’ The Sorcerer’s Apprentice, famously depicted in Disney’s Fantasia. Guest conducted by Brevard music educator Patrick Phillips, the vivid, 11-minute orchestral tone poem musically narrates a tale of magic gone wrong. The world premiere performance of Kenneth Fuchs’ Cloud Slant shifts the focus inward, capturing light, motion and atmosphere. A Fuchs album recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for Naxos won the 2018 GRAMMY Award for Best Classical Compendium. Landscapes Legends continues when Vero Beach music and arts leader, Dr. Jacob Craig joins the orchestra for Edward MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2, a deeply romantic and expressive work in three-movements. Composed in 1885, the work has the distinction of being the first major piano concerto written by an American. Renowned pianist, Van Cliburn chose MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2 at age 18 for his professional orchestral debut. Landscapes Legends concludes with Pines of Rome, the world famous 1924 orchestral tone poem by Italian composer, Ottorino Respighi. Lasting about 22 minutes, it dramatically depicts four different locations around Rome framed by iconic pine trees. Ancient streets, distant echoes, and the sound of a nightingale are sculpted into one of the greatest works of the orchestral repertoire. $35 tickets for Landscapes Legends are available through the orchestra website at www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org or at Marine Bank Trust branches. Tickets at the door are $40. Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. For more information about Landscapes Legends, call 855-252-7276 or visit www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org . Collins, Conductor and Artistic Director for the Space Coast Symphony Orchestra, describes what makes the Landscapes Legends concert special. “A good orchestral concert can make the invisible feel real,” said Collins. “The works on this program aren’t just pretty melodies with dramatic flourishes – they create places, characters, atmospheres, and emotional landscapes for a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience.” Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. For more information about the Space Coast Symphony s 2026-27 season or the Symphony for Everyone discounted ticket program, visit SpaceCoastSymphony.org or call (855) 252-7276.
