The developer behind Fort Pierce's long-stalled King's Landing project told city commissioners this week it's roughly $15 million short of the money needed to complete the development's hotel, and is asking for another 180 days to find it. Live Oak requested the extension in a July 24 email to city staff, and Live Oak CEO Paul Bertozzi answered commissioners' questions on the request during Monday's city commission meeting, saying the shortfall stems largely from rising construction costs since the project's budget was first set. Commissioners didn't vote on the request Monday, but agreed to hold a special meeting September 14 to decide whether to grant the extension or take other action on the project. As we've seen construction costs continue to bloom. We've had those challenges, said Bertozzi. King's Landing is planned for the site of the former H.D. King Power Plant on the Fort Pierce waterfront, and is set to include a hotel, condominiums, restaurants, retail space and public waterfront access. The project has changed hands multiple times since the city first selected Audubon Development to build it in 2019, most recently passing to Live Oak in 2025. City officials say the development agreement has already been amended three times to adjust deadlines and financing terms, and a fourth amendment is now under discussion. City staff and Bertozzi say the financing gap grew as construction and hotel financing costs increased. Commissioners were told hotel financing typically requires a 65-35 split between bank loans and investor equity, and that rising interest and construction costs widened the amount Live Oak needs to raise privately as the project's overall budget increased. Bertozzi told commissioners he's already in talks with potential investors and expects at least one to be part of the September presentation. Not every commissioner is on board with waiting. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said the city's own financial exposure has already grown, with the property's value as a city incentive rising from about $2.5 million to $8.5 million over time, and said he's not willing to support further delay. "There are too many issues for too many years," he said. "At the end of the day, I'm just going to share with you I'm not going to support anything going forward, with this particular situation. See also: Police release photo of toy kitchen involved in Boynton toddler's death; family IDs girl Commissioner Michael Broderick took the opposite view, saying that terminating the agreement and reclaiming the property could mean years of litigation and cost the city hundreds of thousands of dollars, on top of the time needed to find a new developer and restart construction. The city attorney confirmed Monday that Live Oak is currently in breach of its development agreement over missed deadlines. I'm suggesting let's give this a bit of a breather. Let them go do their work and come back and keep us posted on your progress, said Broderick While the funding gap continues for the hotel portion of King's Landing, homes are currently under construction next door with a different developer. Brooke Harris, a realtor selling the luxury townhomes, says she's confident Live Oak will find the money. It's going to continue to go through. That's Live Oak Contracting that's spearheading that. They are very well versed with what they do, and they always see it through. So I have a lot of confidence with the entire project continuing forward, said Harris. Commissioners are set to revisit the issue at the September 14 special meeting, followed by a Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency board meeting the next day, since both bodies must approve any changes to the three-party development agreement. Until then, the fate of the $15 million gap remains unresolved.

With the 2026-27 school year just days away, residents of a Royal Palm Beach community are sounding the alarm over a traffic plan they say is endangering children near H.L. Johnson Elementary School. However, a video message sent to parents by the school during the second week of the 2025 school year instructed drivers to instead "go around and then you’re going to make a U-turn in front of Bella Sera."Brianna Steel, a lifelong Royal Palm Beach resident who has lived in the Bella Sera community for nearly a decade, says the directive simply moved the traffic bottleneck and created a new set of hazards.The daily queue of cars waiting to make the U-turn now blocks the entrance and exit to her community, causing significant backups. More than 100 women's college basketball players have teamed up to form a union for college athletes as part of their growing push to collectively bargain with their schools, an organizing group announced Friday.The United College Athletes Association said as part of the push, members of the Oregon State women's team filed a petition with state regulators, marking a formal effort to seek collective bargaining rights under state law.RELATED STORY | NCAA transfer portal rules, NIL could change under new bipartisan Senate billThe announcement comes two years after a group of women's basketball players co-signed letters to Southeastern and Big Ten Conference leaders in 2024, requesting a formal collaboration process on issues affecting college athletics.Since those efforts were denied, more than 100 female athletes have signed union authorization cards with the UCAA, agreeing to representation in collective bargaining.The announcement comes a few days after the College Football Players Association revealed that Stanford has become the first football team to organize a player-led chapter — another effort by college athletes to unionize.The UCAA says its mission is to represent and protect athletes through collective bargaining, ensuring that college sports are safe, fair, sustainable and that athletes have a say in decision-making."As interim president of the UCAA, I'm proud to help lead a movement that gives college athletes a real voice in the decisions that shape our lives and careers," University of Maryland basketball player Oluchi Okananwa said in a statement.RELATED STORY | NCAA accuses DraftKings of trademark infringement in March Madness marketingNCAA leaders have long opposed the idea of players becoming employees of their schools, though the idea isn't universally opposed by college leaders. Tennessee athletic director Danny White has been among those who have said collective bargaining is the only real solution to the problems that confront schools that are now paying millions to their players.Attempts to create unions for college athletes at Dartmouth and Southern California stalled in 2024 due to the changing landscape in college sports and the then-incoming Trump administration's new National Labor Relations Board, which wasn't expected to approve the moves.

The debate over constructing massive artificial intelligence data centers is intensifying across South Florida ahead of the August primary elections, as proposals like Project Tango in Palm Beach County draw both interest and opposition. Multiple municipalities in the region are exploring or enacting moratoriums on data center construction. While Florida currently has no hyperscale AI centers, residents living near large-scale data centers in other parts of the country report a constant, industrial hum from cooling fans that operate 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Mehran Basiratmand, the Director of Innovations and Programs at Florida Atlantic University and former policy board chairperson for the state's largest data center, said the noise level, the water consumption and electricity impact to surrounding neighborhoods are creating concerns. Basiratmand said these concerns have a legitimate basis, noting the demand is growing and AI is front and center, but officials need to also be equally responsible for the limited resources that are currently available. Several cities and counties in the region are either discussing or have already passed temporary bans, or moratoriums, on the approval of new data centers. These measures are designed to give officials time to study the potential impacts and develop zoning and regulatory frameworks that could mitigate issues like noise and resource consumption before developers break ground. John Dial John ‘Kaz’ Kazanjian Sarah Heard The Hometown News sent the same list of questions below to each qualified candidate in the August 18 Primary Election for the District 4 Martin County Commission Seat. Question 1: What do you view as the most serious issue facing Martin County and how would you propose addressing that if elected? Question 2: There will be a referendum this year on raising the Homestead exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income significantly to municipalities. If you are elected and that passes, what areas of the county budget would you suggest trimming or cutting out altogether if need-be? Question 3: Where do you stand on Martin County’s current plan to fund the Brightline train station and potentially relocating that to the county fairgrounds site? Question 4: Do you think the County Commission should address the lack of affordable housing, and if so, in what way? Question 5: On June 23, the County Commission majority voted to approve the Business Development Board’s annual $450,000 funding as part of the Consent Agenda. District 1 Commissioner Eileen Vargas cast the lone opposing vote, insisting the BDB become self-sufficient like the Economic Development Council of Martin County and potentially merge with that entity. If elected, would you support the BDB’s current funding or side with Commissioner Vargas? Question 6: The possibility of data center applications, particularly in the Indiantown area, have been very divisive. Have you studied this issue yourself, and if so, how do you think it should be addressed if you’re elected? Question 7: If elected, how would you work to improve the quality of life for Martin County voters? The most serious issue facing our county right now is over-development, and that problem has only gotten worse with Senate Bill 180, as well as SB102 and the new mandates coming from Tallahassee. These state actions take power away from local voters and leaders and make it harder for Martin County residents to control the kind of growth in their own communities. If I am elected, I will fight to take that authority back. I will go to Tallahassee as often as necessary to represent local control and push to restore the county’s ability to make decisions for itself. Without a repeal or major reform of this law, we will remain trapped in a cycle of over-development no matter what the people of Martin County want. In my view, we should have been more vocal, more organized, and more aggressive in standing up against these state changes before they were passed. We cannot afford to make that mistake again. The consequences for local government budgets are significant, and we must be prepared to act responsibly if it is approved. Like the families and taxpayers we serve, government must learn to live within its means. Over the past several years, citizens have been forced to make tough choices as housing costs, rent, groceries, and electric bills have continued to rise. If this measure passes, I will work to protect essential services first – fire protection, law enforcement, waste management and education – while carefully reviewing non-essential programs and discretionary spending for reductions. We must make sure taxpayer dollars are directed to priorities that truly serve the public. I also believe new development should pay its fair share and not shift additional burdens onto existing taxpayers. In addition, we should explore ways to turn costly county assets – Sailfish Splash, the golf course and the café on the beach – into revenue-producing opportunities. Facilities such as these could potentially be leased to private operators, allowing the county to reduce losses and create income. Every budget should be scrutinized, including the discretionary spending available to the five commissioners. I support a “use it or lose it” policy so that unused funds are returned to the general fund and put toward real needs in the districts. We should closely evaluate every dollar going to 501(c)(3) organizations to ensure there is a measurable return for the community, and we should look for better public-private partnerships where appropriate. I do not support using taxpayer money to fund a private company, especially one that is not U.S.-owned, carries roughly $2 billion in debt and is reportedly losing more than $220 million a year. That said, I would be open to a train station or stop in our county if a private rail company or a qualified buyer emerging from bankruptcy proceedings wanted to invest their own capital here. I would also consider a fair market land-lease for a smaller-scale facility at the fairgrounds or another appropriate location, provided the arrangement protects the public interest. If the company fails or goes out of business, the property should immediately revert to the county, and taxpayers should face zero financial risk. Yes, I do support it, either with non-profits such as Love And Hope In Action or if a developer is seeking to market a project as affordable housing or workforce housing. They should be required to deliver real affordability for the community. That means negotiating firm standards so that a defined percentage of the total units must be reserved at an affordable or workforce price-point. Permits should be made contingent on compliance with those terms. Affordable housing should serve working families, young people, teachers, first responders, and seniors. This is about fairness, accountability, and making sure that growth actually helps the people who live and work here. I support the Business Development Board in its current role. It plays an important part in helping Martin County grow by attracting quality jobs, strengthening our economic base and recruiting the kind of industries that support long-term prosperity. At the same time, if we are forced to make spending cuts, every use of taxpayer dollars must be examined carefully. No public funding should be automatic or off limits. That said, the BDB has a real value to our county. It helps position Martin County to compete for manufacturing opportunities, workforce recruitment, marine industry expansion, aeronautical jobs and other businesses that bring good-paying employment and responsible growth to our community. I am continuing to study this issue and will keep reviewing new information as it becomes available. If elected to the County Commission, I will give this matter my full attention and direct county staff resources toward gathering the facts before taking a position in support of or opposition to it. This is ultimately a decision for the Village of Indiantown, and whatever course they choose, the county should be prepared to assist and support them appropriately. At this time, I do not believe there is enough reliable information for me to make a final judgment. Protecting our natural resources must remain a top priority. I will work to improve water quality in both our fresh and saltwater systems and address the pollution sources that threaten them. I will also work to preserve agricultural lands, defend our development boundaries and review every available option to strengthen our comprehensive plan and restore appropriate limits on urban service expansion. At the same time, I will keep traffic concerns front and center, because growth must never outpace infrastructure. Within the laws and regulations I inherit, I will do everything possible to protect the character of Martin County and make sure our growth policies reflect the interests of current residents and not just future development pressure. Avoid allowing urban development to occur outside the Urban Services Boundary. The legislature is taking that decision-making out of the Board’s hands. Only essential services are allowed to be funded with ad valorem taxes, which means public safety – the Sheriff and Fire Rescue. All other public services are deemed non-essential. Even if funding only public safety, we would not be able to fund public safety by the third year. I am in favor of a train station here. At present the site is downtown. If the majority of residents overwhelmingly favors a fairgrounds location, I would consider it. We do through partnerships with the state and federal agencies, and we partner with Habitat for Humanity. We should continue to evaluate land trusts. I agree that the BDB is far too dependent on government funding. I don’t want to see data centers in unincorporated Martin County. They are not allowed uses on agricultural lands, so a comprehensive plan amendment would have to be approved to change the future land use. I would oppose such an amendment. My priorities have always been to clean up our water, stop over-development and keep our taxes low. Those remain my priorities. Housing affordability is a hot topic at WPTV Let's Hear It community events. At a recent Delray Beach Let's Hear It, we discovered a local solution that's making homeownership possible for low-to-moderate income families."Considering what we know about the economy and how expensive everything is, we'd entirely be homeless," David Obee said.Obee was eager to discuss with WPTV reporter Victor Jorges about what the Delray Beach Community Land Trust means to him and his brother. WATCH: About a decade ago, the brothers were struggling with rising rent when they heard about a community meeting at Pompey Park. That meeting changed their lives—they learned about the Delray Beach Community Land Trust, a nonprofit that helps low-to-moderate income families buy and rent homes at prices they can actually afford.After a year of paperwork, the Obees moved into a 3-bedroom, 2-bathroom house on 14th Avenue. To put that in perspective, they bought their home for around $142,000 in 2009. Today, according to trust executive director Evelyn Dobson, a comparable home would cost at least $450,000. The trust's homes typically cost around $300,000, but grants and other resources can bring that down to about $275,000. The secret to keeping costs low? The Delray Beach Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) usually buys the land and transfers it to the trust. This means homeowners only pay taxes on their house—not the expensive land underneath it.The savings make a huge difference in people's lives, Dobson explains."You can keep your healthcare up, save money for your kids college, go on vacations that you never went on before, you can make improvements to your home," Dobson said.The trust currently manages 146 units total with zero vacancies and five more projects in development. The CRA also offers grants up to $15,000 for exterior home improvements in certain neighborhoods, covering everything from painting and landscaping to driveway repairs and fence installation."We have eight (more) homes coming, hopefully within the next year," Dobson said.To learn more about the Land Trust, visit https://www.delraybeachlandtrust.org/

A Fort Myers man was arrested after an apparent road rage incident Saturday night on I-95 in Martin County that caused a family’s vehicle to crash into a barbed wire fence and left them hiding in the woods. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident involved a woman traveling in her own vehicle and her brother, his wife, and their young son following in another vehicle while on vacation from North Carolina. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "He tries to run the sister off the road, makes multiple attempts to run her off the road, brake checks her a couple of times. She starts panicking, calling her brother and saying there is something going on, I'm not sure what it is," Budensiek said. He said the brother caught up to the suspect, identified as Michael Spires, who then targeted his vehicle. At one point, Spires performed a pit maneuver, causing the family’s vehicle to spin off the road and crash into a barbed wire fence. Body camera footage shows the family emerging from the woods where they had been hiding after fleeing their vehicle. "The family at that point is extremely alarmed. They think he may be armed; they know he's not thinking clearly, so they jump out of the car, and they flee and they're hiding in the woods," Budensiek said. Spires drove to a nearby gas station and stayed there before speaking with investigators. "I got out of the car, and this blue car ran into me," Spires said. Spires, who is from Fort Myers, was taken into custody and appeared before a judge Monday afternoon. Officials said he had a dog in his vehicle at the time of the incident, which they later learned was stolen from his ex-boyfriend. The dog has since been returned. The sheriff said no one was injured during the incident. "The sister had driven about a few miles further up the road. She came back to the scene to tell her story. They're all safe, but only by the grace of God they are safe because this could have been so much worse," the sheriff said. Detectives said Spires was arrested and charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Palm Beach County’s growing culinary scene is earning international recognition after several local restaurants received honors from the Michelin Guide Florida, including one West Palm Beach restaurant making history.Emelina, a 16-seat tasting-menu restaurant in West Palm Beach’s Flamingo Park neighborhood, earned Palm Beach County’s only Michelin Star this year. According to Discover The Palm Beaches, Emelina also became the first Cuban restaurant in the world to receive a Michelin Star.Several other Palm Beach County restaurants received Michelin recognition through recommendations and Bib Gourmand honors, which recognize quality food at a good value.Michelin inspectors evaluate restaurants based on ingredient quality, flavor harmony, cooking techniques, consistency and the chef’s personality reflected in the cuisine.In Palm Beach County kitchens, chefs are chasing perfection and now, Michelin is noticing.Chef Pushkar Marathe said Michelin inspectors visit anonymously.“They never really shared that they’re going to be in your restaurant,” Marathe said.Marathe’s Palm Beach Gardens restaurants, Stage Kitchen & Bar and Ela Curry & Cocktails, both earned Michelin recommendations this year. His first reaction after learning about the recognition focused on improvement.“First thought was, how could we do better to get a star?” Marathe said.Marathe explained that Michelin recommendations place restaurants within reach of earning a future star.“When you’re recommended, you’ve been considered for the star, but there’s still some things you need to work on,” he said.Chef Tim Lipman’s Coolinary and the Parched Pig also received a Michelin recommendation.“You don’t necessarily strive for the award, but you strive for excellence,” Lipman said.Lipman said the recognition has helped local restaurants stand out in a competitive dining market.“Definitely needle in a haystack, right? There’s so many great restaurants out there,” he said.Aioli in West Palm Beach earned a Bib Gourmand designation for the second consecutive year. Owners Michael and Melanie Hackman said the recognition validates their commitment to scratch-made baking and consistency.“We are a scratch sourdough bakery,” Michael Hackman said. “It’s definitely why Michelin noticed us. We’re doing stuff the right way. We’re not cutting corners."Aioli’s sourdough takes more than three days to ferment. Hackman said even pop culture trends have influenced customer interest.“They said, ‘I’m only here because Taylor Swift makes sourdough. I want to learn how to make sourdough,’” Hackman said.Melanie Hackman said maintaining Michelin recognition can be even more challenging than earning it initially.“Earning it the first time was huge, but retaining it was even bigger for us,” she said.Restaurant owners also said the recognition is helping business during the slower summer months.“We are in the dead of summer and grateful that our restaurant is full every day,” Melanie Hackman said.Milton Segarra, president and CEO of Discover The Palm Beaches, said culinary tourism is becoming increasingly important to Palm Beach County’s economy.“Normally visitors come here for the beaches and the experiences we can offer. Now they are returning, because we became this powerhouse in the culinary scene,” Segarra said.Segarra said tourism investment tied to culinary marketing efforts has generated measurable returns for the county.“For every dollar that we invest on behalf of the county, we have a return of $3.55 in TDTs,” he said, referring to tourist development tax revenue.Why this matters now: Michelin recognition continues to reshape Palm Beach County’s reputation beyond beaches and luxury resorts. As more nationally recognized chefs and restaurants open across the region, local leaders see fine dining and culinary tourism becoming a growing economic driver for South Florida.From scratch bakeries to chef-driven tasting menus, Palm Beach County’s restaurant scene is earning attention from diners around the world — and local chefs say they are still striving for more.2026 Palm Beach County restaurants recognized by Michelin Guide FloridaMICHELIN Star • Emelina — West Palm BeachBib Gourmand • aioli — West Palm BeachMICHELIN Recommended• Stage Kitchen & Bar — Palm Beach Gardens• Ela Curry & Cocktails — Palm Beach Gardens• Coolinary and the Parched Pig — Palm Beach Gardens• būccan — Palm Beach• Moody Tongue Sushi — West Palm Beach• Nicholson Muir Distinguished Meats — Boynton Beach• The Butcher’s Club — Palm Beach GardensWhat do Michelin distinctions mean?• MICHELIN Star: Awarded for exceptional cooking and culinary excellence.• Bib Gourmand: Recognizes high-quality food at a good value.• Recommended: Honors restaurants serving standout meals with quality ingredients and strong execution.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former health official, has narrowly defeated moderate U.S. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, the Associated Press projects.The primary set national spending records, and the result was far closer than recent polls suggested, with Stevens and El-Sayed separated by only a few thousand votes. El-Sayed will now take on Republican Mike Rogers — President Donald Trump's pick — in a contest expected to decide control of the U.S. Senate.RELATED STORY | High-stakes Michigan Senate race could shape Congress in NovemberStevens conceded and offered her support to El-Sayed in a statement following the race."I want to congratulate Abdul El-Sayed on winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. "He is a doctor, a community health official, a Rhodes Scholar, and a dedicated Michigander. I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election."At a Wednesday press conference, El-Sayed struck a unifying tone toward Stevens and issued a direct challenge to Rogers."To my colleague and friend, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, we shared a great conversation this morning," El-Sayed said. "And I know that it was a bitter end to this very long primary, but I also know that Haley brings the best of herself to her work. She is one of the most committed public servants that you'll ever meet. She loves democracy and I love democracy. And whatever differences that we might have had in the primary, that pale in comparison to what unifies us — a recognition that so long as we want to keep our democracy, that democracy better be working for people and now all of us must come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the U.S. Senate."IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Midterm poll shows Democrats with advantage on generic midterm ballotEl-Sayed, who has campaigned on "Medicare for All," has the endorsement of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). However, the biggest task next for Democrats will be finding a way to bring all sides of the party together with just 90 days remaining until Election Day.El-Sayed's victory also represents a dramatic shift in the Democratic Party, as he lost Michigan's 2018 gubernatorial primary to current Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by over 20 percentage points. Stevens, the more moderate candidate, had the backing of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and millions of dollars in outside spending from lobbying groups like the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.Polling showed Stevens would have been the more competitive candidate against Rogers. Republicans are optimistic that scars from the primary will be too deep to heal in just a few weeks, presenting an opportunity for the GOP to flip the seat.

Lucie County Public Schools open for students on Aug. Lucie reporter Tyler Hatfield spoke to the school district about what families can expect this year. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: Families are already preparing for the first-day. Jovani Taylor said he has been getting his daughter, Jayla, ready for the new school year. "Purchase school supplies for books, clothing for school," Taylor said. Jayla said she is looking forward to fourth grade. "I'm very excited," Jayla said. Another parent, Julia Lopez, said her daughter will be starting VPK. Julia also noted the district's growth firsthand. "I see schools like almost every corner," Julia said. WPTV’s Tyler Hatfield sat down with Superintendent Jon Prince ahead of the first day of school. "We're ready to kick it off," Prince said. To keep up with growth, the district has been building new schools. Tradition Lakes K-8 is the newest, welcoming students in western St. "We know in the Tradition area there, that's an area of very, very expansive growth," Prince said. Despite that growth, Prince said enrollment is expected to be flat this year at 42,505 students. Over the past seven years, enrollment has increased by 7 percent, but Prince attributes this year's plateau to more families choosing homeschooling or private schools. "There are so many options for families right now that makes it a little bit uncertain where our enrollment is going to be when the first day starts," Prince said. Last year, the state projected an increase of 350 students, but the district instead lost 150, costing it around $14 million in state and federal funding. This year's tentative district budget is $1.07 billion, nearly $60 million less than last year's final budget. "We had a significant number of cuts. Most of them did not directly impact schools. Most of them were at the district level," Prince said. Prince said no staff were laid off but were instead moved to other positions. Even with the budget cuts, the district is adding new programs. Two new courses focused on artificial intelligence will be available to students this year at Legacy High School. "We need to provide an avenue based on future legislation as to what that's going to look like for students if they're interested in that field of work," Prince said.

Chris Dzadovsky Michael Broderick FORT PIERCE – The Fort Pierce City Commission decided Monday to give King’s Landing plans another look at a special meeting Sept. And while commissioners have agreed to give developers an additional 180 days to attempt to fill a $15 million funding gap, they have said that money won’t come from local taxpayers. Development partner Live Oak Holdings Group LLC, of Jacksonville, will get until early 2027, to see if it can garner the $15 million shortfall from “friends and family” investors who may not demand the 18-22 percent return commanded by typical hotel financiers. But continued work to salvage the mixed-use King’s Landing development that has floundered over the past five years was not universally embraced by city leaders Monday night. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he was “not willing to go one step further,” calling for the city to “cut bait and move on” with the downtown waterfront development. Dzadovsky suggested developers already have defaulted on their timelines for financing and getting buildings up. Now, he claimed, those investors want to save the proposed Marriott hotel portion of the project that’s a linchpin for the remaining housing, office, retail and restaurant facets. However, Commissioner Michael Broderick argued that a 180-day extension to find the remaining $15 million capital was “a responsible ask.” suggesting that pulling the plug now could result in five years of costly litigation for the city to reclaim the land currently owned by a private developer, plus a 10-year delay in any development of the former H.D. Paul Bertozzi, Live Oak president and chief executive officer, said Monday he’s already begun contacting “third tier” potential investors. “A hotel should not fail in this market in this location,” said Bertozzi. Broderick said he believes there also may be a “pool of local money that could be interested as well.” Broderick suggested King’s Landing original developers may have known they could fall short of meeting their capital requirements, but Bertozzi said the gap was created as a $50 million hotel project ballooned over time to more than $60 million. Mainsail Lodging and Development, the primary force behind the proposed downtown hotel, has already missed at least three deadlines in contracts with the city, including a requirement to have the hotel’s financing “fully and finally closed” by July 15. The financing gap that threatens the project first became public in July when commissioners met as the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency (FPRA) board. Live Oak officials said they were surprised to first learn a shortfall existed in April. So far, Live Oak has been the only member of the development group that has appeared before the city commission to answer questions. Commissioners said Monday they want “the whole team” to be present Sept. 14 to discuss whether the project has a future. If commissioners decide Sept. 14 to keep the current King’s Landing deal on life support a bit longer, they will still have to act Sept. 15 as the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency to approve a fourth amendment to the original contract. The city has been embroiled in a series of questionable real estate deals involving city-owned land. A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.

A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old baby who allegedly died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Detectives had obtained an arrest warrant for Gunter in connection with the ongoing investigation into the child's death. He has been charged with felony child neglect causing great harm and is awaiting extradition to St. The arrest comes after three others were previously charged in the case: the child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell; the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell; and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon. See also: Body found in ocean off Boca Raton coast, investigation underway All three were charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. Investigation Began After Baby Was Brought to Hospital The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when Koon and Robert Maxwell brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs that the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed. Detectives assigned to the case conducted interviews with family members at the hospital before serving search warrants and beginning what would become a months-long investigation. Caregivers Allegedly Noticed Warning Signs According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, the infant had been primarily living with Koon and Robert Maxwell after Gunter moved to Virginia. During interviews, detectives learned caregivers had noticed numerous warning signs in the days leading up to the child's death. Investigators say Koon admitted the baby was often fed only a few times a day and claimed he sometimes drank as little as two bottles daily. She told detectives she noticed the child was becoming increasingly thin, pale and lethargic. She also described frequent vomiting, excessive sleeping and a decrease in wet diapers. Despite those concerns, detectives say no one sought emergency medical treatment. Text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong. 12, 2025, messages sent to Nicole Maxwell stated, "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Search Warrant Revealed Conditions Inside Home When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an "extreme environmental hazard." The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Autopsy Findings Led to Homicide Ruling An autopsy later revealed the extent of the infant's condition. According to the Medical Examiner's Office, Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The autopsy found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Examiners also documented numerous lesions and insect bites across the infant's body. The Medical Examiner ultimately determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide, writing that the infant was dependent on caregivers for nutrition and hydration and that the failure to provide those necessities directly caused his death. Father's Role Under Scrutiny Investigators say Gunter was aware of concerns about the child's condition. The criminal complaint states that messages sent to Gunter warned that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. Detectives also recovered messages discussing food shortages and concerns the infant was not being properly cared for. Despite those warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services. A separate text message recovered from his phone stated: "The baby is starving." Detectives included that message among evidence supporting criminal charges. Sheriff's officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the court system. Meanwhile, two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old child following an investigation, the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said. Jason Gunter, 45, the child’s biological father, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service Tuesday morning, at his residence in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office detectives. Gunter has been charged with felony child neglect resulting in great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child’s death. He is currently awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. This arrest marks the fourth individual charged as a result of the investigation. Three people were arrested back on July 24 in relation to this case. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on back in 2025 , after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child’s grandparents. The sheriff’s office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child’s manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said this investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.

A Florida man is behind bars after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and, at one point, passed through Stuart. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the crash happened around 7:30 p.m. on Saturday near Kanner Highway and I-95. Investigators identified the suspect as 36-year-old Michael Jeffrey Spiers, who is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Deputies say the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted. See also: 100-car Florida street takeover sparks 140-mph pursuit ending in 4 arrests According to investigators, Spiers first went after a woman who was driving alone, chasing her through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman frantically called 911 and told dispatchers he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Authorities say Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Investigators say witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. According to the arrest report, the woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. Deputies say the suspect continued chasing the family's SUV. Eventually, the suspect intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car; a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact of the PIT-maneuver sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence, deputies said. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Deputies say Spiers didn't know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. [I] don't know what was in his mind," said Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. He acted as if he was high on some type of of drug, some kind of a stimulant, or he was having some kind of mental episode. We don't really know." Despite the violent crash, no one was injured, including a child who was inside the family's vehicle. "They did all the things that we would recommend they do. They called 911," said Sheriff Budensiek. "Thankfully, our suspect didn't have a gun; it could have ended so much worse." See also: 1 4-year-old killed in three car collision in PBC leaving two dead and four injured Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle. During the investigation, detectives learned the dog had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers use to dated. The dog has since been reunited with its owner, according to the sheriff's office. Spiers was taken into custody and remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely. Tate said the price of housing in Puerto Rico is much less than Florida, especially South Florida. He said property taxes were going up and he could not afford it anymore. His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases: 131.5% in Okeechobee County, 99.4% in Palm Beach County, 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County. Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue. A woman was killed and a man was found dead Saturday evening following what investigators believe was a domestic-related shooting in Port St. Lucie Police Department officers responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Lucie police said the suspect in the domestic disturbance Saturday evening has been identified as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. and the victim has been identified as 50-year-old Elizabeth Ortega. The investigation revealed that Varela and Ortega had been involved in a long-term cohabitation domestic relationship and resided together with their adult son, police said. It was learned that Varela and Ortega were in the process of separating. On Saturday at around 7:30 p.m., the adult son left the residence to pick up dinner from a local restaurant, investigators said. Investigators determined there was no known argument or disturbance inside the home prior to his departure. At some point after the adult son left, investigators believe Varela utilized an AR-style .223 caliber rifle and began shooting Ortega inside the residence, detectives said. Ortega fled the home in an attempt to escape, while Varela continued firing. Investigators recovered home surveillance video that captured portions of the incident and the video shows Ortega attempting to flee into the front yard, while Varela continued to fire at her before she collapsed. After the shooting, Varela returned inside the residence, police said. Responding officers located Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was later pronounced deceased. Following the shooting, Varela was later observed inside the home, where he appeared to have died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and awaiting the final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Lucie Police Department extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones affected by this tragic incident. Wesley Bell won a rematch Tuesday in a Democratic primary against former U.S. Cori Bush, and Missouri voters rejected a ballot measure that could have made ii harder to pass citizen-led amendments in the future.Bell’s primary victory is likely to propel him to reelection in November in the heavily Democratic 1st Congressional District in St. Louis County prosecutor, was backed by a political group affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. The pro-Israeli group also financed his ouster of Bush in the 2024 primary after Bush criticized Israel’s response in Gaza to Hamas’ attack on Israel in 2023.Bush had been a part of a progressive group of House members known as the Squad.The rematch was one of several consequential primaries. In western Missouri, Republicans are picking a candidate to try to unseat Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver in a dramatically reshaped district that is part of President Donald Trump’s attempt to retain a slim House majority in the midterms.In northern Missouri, Republicans are choosing a potential successor to retiring Rep. Sam Graves, chair of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.Meanwhile, Missouri voters were deciding a pair of unique ballot measures backed by the Republican-led Legislature. One defeated measure would have required all citizen-initiated constitutional amendments to pass in each of Missouri's eight congressional districts instead of by a simple statewide majority — a high standard used by no other state. Another amendment under consideration would direct lawmakers to repeal the state’s individual income tax while authorizing a state sales tax expansion.St. Louis primary pits Israel critic against supporterThe contest between Bush and Bell tested how much the Democratic Party has shifted over the past two years.The deep-pocketed American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent millions to help oust Bush in 2024. Bell was again supported by AIPAC.But public opinions of Israel have since shifted, particularly among Democrats. A recent survey by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that about 58% of Democrats now say the U.S. is “too supportive” of Israelis, up from 45% in an AP-NORC poll from January 2024.This year's primary also tested the clout of democratic socialists, who traveled from across the country to help campaign for Bush.Bush and Bell both honed their leadership skills in Ferguson amid the racial unrest that followed the fatal shooting of Michael Brown by a police officer in 2014. Bell won election to the Ferguson City Council the next year, then defeated a seven-term St. Louis County prosecutor in the 2018 Democratic primary.Bush, a protest leader, defeated longtime Rep. William Lacy Clay in the 2020 Democratic primary. A six-person Republican primary features state Sen. Rick Brattin, a Marine veteran and founding member of the Missouri Freedom Caucus, a conservative faction that has challenged the legislature’s GOP leadership. Brattin now has the backing of some of Missouri's top Republicans, including Gov. Mike Kehoe, and received an endorsement from Trump on the evening before the election.His main advertising competitor has been Taylor Burks, a Navy officer who previously served as Boone County clerk, which oversees elections in the home county of the University of Missouri.Retirement creates an opening for a Republican-held seatGraves, who has represented rural northern Missouri for a quarter century, set off a political scramble when he announced in late March that he wasn’t seeking reelection. Lucie County sheriff's deputy was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's "Standards of Performance." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, on Oct. 10, 2025, Sheriff Richard Del Toro was made aware of a Facebook post on Deputy Tina Speicker's personal social media account featuring an image titled "Standards of Power." The report says the image closely resembled Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," which was introduced after he was sworn into office. The Standards of Performance outlined eight performance expectations for employees, agency divisions and the Sheriff's Office's core values. Investigators alleged the post was intended to disparage the Sheriff's Office and Sheriff Del Toro and violated agency rules and regulations. According to the Internal Affairs report, Speicker's "Standards of Power" graphic stated: Top-down domination. Keep everyone beneath you guessing who's next to take the blame. Set confusion for others to follow. The less they know, the more control you have. Display a ruthless work ethic with a focus on self-preservation. Take credit for wins, redirect the failures. Demonstrate selective respect. Favor those who serve your goals; silence those who don't. Being unfair-strategically. Tip the scales to your advantage. Remain obsessive and paranoid. The Internal Affairs investigator identified several similarities between the "Standards of Power" graphic and Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," including that both contained eight principles, used similar wording and sentence structure, began each bullet point with the same first word and featured a similar two-tone outline. The investigation concluded that Speicker violated Sheriff's Office policies regarding criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony.

A Leon County circuit judge has blocked the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, Florida's sweeping property-tax measure, ruling the language is biased, misleading and factually inaccurate.Judge David Frank ordered Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite the title and summary but did not remove Amendment 3 from the November ballot. The ruling changes what voters will read before making their decision — not whether they will make one.WATCH FORREST SAUNDERS' COVERAGE BELOW:"The title and summary simply must pass muster under longstanding Florida law that demands fairness and accuracy," Frank wrote in the 18-page order. "They fail both prerequisites and must be rewritten."Frank found the current ballot title — "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes" — reads more like a political slogan than a neutral description."The title is more akin to a political slogan," he wrote. "It is not fair or neutral. It advocates a policy position: to stop excessive property taxes."Frank said the word "save" was designed to provoke an emotional response. He also found that "Save Our Homes" could confuse voters because the phrase is already associated with Florida's existing 3% cap on annual assessment increases for homesteaded property. Amendment 3 would not change that cap.The judge also found the title could falsely suggest the amendment guarantees lower overall property-tax bills. Local governments could respond to a smaller tax base by raising millage rates or adopting special assessments, potentially offsetting some homeowners' savings. Renters could also face higher costs if landlords pass along increased taxes."Simply put, the proposed ballot title does not state the basic legal purpose of the amendment; it endorses it and diverts voters from its actual effect," Frank wrote.Frank also rejected the summary's declaration that the amendment "benefits Florida taxpayers" and its promotional labels promising to protect small businesses, ensure funding for core services and guarantee fairness."The purpose of a ballot summary is to explain what an amendment would do, not to advocate for its adoption," he wrote.Among the specific problems identified in the ruling:The summary promises a $250,000 homestead exemption while saying the amendment takes effect in 2027. The exemption would initially be $150,000 in 2027 before increasing to $250,000 in 2028.It refers to protecting "small businesses," although the lower assessment-growth cap would apply to all non-homestead property — not only small businesses.It says the amendment requires a schedule for the "full elimination" of non-school homestead property taxes. Frank found the proposal would instead create a process allowing local governments to increase exemptions up to a property's full assessed value.It promises to "ensure" funding for core services, even though the amendment would substantially reduce the local property-tax base and does not guarantee funding for police, firefighters, infrastructure or other services.It inaccurately describes which new Florida residents would face a waiting period before receiving the expanded homestead exemption."Voters are entitled to a fair, clear, accurate and non-misleading ballot statement," Frank wrote.Lawmakers approved the amendment during a June special session, passing it 75-26 in the House and 30-9 in the Senate.Even then, House sponsor Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, acknowledged its legal future was uncertain. Asked June 2 whether the amendment would survive a court challenge, Overdorf responded, "That remains to be seen."Two months later, Frank found the ballot title and summary "clearly and conclusively defective."Former Republican state Sen. The court will retain jurisdiction, and challengers will have 10 days after the replacement language is submitted to raise new objections. The state could also appeal."The ball is in the Attorney General's court at this point," plaintiffs' attorney Jamie Cole said. "They can either appeal this decision, or have the Attorney General fix the language."Uthmeier said Tuesday that his office had not decided how it would proceed."The team is looking at that," Uthmeier said. So, we're giving it a hard look, and we'll have updates soon."If approved, Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from the typical $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. The exemption would rise with inflation beginning in 2029.School-district property taxes would remain unchanged.The amendment would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, impose a waiting period before certain new Florida residents could receive the expanded exemption and limit how counties and cities use remaining property-tax revenue.A Florida House analysis estimates the amendment would reduce local non-school property-tax revenue by $4.95 billion during its first fiscal year and $8.78 billion the following year. The recurring annual reduction is projected to reach $11.86 billion once fully implemented.Amendment 3 needs support from at least 60% of voters to become part of the Florida Constitution.A July University of North Florida poll found 61% initially supported the amendment — barely enough for passage — when respondents were told it would reserve property-tax revenue for core services. Support fell to 45%, with 47% opposed, after respondents were told about projected local-government budget losses.The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points.The results underscore the stakes of the court-ordered rewrite: Amendment 3 will still be decided by Florida voters, but the words they see on the ballot could help decide its fate.

"Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to open its doors on Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county’s fastest-growing communities. Crews have worked throughout the summer to prepare the campus for its first group of students. Principal Latanya Greene said the school’s motto, "Traditions begin here," reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. Your neighborhood: Local coverage from WPBF 25 News "Throughout this process, we have talked a lot about traditions and accomplishments and the achievements that we want to build and grow at this school. Hence, our motto for the school year is that tradition leads K through eight. Traditions begin here," Greene said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Greene emphasized that months of planning have gone into creating an environment where students can grow academically and socially. "It's about being in an environment that you can grow and continue with great levels. But bigger than that, you begin to set the tone of creating those strong academics that move with you from year to year to year. You develop friendships," Greene said. The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school’s convenient location. "We are busting at the seams in the south and the west. And this school is so conveniently located to families that we're going to have a tremendous number of students that are walking or even other parents dropping the kids off in a golf cart," said John R. Prince, superintendent of St. Lucie County Public Schools. As the first day approaches, Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school’s inaugural year. "The academics component is going to be there, but it is going to be walking through this inaugural year and looking back on all the traditions that we have created as a team, as a family, and the strength of our culture, and how we just grow throughout the first year will be beyond the definition of success for us," Greene said. Tradition Lakes K-8 will officially open on August 10, marking the beginning of a new chapter for students and families in the Tradition area.

A prosecutor says they have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 in Port St. Lucie when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads. According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. "Basically, under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony, occur in their presence. So that's basically what happened here. When someone effects a citizen's arrest, basically, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. Bruin says if the case had gone to a jury, they would've returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis, in this case, gets out of the vehicle and holds the the people that were in that car at gunpoint. No, we don't recommend that people take the law into their own hands like that. Let the police do their job. Call the police, let the police do their job," Bruin said. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. "I am very grateful as I am a father of three and everything I do is for my kids. The thought of being away from them is horrifying. I have a daughter that is the same age as the person who did the shooting, and I spend my time teaching my children not to do dumb things like that. Obviously I would never want anyone to ever get hurt. Especially over what they consider to be a prank. I believe behavior like this starts with the parents. It is our job to teach our kids right from wrong and be their parent first and their friend second," Davis said in a text message to CBS12 News, reacting to the fact that the charges against him were dropped. Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore — one that washed up dead and another of fishermen struggling with a hooked one. Both incidents occurred Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident and avid beach walker Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the deadly beast and released it back into the water. Shark expert and conservationist Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark by looking at the video. Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County, which also includes Hutchinson Island, to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

The Florida Sheriffs Association says a November ballot measure to increase the homestead exemption could create longer law enforcement response times.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:The Florida Sheriffs Association has entered the tax reform debate, raising concerns about a November ballot measure that would increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners.The association states it has "significant concerns" with the referendum, warning it could potentially "create longer law enforcement response times."Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said the association's position carries weight."Florida sheriffs are always moderate in their responses they tend to be very supportive of the governor and for them to come out strong in this case opposed to the governor should send a very clear signal," Snyder said.The debate over cutting taxes and its impact on public safety is central to the amendment question facing voters in November. County and city leaders are grappling with how they would manage significant cuts in revenue as homeowners look to Tallahassee for relief from high tax bills.Snyder said he understands the frustration driving the push for tax relief."I understand the individual homeowner and the taxpayer desire to reduce taxes," Snyder said.But he warned the savings may come with hidden costs."But what they will be doing is instead of paying for services out of their left pocket they'll pay for it out of their right pocket," Snyder said, explaining how sheriffs' offices and fire departments would look to other taxes and fees to make up the difference.Snyder served as Martin County sheriff for 12 years and managed the department's budgets throughout that time."I will tell you we looked at every single nickle and you shave a little off the edges but when 80 percent of your budget is personnel services unless you let deputies go, or firefighters go, you really can't do all that much with the budget," Snyder said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.
