The city offered the land lease to bidders, drawing an outcry from residents."Our biggest fear is we don't want this to change and be a chain restaurant or a big box store," restaurant co-owner Donna Qvarnstrom said. "It's local and the people love local."After an outpouring of community support, the city kept the restaurant open month to month. Despite five formal proposals submitted to the city — including one from the current operators — the city said none met the criteria and scrapped plans to select a new tenant.Keene argues the handling of Little Jim's is part of a broader pattern of poor waterfront stewardship, pointing to two other controversial city projects: Fisherman's Wharf, where state records show the city promised land it didn't own, and King's Landing, where a developer claims the city promised buildable property that contained 1,500 tons of old power plant concrete. The Fisherman's Wharf situation led to a current multi-million dollar lawsuit filed by that project's developer and threats of a lawsuit from the King's Landing developer.Broderick said the city's management of leased properties needs to change."In my opinion, the handling of city-owned real estate that we subsequently lease out to tenants is — it's not being managed. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office announced Monday that one of its longtime communications officers was the woman killed in what investigators say was a murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie over the weekend.WATCH BELOW:The sheriff's office identified the victim as Elizabeth "Liz" Ortega, a communications officer who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years."Our Communications Division is deeply saddened to announce the sudden and tragic passing of Communications Officer Elizabeth 'Liz' Ortega," the sheriff's office said. "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room."Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016.According to Port St. Lucie police, officers responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.Investigators identified the suspect as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. and confirmed Ortega was also 50 years old. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating.Investigators said the couple's adult son had left the home around 7:30 p.m. Detectives found no indication of an argument or disturbance before he left."He did not witness any arguments or disturbance prior to his departure from the residence," Officer Brittany Holly told WPTV.Police believe Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Investigators said Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting, according to detectives."One of the neighbors actually located that victim, after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive suffering from gunshot wounds," Holly told WPTV.Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died.Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.PBSO said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, and asked the community to keep both agencies in their thoughts during this time. Funeral arrangements are pending.The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Lucie police extended their condolences to Ortega's family and loved ones.The department said anyone experiencing domestic violence should not be afraid to speak up."We encourage anyone who is experiencing domestic violence, or knows someone who is experiencing domestic violence to ask for help, seek help," Holly said. "That's what we're here for."

Palm Beach County health officials have confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue fever, prompting a mosquito-borne illness advisory and warnings from health experts for residents to take mosquito prevention seriously.WATCH BELOW: 'If it happens to bite someone, that someone will likely get the infection,'Unlike most dengue cases seen in South Florida, the patient did not travel outside the area before getting sick."The importance of this announcement is that this is the first case that would happen in someone who has not left Palm Beach County," Dr. Kleper De Almeida, an infectious disease specialist working at several hospitals in Palm Beach County, including Good Samaritan Medical Center, said.Every year, Florida sees what doctors call "imported cases" of dengue, where travelers become infected overseas and return home carrying the virus. But local transmission means mosquitoes in Palm Beach County are now carrying dengue and spreading it to people in the area."What this means is that there are mosquitoes floating around, flying around, carrying the dengue virus," De Almeida said. "If it happens to bite someone, that someone will likely get the infection."Palm Beach County Mosquito Control has already been dispatched in response to the confirmed case. Health experts say the situation will likely not turn into a massive outbreak, but they do expect additional infections."Usually one of these, having one case is a signal that there are mosquitoes flying around with the dengue virus," De Almeida said. "If infected mosquitoes bite an uninfected person, there is a good chance that the person will catch the infection.""We'll probably see a few people, and there would not be a huge number, hopefully," De Almeida said.Dengue symptoms can be intense and often begin with fever and severe pain."The telltale symptom is severe body aches, body and joint aches accompanied by a fever," De Almeida said. The lower back hurts, the joints hurt."Some patients may also develop a rash."There is a rash that comes and goes," De Almeida said.In more severe cases, bleeding complications can develop, including a rash on the skin that does not blanch."There are unfortunately no direct treatment," De Almeida said. "One has to wait it out."Doctors recommend using acetaminophen, like Tylenol, to manage fever and pain instead of medications like ibuprofen or aspirin, which could worsen bleeding complications."If using aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen or other anti-inflammatory medications, it might exacerbate these bleeding complications," De Almeida said.Mosquito experts say one of the best ways to stop the spread starts in your own backyard. Harold Fortes with Mosquito Shield of Palm Beach said standing water is the primary concern."What we're gonna do is spray all the vegetation," he said. "You see these pots right here? So, what mosquitoes does is they lay eggs in there."Fortes said standing water can produce mosquitoes in as little as eight days, with some species breeding in as few as four days."It's rainy season, big time for them to reproduce," he said.Residents are being urged to clean gutters, remove yard debris, and empty trays underneath flower pots. Experts also said bromeliad plants should be rinsed regularly, because they naturally collect water that can allow larvae to grow.De Almeida said dengue is just one of several dangerous illnesses spread by mosquitoes in Florida."There is West Nile that causes a brain infection. There is chikungunya that causes severe joint and muscle pains. We remember Zika that happened a number of years ago," De Almeida said.His message to Palm Beach County residents is simple: avoid mosquito bites whenever possible."We need to be more conscious, more attentive to not being bitten by mosquitoes during the summertime in Florida, because we can be acquiring one of these infections," De Almeida said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes.WATCH BELOW: 'The price of housing here is much less than Florida,' Jock Tate tells WPTV's Consumer Reporter Matt Sczesny"The property taxes are going up and up and I'm like I just can't afford it," Jock Tate said.Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Lead sponsors supporting the Education Foundation of Martin County’s Your Classroom Connection programs are, from left, Patty McAuley of Seacoast Bank; Tami Karol of Tami Karol Insurance; Kelley Decowski of RE/MAX of Stuart; Dr. Ajay Goyal of Diagnostic Radiology Center of the Treasure Coast; Lisa Rhodes of the Education Foundation of Martin County; and Dr. Vincent Napoli of Napoli Orthodontics. STUART — Martin County residents can help teachers prepare for the new school year by adopting a classroom, funding a project or donating supplies through the Education Foundation of Martin County. As Martin County students prepare to return to school Aug. 10, the Education Foundation of Martin County is inviting residents, civic groups, nonprofits and businesses to help meet classroom needs through three online programs. Adopt-A-Class allows supporters to adopt a specific classroom or school program with a donation of $100 or more. Classrooms and programs may be adopted multiple times, and the foundation hopes to have every classroom adopted at least once during the school year. To adopt a class and make a donation to a classroom or program, visit www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/251/adopt-a-class . Through Fund-A-Project, teachers can post requests for classroom projects designed to support student learning. Donors can select and fund specific educational projects. To view teacher requests, visit www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/285/fund-a-project . Bulletin Board Listings connect community members with nonmonetary classroom needs. Participants may volunteer their time or donate materials, gently used equipment, books, magazines, shoe boxes and other reusable supplies. Community members also may offer subject-matter expertise or advisory board support. To support the Bulletin Board, visit https://www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/284/community-opportunities . “Every great classroom innovation begins with an idea,” said Chanda Leon, a pre-AICE biology teacher at Martin County High School and the Education Foundation’s 2025-2026 Martin County Teacher of the Year. “Too often, that idea never becomes reality because of cost. Adopt-a-Classroom and Fund-a-Project have helped to remove financial barriers, allowing me the opportunity to convert creative solutions into meaningful learning experiences for my students.” The foundation said 100 percent of donations go directly toward classroom needs because program sponsors cover administrative costs. Lead sponsors include Napoli Orthodontics, the Kelley Decowski Team at RE/MAX of Stuart, Tami Karol Insurance, Diagnostic Radiology Center of the Treasure Coast, Seacoast Bank, and Rosenthal, Levy, Simon Sosa Injury Lawyers. Other sponsors include Precision Site Contracting, Stuart Pediatric Dentistry, Sullivan Electric Pump, Searcy Law, New Wave Compass – Sara Crombie, Ampersand Graphics, JoAnna Oster, RE/MAX of Stuart, Pinder’s Nursery, All Jetting Technologies, Elegant Entries, Lesser Landy Smith Siegel PLLC, SwissMango and Sal’s Air. “Every adopted classroom, funded project and donated resource sends a powerful message to our teachers and students that this community believes in them,” said Lisa Rhodes, executive director of the Education Foundation of Martin County. “When local residents and businesses step forward, they help turn classroom ideas into learning experiences that can inspire achievement all year long.” Steven C. Simon, managing shareholder at Rosenthal, Levy, Simon Sosa Injury Lawyers, said his firm was pleased to support the foundation’s Your Classroom Connection program. “Educators make a lasting difference in the lives of students, and we are grateful for the opportunity to help strengthen classrooms across Martin County. It is a privilege to stand with many leading community businesses and join the Education Foundation in investing in educational excellence and student success,” he said. The Education Foundation of Martin County is the Martin County School District’s nonprofit partner. It raises and distributes private and corporate donations through classroom enrichment grants, literacy and STEAM programs, teacher professional development, scholarships and other educational initiatives. To adopt a classroom, fund a project, respond to a classroom need or learn more about the Education Foundation of Martin County, visit www.EducationFoundationMC.org or call 772-600-8062. The aerial view for the P-1 Motor Club being developed on a 626.3-acre property located on the south side of Okeechobee Road near Summerlin Road. The site plan for the P-1 Motor Club being developed on a 626.3-acre property located on the south side of Okeechobee Road near Summerlin Road. Lucie County Commission approved the major final site plan on July 21 with a few modifications to conditions of approval primarily related to the timing of landscape installation. Lucie County Commission voted unanimously July 21 to approve the final major site plan for the P-1 Motor Club while also agreeing to the developer’s request to modify a few of the 33 staff conditions of approval. Senior Planner Thad Crowe presented the request that evening for the 626.3-acre property located on the south side of Okeechobee Road near Summerlin Road. “This is a final site plan for the P-1 Motor Club on Okeechobee Road, [about] 3.8 miles outside the Urban Service Boundary,” he said. “First, a little history: In 2023, the original comprehensive plan amendment was passed to establish the special district for the P-1 Motor Club. That was followed by a second comprehensive plan amendment in 2025, specifically allowing for public or private provision of potable water. The planned mixed use development was approved in 2025 as well.” Crowe then provided specific details of the plan as he pointed to a map on the overhead screen. “On the right-hand side is one of the tracks,” he said. “On the left-hand side, is the second track, the Treasure Coast Circuit and the P-1 Circuit. A lot of this stuff – the garagemajals, the residences, the R D park – is way into the future. Right now, the applicant is focusing on these two tracks.” Crowe also touched on the applicant’s preliminary landscape plan for the property, which no longer has any native vegetation. “The applicant did have a conceptual landscape plan they submitted with this application,” he continued. “It’s their intent to work with their landscape firm to develop comprehensive landscaping across the whole site, establishing ecosystems such as native oasis with palms and shade. This is a blank slate and an opportunity to establish reforestation and reintroduce native communities to the site.” The senior planner provided his own recommendations on that aspect before reading through the conditions of approval. “We are recommending that the northern and eastern buffer at a minimum should be required in this first phase,” he said. “The landscaping is a work in progress; the applicant has not provided complete details and the Environment Resources Department has been working with us. Their stance on this is that a finalized landscape plan be required prior to development and required landscaping in place prior to the site-development permit. With the recommended conditions, we believe the major site plan is consistent with the adopted P1MC Special District, the PMUD site plan [and] landscape plan.” When no members of the Board had questions, the developer Ari Strauss came to the podium to request relief from a few of those conditions of approval, some actually related to the landscaping. “We have a handful of really minor conditions that we would like to ask the Board to consider modifying,” he said. “We’ve had a number of delays [and] we’re still working through some water agreements. While it’s in discussion, it’s really critical that we demonstrate some progress. We’re anxious to get the first circuit up and running hopefully in several months for our members.” Strauss then enumerated conditions, 6, 7, 27, 31 and 32 for modification. The sixth condition was the only one unrelated to landscaping, but rather required the developer to separate the bicycle or walking lanes from internal roadways. “We intend to build the cross-sections that are included in the PMUD plans, which actually has a seven-foot travel lane on both sides of the road,” he said. “We would adhere to these cross-sections unless we provide an alternate travel path that pulls members or guests away from the travel lanes. In some of our landscape renderings, we show areas where a pedestrian or bike could actually leave the travel lane and then go through unpaved sections.” The seventh condition required him to plant shade trees along the roadways 30 feet apart. “We’re asking if we can change it from shade trees to native trees,” he explained. Instead, we want it to appear more like native plantings.” While Conditions 31 and 32 were related to his desire to preserve native trees along the Summerlin Road right of way, Strauss’ requested relief from number 27 eventually got pushback from county staff. “We would ask for – rather than prior to commencement of development – that we would provide the finalized landscape plan within 12 months of the commencement of development,” he said. “Then within 24 months of commencement, we will complete all the landscaping plans for Okeechobee Road, the entrance, all the completed interior roads and the littoral plantings around the stormwater ponds and lakes. As we get the first track running, we’ll have a lot of work around the site with earth-moving equipment and ponds being dug. It would be difficult to have all of the landscaping done and in place.” District 1 Commissioner James Clasby immediately asked Planning Manager Kori Benton to confirm that his staff had no objections to the applicant’s modifications. “I don’t think we have concerns or conflicts with the provision of time, as long as we have a plan or goal,” Benton replied. Commissioner Clasby then admitting to having met with ERD staff in his office and expressed his support for the modifications. “I don’t mind delaying when they are compliant with their landscaping requirements, only that they eventually do [comply],” he said. “That portion on number 27… seems like a reasonable timeline.” Environmental Regulations Manager Aimee Cooper, however, still wasn’t convinced, asking Strauss to reiterate that timeframe. “Within 12 months of commencement, the applicant shall provide all the way to the landscape typicals plan,” he explained. “Within 24 months of commencement, we will complete the landscaping plans for Okeechobee Road, the entrance, all of the completed interior roads and all of the littoral plantings. If that modification is approved, I believe that eliminates number 28.” His last comment on a separate condition concerned Environmental Planner Brian Ingram, however. “I think ERD’s okay with deferring some of it,” he said. “But by eliminating Condition 28, they would be authorized to use the track without the code-required landscaping.” After back-and-forth clarification questions between commissioners and Strauss, Cooper posed her own question directly to the developer. “I need some details here on what minimum landscaping would be installed for the first track so that we have a better understanding,” she said. “Then for the second track, would it be possible to have a majority of the landscaping installed?” “We could commit to that,” Strauss answered. “For clarification, within 12 months of commencing development, we’ll provide the finalized landscape plan. And where I suggested within 24 months of commencement, we will complete the plans for Okeechobee Road entrance and littoral plantings around the ponds. We could commit to having that done before the second track, the P-1 Circuit, is open, since we believe it will be roughly a year and a half instead of the two years we asked for. If that is amenable to you, we would be amenable to that as well.” After Cooper found that acceptable, the County Commission voted unanimously to approve the major final site with the modifications to the conditions of approval. STUART — Stories of beloved pets and second chances brought readers and animal advocates together as local children’s author Sherry Dunn celebrated the release of her newest book, “The Quiet Bond.” The book signing at the Court House Cultural Center in downtown Stuart was presented in partnership with MartinArts and catered by Riverwalk Café Oyster Bar. Cobie’s Cottage, a local nonprofit that rescues senior dogs and helps find them homes, also participated. Several of the organization’s dogs greeted guests throughout the evening, reinforcing one of the book’s central messages that some of life’s deepest connections are often the quietest. Following a reading, Dunn met with attendees during a book-signing reception. Guests shared stories about pets that had changed their lives. “The goal was never simply to sell books,” Dunn said. “It was to encourage people to cherish the quiet bond they already share with their pets, consider opening their hearts to a senior rescue animal and leave inspired to make a difference.” “The Quiet Bond” is a collection of engaging anecdotes exploring the connection between animals and humans. Through wise and often humorous stories about Dunn’s rescue cat, Jasmine, and quieter reflections, including the meditative experience of watching an aquarium, the book illustrates how animals can bring comfort, improve moods and enrich people’s lives. The evening also showcased the power of community partnerships. The Court House Cultural Center provided an inviting setting. Riverwalk Café Oyster Bar delighted guests with an assortment of hors d’oeuvres including a crowd-favorite baked Brie. Cobie’s Cottage reminded everyone that compassion can change an animal’s life forever. Dunn said she hopes the book will encourage readers to appreciate their pets and consider visiting a local shelter or rescue organization. For information, visit sherrydunn.com or cobiescottage.org . Two senior FIFA officials criticized Gianni Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan Friday with one resigning as a presidential adviser and a second saying staff were deceived by project that must not go ahead.Carlos Cordeiro, who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned in protest at the private equity plan."I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker, said in a statement resigning as adviser to FIFA President Gianni Infantino that urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.RELATED STORY | UEFA members threaten FIFA boycott, Concacaf rejects World Cup investor planFIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to The Associated Press staff were "deceived" by Infantino's lack of openness planning the private investor scheme and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation.""It is the project of one person," Lamour, a long-time colleague of Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA, wrote. "Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."Lamour did not resign the post he held since 2024 but said he had a duty to his colleagues."And if that means I lose my job, then so be it" the French official said. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."Cordeiro often joined Infantino on working visits to meet U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in recent years."Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," Cordeiro, the former U.S. Soccer Federation president said, calling the $20 billion commercial subsidiary "a bad deal for football.""Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking, I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away" he said. "That is why this proposal should be rejected."RELATED STORY | FIFA's Infantino sets deadline to members in Kushner-backed World Cup planInfantino has proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $20 billion subsidiary with 20% owned by private investors.The "anchor investor," described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner."FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organization sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt," Cordeiro said, noting FIFA's revenue of $15 billion over the last four years tied to the men's Wold Cup just ended."Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification," he said.Cordeiro said he shared five years working for FIFA alongside Infantino with "dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game.""I hope they, too, will speak up," he wrote, "because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."Infantino has been president of FIFA for more than 10 years and had seemed sure to be reelected unopposed next March. 18 deadline for challengers to come forward.

VERO BEACH – The members of the Vero Beach Planning Zoning Board unanimously recommended July 16 that the City Council change the land use of a seven-acre parcel from residential to commercial so a developer can repurpose the property at 2300 5th Ave. for mixed-use development as part of a northern extension of the Miracle Mile Business District. Planning Development Director Jason Jeffries provided a brief introduction that afternoon for the three related agenda items, of which the last for the rezoning had already been withdrawn. “The applicant, 2300 5th Avenue LLC, has purchased an office building just north of the Miracle Mile Business District,” he said. “Many people locally know this property as the Doctors’ Clinic. Through redevelopment, they’re looking for this site to become integrated into the Miracle Mile area. That required three separate applications: One is the future land use map amendment, the first hearing; then a text amendment to update one of the figures in the map series, which designates the commercial districts; and the rezoning. Most of the presentation is going to occur in the first hearing.” Principal Planner Cheri Fitzgerald then kicked off that presentation. “The request is to change the future land use map from the existing residential medium to the proposed commercial,” she said. “The property is just north of the Miracle Mile commercial district [and] is currently an office/pre-school. To the north is an office complex, and the land use is residential medium; To the south is the Miracle Mile area; to the east is a multifamily residential apartment complex; and to the west is a pre-school/daycare. The amendment is to extend the Miracle Mile commercial district to the north, which would allow mixed-use residential and commercial uses that could better align with more recent development trends.” Fitzgerald based her recommendation of approval on the application’s compliance with city code. “The future land use map amendment is found to be consistent with the standards for review in Section 6525 of the land development regulations,” she explained. “It is compatible with the surrounding area in terms of existing uses and future land-use designations.” Board Member Samantha Irvin was the first to question what the future development might contain. “Do we know yet what type of commercial businesses are going to go there?” she asked. Jeffries tackled that inquiry. “It depends on what’s been submitted to staff,” he replied. That is one of the reasons why our recommendation was not to approve the zoning so that we would get a more specific development plan or some further updates that we’re working on with the B-4 Zoning to ensure it is pedestrian oriented.” Vice-Chairman Thomas “TP” Kennedy then asked about potential traffic impacts but discovered it was probably too early in the process to get clear answers on that concern as well. “Does making it more pedestrian friendly decrease the traffic?” he asked. “Is that what you guys are looking for in the B-4 Zoning?” “Because they say it’s going to be pedestrian oriented, they say there’s more internal capture in the modeling,” Jeffries answered. “Again, this goes back to making sure in the zoning you actually get the pedestrian-oriented development. I think on Indian River Boulevard... some intersection improvements are needed.” Fitzgerald offered her insight as well. “At this level like Jason explained, it’s more theoretical,” she said. “You do the overall analysis and you look at the most practical case with those assumptions, and that’s what the traffic impact analysis did. Once you get a project-specific development, the traffic report will be specified to that site plan.” After more Board member questions related to both traffic and the pedestrian-friendly focus, the applicant’s contracted developer Keith Kyte and contracted Land Planner Rebecca Grohall both came to the podium. “The reason we’re here today is we need the Commercial Land Use Designation to answer those questions,” Kyte said. “We’re aligning it with the city’s 2005 Vision Plan.” Grohall then provided details on the current status of the property and the ideas for repurposing it. “This was originally the Doctors’ Clinics specialized in heathcare,” she said. “A lot of specialty medical practices eventually migrated toward the hospital and opening their own facilities. Today, it’s generally utilized as office and a pre-school and it does face vacancy rates and under-utilization.” Grohall emphasized that the site plan was in limbo until the Commercial Land Use is approved. “The site plan hasn’t even been started because we need to put the foundation in place,” she explained. “Possibly one of those pieces could be a hotel. We’re looking at multifamily units, a true mixed-use development where there’s ground-floor retail and upper floor residential uses. You’ll see the map of how this interfaces with the neighborhood. This is a visualization, and this would be a non-vehicular pedestrian connection that would bring you into the Miracle Mile shopping plaza.” After much further discussion, Vice-Chairman Kennedy wondered why the Parc24 office building currently under construction by Kimley-Horn wasn’t included since it sits just north of the 2300 5th Avenue LLC property. “When I read through this over the past week, I thought for uniformity it might be better for Kimley-Horn to come in too,” he said. “Was there any conversation there with them?” The answer according to Jeffries was cut and dry. “That was staff’s recommendation, but they decided not to become part of this application,” he said. What the Martin County Sheriff describes as the worst animal hoarding case he has ever seen has grown larger, with 108 animals now rescued.When investigators searched 77-year-old Gail Gustino's home near Hobe Sound on July 20, they found 92 dogs and cats living in triple-digit heat with no ventilation and surrounded by inches of waste.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Gustino has since been released from jail on bond, with her next court date scheduled for September.The Martin County Sheriff described how Gustino was able to avoid detection."She walled herself off and made her house where you couldn't just walk up to the front door and see what was going on in there, where code enforcement couldn't just come out there. So while she's got some mental illness component in her life, she's also pretty savvy with law enforcement," the sheriff said.Since the initial rescue, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says the total number of animals recovered has climbed to 108, with more arriving daily."Every single day more animals are coming forth from the same case. Apparently Gail had friends that she dropped off animals too and the friends have been bringing the animals to us to surrender them," the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said.The shelter says it has been overwhelmed by community support since the rescue."It is so heartwarming to see the community come together. Our hallways are filled with donations. We are using the donations as quickly as they're coming in," the shelter said.Staff says more animals are being medically cleared for adoption every day, but the shelter still needs help."We need resources. We need fosters," the shelter said.Longtime animal rescuer Tish Ott has been waiting for the chance to bring one of the rescued animals home."This little girl has been through hell and back, and I just wanted her to finally realize what a real life was," Ott said.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging people to check its website for the latest adoption listings. Three men from Palm Beach County have been sentenced in federal court for trafficking and sexually exploiting three teenage girls who had run away from foster care, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced Monday. Antonio Michel, 36, of Delray Beach, was sentenced to 15 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to sex trafficking of a minor; Jaime Figueroa, 36, of Boynton Beach, to 19 years and seven months in prison after he pleaded guilty to production of child sexual abuse material; and Raymond Jean, 46, of Greenacres, to 12 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to sex trafficking of a minor. HSI West Palm Beach and the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office Human Trafficking Task Force investigated the case.“These defendants found missing foster children who needed protection and chose instead to exploit them, supply them with drugs, and sell them for profit,” said U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida.According to court documents, the defendants preyed upon three teenage girls who had run away from foster care. Taking advantage of the victims’ youth, instability, and lack of family support, the defendants transported, harbored, and commercially exploited the minors for financial gain.Michel, often accompanied by Jean, transported the victims to and from hotels, motels, and other locations where commercial sex acts occurred. Michel also rented and paid for multiple hotel and motel rooms used to facilitate the exploitation of the minor victims.Figueroa directed the victims on how much money to charge for commercial sex acts and how to conduct the “dates.” He also regularly supplied crack cocaine to the victims during the course of the trafficking scheme. The victims turned over proceeds from the commercial sex acts to Figueroa. Following Figueroa’s arrest, law enforcement searched his cellphone and discovered that he had produced child sexual abuse material involving one of the victims.“No child should ever be subjected to such cruelty," Special Agent in Charge José R. Figueroa of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Miami said. "These sentences represent an important step toward justice for the victims and demonstrate that HSI and our partners will use every tool available to identify, investigate, and bring child predators to justice.”

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police investigate campaign sign confrontations between mayor and challenger
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police are investigating two separate incidents involving mayoral campaign signs being removed or tampered with, occurring two days apart and about a mile from each other. The confrontations involve incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin and challenger Steven Giordano in the race ahead of the August election.

Surveillance footage shows a woman removing one of Mayor Shannon Martin's campaign signs on SW Thanksgiving Avenue on Wednesday night. Police say the footage also shows Giordano at the scene. Giordano stated that the homeowner had given his volunteer permission to remove the sign. Another incident occurred early Friday morning on SW Thornhill Drive, where Giordano said he witnessed someone vandalizing his campaign sign. Police later identified the individual as Aaron Martin, the mayor's husband and a lieutenant with the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Aaron Martin, with the two shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission.

Officers said homeowners had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property, and a language barrier may have caused confusion about the signs. Investigators learned that one homeowner had given permission for one campaign sign to be placed on the property, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, told members of the opposing campaign they could also place a sign there. On Friday evening, Shannon Martin addressed the incidents on social media, stating that she was aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of her campaign signs over several days. She said some of her signs had been taken down without permission and replaced with Giordano's signs. Martin stated that at no time did her husband steal Giordano's sign nor did he damage or vandalize it, and that the sign remained at the location.

Police emphasized that the fact that the mayor's husband is a lieutenant will not affect the investigation. The Port St. Lucie Police Department said it remains committed to conducting a fair, impartial and fact-based investigation. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged. Detectives are reviewing physical evidence, speaking with witnesses and verifying statements provided to investigators. The investigations remain active.

cards.headline: 77-year-old Port St. Lucie man found dead in pond near his home
cards.teaser: Michael Joseph Kramer, 77, was found unresponsive in a pond directly across the street from his residence on SW Mockingbird Drive.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police are investigating the death of a 77-year-old man who was found in a pond on Friday. Around 1:18 p.m., officers were called to a residence on SW Mockingbird Drive in reference to a missing adult who was later identified as Michael Joseph Kramer, 77.

The investigation revealed that Kramer was last seen by his wife inside of their residence at around 10:00 p.m. Thursday. When Kramer's wife woke up at approximately 7:00 a.m. on Friday, Kramer was nowhere to be found despite all of his personal belongings remaining in the residence. After an extensive search of the area, police located an unresponsive man that matched Kramer's description in a pond directly across the street from the residence at around 2:00 p.m. The Port St. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water, and he was pronounced deceased. The circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear, but no indications of foul play seem apparent.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after video shows alleged abuse of small dog
cards.teaser: Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, was charged with animal cruelty after video showed him appearing to kick a small dog in his backyard.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested following an investigation into a social media video that shows a man abusing a small dog, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Video from the Sheriff's Office shows Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, appearing to kick a small dog in his backyard near a pool.

The video made rounds on social media, and the outrage sparked an investigation from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Following the investigation, the Sheriff's Office's findings gave detectives probable cause to charge Shieferstein with animal cruelty. Shieferstein is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $7,500 bond.

hero.headline: Early voting begins Saturday for Florida's August primary in Martin County
hero.teaser: Martin County voters can cast early ballots starting Saturday at designated sites through Aug. 15.
hero.body:
Early voting for Florida's August primary begins Aug. 8 in Martin County, with voters able to cast ballots at any designated early voting site from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily through Aug. 15. Voters can cast their ballots at any of the designated early voting sites in the county. This differs from Election Day, when voters must go to their assigned polling place.

Voters should bring a current, valid photo ID with a signature. If the photo ID does not include a signature, a second form of identification may be required. Election officials recommend checking voter information and reviewing sample ballots before heading to the polls.

Florida has closed primaries, meaning party registration determines which primary ballot voters receive. The deadline to change party affiliation has passed. However, all registered voters may still be eligible to vote in nonpartisan or universal-primary contests, depending on their location. Election Day is Tuesday, Aug. 18.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie postpones Riverland sports complex rezoning after Tradition residents protest
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council voted unanimously on July 27 to postpone a rezoning request for a 135,000-square-foot indoor and outdoor sports recreation complex in the Riverland area after dozens of Tradition-area homeowners packed City Chambers in protest. The council tabled the request from Riverland/Kennedy II LLC until August 24 to give the developer time to hold a neighborhood meeting with concerned residents. The developer GL Homes is seeking to rezone approximately 33.23 acres south of Southwest Discovery Way and east of Southwest Sundance Vista Boulevard from St. Lucie County Agricultural to Riverland-West Sports Recreation Master Planned Unit Development.

Residents who spoke at the hearing said they purchased their homes with the understanding that the parcel would be a city park, not a commercial recreation facility. Southwest River Rock Road resident Jim Riordan told the council GL Homes has 1,300 other acres where they could build the complex and that the company is already advertising the fitness center in sales materials for new parcels. Harriet Gallas said she was told when she bought her house there would be a park over the berm next to her property. She told the council the planned 72 pickleball courts, bocci courts, tennis courts, dog park and RV park would destroy her quality of life through noise pollution.

Planning Zoning Director Mary Savage-Dunham told the council the rezoning is consistent with the city comprehensive plan and a pre-existing Development of Regional Impact for the area. The site is designated Neighborhood Village Commercial, which allows a mixture of residential and non-residential uses including commercial offices, personal and household services, institutional facilities, public facilities, parks, playgrounds and similar services. Land Use Attorney Azlina Goldstein, representing the applicant, initially resisted postponing the request and said details about landscaping, buffers and specific indoor and outdoor features would be addressed during the site-plan process, not the rezoning.

Mayor Shannon Martin asked Goldstein if GL Homes would be willing to meet with residents to address their concerns. Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo urged Goldstein to table the request, saying residents did not comprehend the quasi-judicial rezoning process. After loud protest from the audience, the council voted to postpone the hearing until August 24. City Attorney Richard Berrios explained that the rezoning is a quasi-judicial process limited to sworn testimony and facts applied to the specific rezoning request, with details about landscaping and specific features reserved for the site-plan process.
hero.article_text: The location and aerial maps of the 33.23-acre parcel that G.L. Homes wants to rezone in order to build a 135,000-square-foot indoor and outdoor recreation area known as the Riverland-West Sports Recreation complex. Because so many residents both emailed the city and spoke out in protest during the July 27 quasi-judicial rezoning hearing, the City Council voted unanimously that day to table the request until Aug. 24 to give the applicant time to hold a neighborhood meeting. LUCIE – City Council members found themselves defending their actions to frustrated Tradition-area residents July 27, prompting them to table a quasi-judicial rezoning request from the developer of the Riverland/Kennedy Development of Regional Impact. The delay will give the developer’s representatives time to meet with area homeowners and address their concerns. Planner Francis Forman introduced the controversial agenda item that evening to a packed Chambers. “The item before you is the Riverland-West Sports Recreation Master Planned Unit Development rezoning,” he said. “The applicant is Azlina Goldstein with Riverland/Kennedy II LLC. This site is located south of Southwest Discovery Way and east of Southwest Sundance Vista Boulevard. The request is to rezone approximately 33.23 acres from St. Lucie County Agricultural to Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD.” Forman proceeded to provide more details on the GL Homes request to develop the site in a manner that many Riverland homeowners claim is different than what was planned when they purchased their properties years ago. “This site is designated Neighborhood Village Commercial, which allows a mixture of residential and non-residential uses such as commercial and offices, personal and household services, institutional, public facilities, parks, playgrounds and similar services,” he explained. “Any Neighborhood Village Commercial area must contain at least two of those uses. Currently the Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD is proposing to provide about 135,000 square feet of indoor recreation with some commercial as well as some outdoor RV/boat storage areas.” Because the city had received numerous emails from nearby residents in opposition, Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo immediately asked City Attorney Richard Berrios to describe the formalities of the quasi-judicial process. “This is a rezoning, which is limited to what Mr. Forman presented,” Berrios said. “Not part of it are things like landscaping, indoor and outdoor features and specifics of what it will ultimately be. Those things are better suited for the site-plan process. As far as the process here, the legislators take off their legislative hats and put on their judge robes, and it’s limited to taking sworn testimony and the facts presented and applying them to a specific problem.” Councilman Anthony Bonna, however, believed more information was needed for the area residents. “Can you go into more detail about what evidence is allowed to be weighed [and] is a rezoning discretionary?” he asked. While Berrios admitted the Council’s hands were tied as far as any pre-existing DRI entitlements, he deferred Councilman Bonna’s question to Planning Zoning Director Mary Savage-Dunham. The latter emphasized the legal framework of controlling agreements and city codes. A pre-existing Development of Regional Impact (DRI) is a large-scale project approved under older Florida growth laws that retains vested development rights despite later changes to local plans or the elimination of the state’s formal DRI program. “The DRI document talks about what’s going to be built there,” Savage-Dunam said. “We also have the comprehensive plan. As staff testified, this rezoning was found to be consistent with the comprehensive plan, [which] follows the DRI. Those are the road maps that guide development in that section of the city. So, you would be looking at the totality of what the applicant submitted showing their intended uses there and how that aligns with the comp plan and the DRI.” Vice-Mayor Caraballo then chimed back in with her own perspective. “If you’re confused, I understand,” she said. “It’s not our process – it’s the way it’s legally required by the state. It’s definitely not the simplest thing for anybody to understand.” After the applicant’s contracted Land Use Attorney Goldstein provided her own presentation, 10 nearby homeowners aired their complaints, beginning with Southwest River Rock Road resident Jim Riordan. “My property is located at the southern end of the proposed Riverland-West Sports Recreation Center,” he said. “I spoke at the July 7 Planning Board meeting, and the chairman encouraged me to meet with Ms. At that time, I gave her our primary concerns with the project. On Friday, she did contact me, but none of those concerns were addressed. What she did say was exactly what she said right now: This is not the time – the time is later – but we feel this is the time before we move forward.” Riordan pointed out that GL Homes had “1,300 other acres where they could build this complex.” “GL has already sold parcels in the new section advertising the fitness center,” he continued. “So, I guess it’s a done deal based on this picture and what they’re advertising. We purchased our property, as well as every citizen here, from The Grove with the understanding that this parcel will be a city park. Now they’re basically trying to make this something different.” Both Harriet Gallas and her husband Lawrence agreed. “We chose to move here for quality of life,” the former said. “When we bought our house, we were told there was going to be a park over the berm next to us. They’re [now] talking 72 pickleball courts, bocci courts, tennis courts, a dog park and RV park, and that’s going to destroy my quality of life. Noise pollution’s a real thing: It causes stress, and pickleball is loud, stabbing and sharp. I respectfully beg you to not pass this rezoning.” The other residents echoed similar fears, resulting in more staff explanations and Council debate until Mayor Shannon Martin asked Goldstein a pivotal question. “Has their been a public meeting with the neighbors with regard to this issue?” she asked. Riordan regarding the issue of the buffer,” Goldstein responded. That response gave Mayor Martin the impetus she needed. “Being that there are so many concerns from the residents, is GL willing to have a meeting with the residents in order to address the issues?” she prodded. Goldstein, however, resisted the delay at first. “This is a straight-forward rezoning,” she insisted. “We don’t have all those details yet for the site plan because that’s not this process. When we’re ready to get there and we have those details, we’d be more than happy to meet with everybody to discuss what’s planned.” That response brought a loud uproar of protest from the audience and a plea from the vice-mayor. “I would really appreciate very much if you’d be willing to just table this,” Caraballo said. “I’m sorry to slow it down, but even this part of the process I don’t think they comprehend.” The City Council then voted unanimously to table the request until the Aug. hero.teaser: A profanity-laced confrontation over campaign signs erupted overnight Friday between mayoral candidate Steve Giordano and the husband of incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin, prompting a police investigation.
hero.body:
Mayoral candidate Steve Giordano says he and his campaign manager were putting up signs in Port St. Lucie during the overnight hours on Friday, Aug. 7, when he saw a man take a sign out of the ground and throw it. Giordano grabbed his cell phone and began recording the incident. The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant in Port St. Lucie's Police Department. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and the other man, with both shouting at each other and making accusations about putting up signs in the community without property owners' permission.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department says it is actively investigating two separate reports involving political campaign signs that occurred this week in the city. Officers responded to the reported incidents, documented the scenes, collected available evidence, and began interviewing those involved. Detectives are reviewing physical evidence, speaking with witnesses, and verifying statements provided to investigators.

Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement that her campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of her campaign signs at different locations over several days. Signs were taken down without permission and replaced with Giordano's signs, Martin said. "In response, my husband simply restored the signs that had been removed," Martin said. "At no time were my opponent's signs stolen or damaged, one small sign was temporarily moved and put back in the ground." Martin and Giordano are running in the August election to determine who will hold the mayor's office.

cards.headline: Tradition Lakes K-8 opening delayed one week, leaving St. Lucie parents scrambling for child care
cards.body:
St. Lucie County's new Tradition Lakes K-8 school will not open on Monday, Aug. 10 as planned, pushing the start date back one week to Aug. 17 and leaving approximately 1,100 enrolled students and their families scrambling to arrange last-minute child care. St. Lucie Public Schools announced the delay on Thursday, just four days before the originally scheduled opening.

Superintendent Dr. Prince said he made the decision after personally inspecting the school site at 10701 SW Sundance Vista Boulevard in Port St. Lucie and consulting with teachers and staff. Prince said he did not want students to navigate what essentially remained a construction zone on their first day. "That's not the first impression that I wanted to make where you're kind of walking and you're kind of part of a construction zone and I just didn't think it was fair," Prince said. "After kind of seeing things for myself, I was really worried that when people rush they make mistakes and I just felt like it was in our best interest to take a pause."

Parents expressed frustration at the short notice. Asia Shouford, a working mother of four children, said the timing completely disrupted her carefully planned arrangements. "I was honestly annoyed, because school starts on Monday, it was Thursday when we got that call. You could have told us a week ago," Shouford said. "Working mom, four kids, I have two little ones at home. I already had everything planned to start on Monday and now I don't know what we're going to do." Parent Taylor Atkins said the delay put families in a tough situation with limited options on short notice. "It's hard because he can't go back to summer camp. It's closed it's another school, you know, they're going to be starting," Atkins said.

The school district said the one-week delay will not impact overall instructional time and the school's academic calendar will remain unchanged. To help working families manage the unexpected delay, the district is coordinating with the Boys and Girls Club and the YMCA to offer affordable child care options during the interim week. Open House is scheduled for Friday, Aug. 14, from 4:30 to 6:30 p.m., where families can meet teachers and tour the campus before the first day.

hero.headline: Costco in Stuart reopens after electrical fire, refrigeration still down
hero.body:
Costco at 3173 Kanner Highway in Stuart reopened Friday following an electrical fire that temporarily closed the store on Thursday. The Stuart Police Department says store management confirmed only dry goods are available for purchase because the refrigeration unit remains non-operational.

The Stuart Police Department reported the electrical fire has been extinguished. Shoppers and travelers were asked to avoid the area while the store was closed Thursday.

The store is now open but customers cannot purchase refrigerated or frozen items until the refrigeration system is restored. The Stuart Police Department shared the update from store management about the limited inventory.

The Costco location serves Stuart and surrounding Martin County communities. The electrical fire forced the temporary closure on Thursday before the store reopened with limited services Friday.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets fall 17-3 to Daytona as Tortugas score 11 unanswered runs at Clover Park
hero.body:
The Daytona Tortugas scored 11 unanswered runs over the final three innings Thursday to defeat the St. Lucie Mets 17-3 at Clover Park. The Mets cut the Daytona lead to 6-3 in the fifth inning with three doubles, including back-to-back RBI doubles by John Smith III and Julio Zayas. The Tortugas broke the game open in the seventh inning, taking advantage of six walks issued by Mets relievers Jean Brito and Luis Sotillo to score six runs and build a 12-3 lead.

Daytona added five more runs in the eighth inning off Zayas, who pitched the final two innings for the Mets after serving as the designated hitter. Zayas pitched a scoreless ninth inning and induced a double play. The Mets scored first on a RBI single by Reed Stallman in the second inning, but Tortugas starter Mason Morris escaped further damage with the bases loaded by starting a 1-2-3 double play off the broken bat of Kooper Schulte.

The Tortugas used that momentum to score five runs on five hits off Mets starter Jose Lopez in the third inning. Bernard Moon hit a two-run double in the inning, his Florida State League-leading 28th double. Lopez pitched 5.1 innings overall and gave up six runs on seven hits with one walk and six strikeouts. It was the longest outing by a Mets pitcher since the first game of the second half on June 19.

Elian Pea went 2 for 5 with a double, his third straight two-hit game. Smith III finished 2 for 4 with a double and RBI. The Mets, now 14-23 in the second half and 47-56 overall, continue their series against the Tortugas at Clover Park on Friday. All veterans and active duty military receive free admission courtesy of LYNQ Real Estate, and kids 14 and under can run the bases after the game.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on animal cruelty charge after video circulates on social media
hero.body:
Ricky Lee Schieferstein, 68, of Port St. Lucie was arrested on Aug. 6 on an animal cruelty charge following the circulation of a video on social media that appeared to show the abuse of a small dog. Schieferstein was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail as of Aug. 7 on a $7,500 bond, according to the jail website.

The investigation began after numerous members of the community shared the video and tagged the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office across its social media platforms, according to the sheriff's office Facebook posting. The information was then turned over to the sheriff's office criminal investigations division for investigation. Detective Dawn Dale developed probable cause through her investigation and obtained an arrest warrant to charge Schieferstein with animal cruelty.

In the 16-second video posted on the sheriff's office Facebook page with a viewer discretion warning, a man can be seen walking behind a dog at a concrete pool and yelling out, out, out ... in the grass several times and kicking the dog in its right hip at least once before the dog and the man went out of range.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office stated in its Facebook posting that it appreciates the public's assistance in bringing this incident to its attention. However, the sheriff's office also reminded residents that the fastest and most effective way to report a crime in progress or suspicious activity is by calling 911. While the sheriff's office actively monitors its social media platforms, they are not monitored continuously and should never be relied upon to report emergencies or crimes requiring an immediate law enforcement response.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Kings Landing development faces new delay as developer seeks $15 million to finish Marriott hotel
hero.teaser: Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on Fort Pierce's Kings Landing project, told city commissioners they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project.
hero.body:
The Kings Landing development in Fort Pierce is facing another delay as Live Oak Development, the secondary developer on the project, told city commissioners they are $15 million short of the $60 million needed to complete the Marriott hotel and restaurant portion of the project. City commissioners are divided on what to do next. Live Oak Development told commissioners the $15 million shortfall is due in part to rising construction costs. CEO Paul Bertozzi said the company has seen construction costs continue to balloon across multiple industries, and that is a portion of the cause of the delta being created.

City leaders said developers initially asked the city to cover the gap through a loan or grant. Commissioner Michael Broderick said that request was denied, and the city does not have $15 million. Live Oak Development is now asking for 180 days to find the money through private sources. Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun, and the company is looking at friends and families and investment and private equity versus institutional investors. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming, and would rather give developers the time they are asking for.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait and thinks it is time to cut bait and move on. Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished. Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area, and he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing, but the delays are wearing on him. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

Bertozzi told commissioners the outreach has already begun."We're already in the process of reaching out to participating parties,” said Bertozzi. "We're looking at friends and families and investment and private equity verses institutional investors."But commissioners are debating about the city reclaiming the property. Broderick said he believes trying to reclaim the property through legal action would be expensive and time-consuming."Clawing the property back through reverter clauses is going to be litigation for years and a ton of money,” said Broderick.He said he would rather give developers the time they are asking for."What are we going to lose by 180 days? That's the question I would ask,” said Broderick. “What are we going to lose? It's just time."Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not want to wait."I think it's time to as they say, cut bait and move on," he said.Jon Nolli, owner of Funky Cuda in Fort Pierce, said he has been waiting on the development and is ready for it to be finished."It's been taking some time,” said Nolli.Nolli said the completed project would benefit the surrounding area. He said he even has plans to open businesses inside Kings Landing — but the delays are wearing on him."I've got a couple deposits on the commercial side. I was looking to a beer garden, and a deli, and I mean it's taking so long that I don't even know the trends have changed,” said NolliWPTV reached out to Live Oak Development and still working on a response. The city commission has scheduled a special meeting on September 14 to discuss next steps.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police investigate death of 77-year-old man found in pond near his home
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day. At approximately 1:18 p.m. Friday, officers responded to a residence on the 1400 block of SW Mockingbird Drive regarding a missing adult. Kramer was last seen by his wife inside their home at approximately 10 p.m. Thursday. The following morning, Kramer was no longer inside the residence. Kramer's personal belongings, including his shoes, wallet, and cellphone, were still inside the home.

Kramer's wife searched for him and contacted local hospitals before reporting him missing to law enforcement at approximately 1:18 p.m. Officers began searching the neighborhood and, during the canvass, located an unresponsive person in a pond directly across the street from Kramer's residence at approximately 2 p.m. The individual and clothing matched Kramer's description. Port St. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water near the shoreline of the pond, where he was confirmed deceased. The circumstances surrounding Kramer's death remain under investigation. Police said there are no known indications of foul play at this preliminary stage of the investigation.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police investigate two separate campaign sign incidents involving Mayor Martin's husband
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police Department released an update Friday on two separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard. The first incident occurred August 5 near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue, where a Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard. Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.

The second incident occurred August 7 near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs. During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence. Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence. The confrontation occurred after Giordano says he saw a man take a sign out of the ground and throw it, according to CBS12 News. The man in the video appears to be Aaron Martin, Shannon Martin's husband and a lieutenant in Port St. Lucie's Police Department.

Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign. Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced. The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department. The department said the fact that Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process, and the investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy. The department said that should the investigation identify any potential policy violations involving a department employee, the matter will be handled in accordance with established department procedures. Any related administrative review will proceed following the completion of the ongoing criminal investigation. Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement that her campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of her campaign signs at different locations over several days, and that her husband simply restored the signs that had been removed.

cards.headline: Road rage confrontation leads to four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 in Port St. Lucie, one arrested
cards.teaser: A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Lucie man arrested.
cards.body:
A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Lucie man arrested. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road rage incident. Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Lucie Police Department said the two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, based on dash camera and witness statements collected.

Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Lucie Medical Center.

Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition. Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The investigative findings indicate that the pickup truck was actively pursuing that motorcyclist just moments prior to that crash, McNally said. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after video shows him kicking small dog
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man was arrested following an investigation into a social media video that shows a man abusing a small dog.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested following an investigation into a social media video that shows a man abusing a small dog, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Video from the sheriff's office shows Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, appearing to kick a small dog in his backyard near a pool. The video made rounds on social media, and the outrage sparked an investigation from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

Following the investigation, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office's findings gave detectives probable cause to charge Shieferstein with animal cruelty. The sheriff's office says that Shieferstein is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $7,500 bond.
