cards.headline: Fort Pierce fraud investigation leads to search warrant at home of Southern Truss bookkeeper
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies executed a search warrant at the Fort Pierce home of Laura Beth Grasso, the bookkeeper and comptroller accused of defrauding Southern Truss Companies of nearly $7 million.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at the Fort Pierce home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box.
cards.article_text: A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Martin County residents lose over $1,200 to fake Pokémon card scam
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning residents after two people lost more than $1,200 combined while buying counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning residents after two people lost more than $1,200 combined while buying counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic. Deputies said the reports were made within the past few weeks. While Pokémon cards are often seen as collectibles, some rare cards can be worth hundreds or even thousands of dollars, making them a target for scammers and counterfeiters.

The sheriff's office said fake cards are being sold through online marketplaces, social media and other online sales platforms across the country. Officials encourage buyers to do their research before making a purchase and to be wary of deals that seem too good to be true. They also recommend checking a seller's reputation and having high-value cards authenticated by a reputable expert before handing over money. When buying cards in person, deputies advise taking time to inspect the items carefully and verify they are authentic.

The sheriff's office noted that recovering money can be difficult once a counterfeit item has been purchased. For added safety, the agency recommends meeting in one of its designated exchange parking spaces, which are monitored by cameras around the clock.

hero.headline: Early voting begins Saturday in Indian River County for August primary election
hero.body:
Early voting for Florida's August primary election begins Saturday in Indian River County and continues through Aug. 16. Voters can find a complete list of early voting locations and additional information by visiting voteindianriver.com.

The early voting period is also underway in neighboring counties across the Treasure Coast region. In Martin County, early voting runs Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16, with locations and additional information available at martinvotes.gov. St. Lucie County offers the same early voting schedule, running from Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16, with details available at stlucievotes.gov.

Palm Beach County is providing early voting during the same timeframe, from Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16. Voters in Palm Beach County can access a full list of early voting locations by visiting votepalmbeach.gov. Okeechobee County is also offering early voting from Saturday, Aug. 8 through Aug. 16, though specific hours were not immediately available. Voters seeking more information about Okeechobee County early voting can visit voteokeechobee.gov.

The early voting period gives voters across the region an opportunity to cast their ballots ahead of the primary election day. By offering multiple days and locations for early voting, election officials aim to provide flexibility for voters who may be unable to visit polling places on election day itself. Voters are encouraged to check their respective county election websites for the most current information about early voting locations, hours, and any requirements for casting ballots during the early voting period.

hero.headline: U.S. 1 closed in both directions near Tiffany Avenue in Port St. Lucie after crash
hero.body:
A traffic crash closed U.S. Highway 1 in both directions near Southeast Tiffany Avenue in Port St. Lucie on Thursday morning. The Port St. Lucie Police Department directed northbound U.S. 1 traffic to exit at Port St. Lucie Boulevard, while southbound U.S. 1 traffic was rerouted to Veterans Memorial Parkway.

The department asked travelers to avoid the area and use alternate routes while officers and emergency personnel worked at the scene. Police did not release information about injuries in the crash.

The closure affected one of the major north-south corridors through Port St. Lucie during morning hours. Emergency responders remained on scene Thursday morning to investigate and clear the roadway.

Police did not provide an estimated time for reopening the highway. Motorists traveling through Port St. Lucie were advised to plan for delays and consider alternative routes.

cards.teaser: Friends, family and strangers are raising money for 30-year-old Ralphy Varela, a Palm Beach County firefighter-paramedic whose mother was killed by his father in a Port St. Lucie murder-suicide over the weekend.
cards.body:
An online fundraiser for 30-year-old Ralphy Varela has raised thousands of dollars after he lost both parents in a murder-suicide at a Port St. Lucie home over the weekend. The fundraiser has been widely shared across social media, along with a photo of Varela and his mother, Elizabeth Ortega.

Ortega, a longtime Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office communications officer, was killed Saturday at her home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace, according to Port St. Lucie police. Investigators say her longtime partner, Ralph Varela Sr., shot her before taking his own life. Detectives say the couple had recently ended their long-term relationship but continued living together while other arrangements were being made. Police said the couple's adult son had left the home shortly before the shooting occurred.

The fundraiser was created by Jorge Uricoechea to support Ralphy Varela, who serves as a firefighter-paramedic with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. One lifelong friend described Ortega simply as very loved. Supporters say the fundraiser is a way to honor Ortega's memory while helping her son rebuild in the days and weeks ahead.
cards.article_text: Friends, family members, and strangers across South Florida are coming together to support a Palm Beach County firefighter-paramedic who lost both of his parents in a tragic murder-suicide over the weekend. An online fundraiser for 30-year-old Ralphy Varela has already raised thousands of dollars as supporters work to help him navigate the unimaginable loss. The fundraiser has been widely shared across social media, along with a photo of Varela and his mother, Elizabeth "Liz" Ortega. Ortega, a longtime Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office communications officer, spent years helping callers through emergencies and crises. Colleagues and friends say she was deeply respected and loved by those who knew her. Related article: Newly released 911 call reveals frantic moments after Port St. Lucie murder-suicide According to Port St. Lucie police, Ortega was killed Saturday at her home. Investigators say her longtime partner, Ralph Varela Sr., shot her before taking his own life. Detectives say the couple had recently ended their long-term relationship but continued living together while other arrangements were being made. Police said the couple's adult son had left the home shortly before the shooting occurred. Neighbors called 911 after hearing gunfire. As the investigation continues, much of the community's focus has shifted to supporting Ralphy Varela, who serves as a firefighter-paramedic with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. One lifelong friend described Ortega simply as "very loved." Supporters say the fundraiser , created by Jorge Uricoechea, is a way to honor Ortega's memory while helping her son rebuild in the days and weeks ahead.

cards.headline: 12-year-old describes hit-and-run that injured sister in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Malachi Jenkins, 12, was with his 8-year-old sister Serenity when she was struck by a driver who fled the scene at North 25th Street and Avenue M in Fort Pierce over the weekend.
cards.body:
Malachi Jenkins, 12, said he was mad when a driver struck his 8-year-old sister Serenity and then drove off at the intersection of North 25th Street and Avenue M in Fort Pierce over the weekend. Malachi described the moments after the crash, saying Serenity was on the ground with her legs bent in different directions. People ran up to check on her, and she started crying before briefly losing consciousness and then waking back up.

Malachi said the driver initially offered to take them home but fled the scene when others approached. When he saw the other people coming and looked at Serenity, he just drove off fast, Malachi said. Police confirmed that Serenity sustained a fractured femur in the crash.

Fort Pierce police believe the driver is a man between the ages of 20 and 30 years old, driving an early 2000s gold Mercedes-Benz that may have damage to the driver's side. Detectives are reviewing surveillance footage from nearby businesses to gather more information about the incident. Anyone with information is urged to contact Fort Pierce detectives.
cards.article_text: Police in Fort Pierce are investigating a hit-and-run that injured 8-year-old Serenity Jenkins over the weekend at the intersection of North 25th Street and Avenue M. Detectives are reviewing surveillance footage from nearby businesses to gather more information about the incident. "I just think it's sad overall because it's a little girl. I mean, you have to have some type of humanity not to just drive away and not make sure she's OK; that's somebody's child," said a woman who works near the intersection where the crash occurred. Serenity’s 12-year-old brother, Malachi Jenkins, said he was with her when the crash happened. "I was mad," Malachi said. He described the moments after the crash, saying, "She was on the ground, and her legs were like this, one like that, and that's when people ran up and were checking on her, and that's when she started crying, and then she dozed off for a little bit and then woke back up." Malachi said the driver initially offered to take them home but fled the scene when others approached. "But then when he saw the other people coming and looked at Serenity, he just drove off fast," Malachi said. Police confirmed that Serenity sustained a fractured femur in the crash and are continuing their investigation. "We have now an individual out in our community that has not been held accountable for this as of yet," police said. Authorities believe the driver is a man between the ages of 20 and 30 years old, driving an early 2000s gold Mercedes-Benz that may have damage to the driver’s side. "I can tell you that the police department is actively working this case. We have different disciplines within the police department looking into this to ensure that we get this person and hold this person accountable for what actually occurred that day," police said. Anyone with information is urged to contact Fort Pierce detectives. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

hero.headline: Flood Advisory issued for western Martin County through 7:30 p.m. Thursday
hero.body:
A Flood Advisory remains in effect until 7:30 p.m. Thursday for western Martin County. Radar estimates indicate anywhere from 1 to 3 inches of rain have already fallen across the area.

An additional 1 to 2 inches of rainfall is expected before the advisory expires. The National Weather Service issued the alert as heavy rain continues to move through the western portion of the county.

A Flood Advisory means that flooding is occurring or is imminent in low-lying and poor drainage areas. Motorists should avoid driving through standing water and should be prepared for potential road closures.

Residents in western Martin County should monitor weather conditions and be alert for rapidly rising water in streams, creeks, and roadways. The advisory was issued early Thursday morning and covers areas away from the coastal communities.

cards.headline: Martin County sheriff warns of counterfeit Pokémon card sales after $1,200 in losses
cards.teaser: Two Martin County residents lost more than $1,200 after purchasing counterfeit Pokémon trading cards in recent weeks, according to the sheriff's office.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning collectors to watch for counterfeit Pokémon trading cards after two local residents reported losing more than $1,200 in recent purchases. The reports were filed within the past few weeks. In both cases, the buyers believed they were purchasing authentic Pokémon cards but later learned the cards were not legitimate.

Rare cards can sell for hundreds or even thousands of dollars, making them a target for counterfeiters and online scammers. Fraudulent cards may be offered through online marketplaces, social media pages, and other sales platforms. The sheriff's office cautioned buyers not to assume an item is authentic simply because it appears legitimate or is listed on a well-known website.

Before making a purchase, buyers should research the card's typical value and investigate the seller's reputation. For expensive cards, authorities recommend having the item examined by a reputable trading card expert or professional authentication service before payment is made. Residents conducting in-person transactions may use the designated exchange parking spaces at the Martin County Sheriff's Office, which are monitored by cameras 24 hours a day.
cards.article_text: The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is warning collectors to watch for counterfeit Pokémon trading cards after two local residents reported losing more than $1,200 in recent purchases. The reports were filed within the past few weeks, according to the sheriff’s office. In both cases, the buyers believed they were purchasing authentic Pokémon cards but later learned the cards were not legitimate. Although Pokémon cards are often viewed as children’s collectibles, rare cards can sell for hundreds or even thousands of dollars. Their potential value has made them a target for counterfeiters and online scammers, authorities said. Fraudulent cards may be offered through online marketplaces, social media pages and other sales platforms. The sheriff’s office cautioned buyers not to assume an item is authentic simply because it appears legitimate or is listed on a well-known website. Before making a purchase, buyers should research the card’s typical value and investigate the seller’s reputation. Deals priced far below market value should be treated with caution. For expensive cards, authorities recommend having the item examined by a reputable trading-card expert or professional authentication service before payment is made. Buyers meeting sellers in person should also take time to inspect the cards carefully. See also: Police release photo of toy kitchen involved in Boynton toddler's death; family IDs girl The sheriff’s office noted that recovering money can be difficult once a transaction is complete, particularly when the item is later found to be counterfeit. Residents conducting in-person transactions may also use the designated exchange parking spaces at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The spaces are monitored by cameras 24 hours a day.

cards.headline: North Carolina family chased off road near I-95 in Martin County describes attack
cards.teaser: A North Carolina family visiting Florida with their young son was forced off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95 in Martin County over the weekend.
cards.body:
Body camera footage shows a North Carolina couple and their young son walking out of the bushes and explaining to a Martin County sheriff's deputy what happened after being chased off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95, over the weekend. The family appeared visibly shaken as they recounted the incident.

The couple said the suspect chased the man's sister for miles, prompting the wife to call 911. The man explained that he and his wife tried to intervene, but the driver then turned his focus on them. After pulling over, the man said the driver came back. The driver continued to follow the couple, eventually forcing them off the road. The man's sister managed to escape.

The driver, identified as Michael Spires, was taken into custody at a nearby gas station. Sheriff John Budensiek said the family did not know what was coming next and were extremely grateful that they did not get injured. Budensiek added that the suspect did not have a gun and that it could have ended much worse.
cards.article_text: Body camera footage shows a North Carolina family walking out of the bushes and explaining what happened after being chased off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95 in Martin County over the weekend. The couple, visiting Florida with their young son, appeared visibly shaken as they recounted the incident to a sheriff's deputy, explaining what happened to them and the man's sister, who was driving ahead of them. "He was trying to run her off the road," the man said, referring to his sister. Were you guys traveling together? Okay," the deputy responded. The family said the suspect, seen in the body camera footage, chased the man's sister for miles, prompting his wife to call 911. "The lady that he's chasing, she has a little baby in her car," the wife said. "He's literally chasing her with his lasers on. She's trying to get away from him. She said he's pressing brakes, trying to get away, and he said he's chasing her." The man explained that he and his wife tried to intervene, but the unknown driver then turned his focus on them. "You all pulled over?" the deputy asked. "Yeah, we all pulled over essentially because he stopped us again. So, I figured if we let him go far enough ahead, maybe we'll keep going. He got out, and he came back," the man said. The man's sister managed to escape, but the driver continued to follow him and his wife, eventually forcing them off the road. "And he's chasing you in the car?" the deputy asked. He evasive maneuver just off the road. He pit you," the man said. The driver, identified as Michael Spires, was taken into custody at a nearby gas station. "They did not know what was coming next, so they are extremely grateful that they didn't get injured and that it wasn't worse," Sheriff John Budensiek said. "Thank goodness our suspect didn't have a gun. It could have ended so much worse." hero.headline: Early voting begins Saturday across Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River counties for August primary
hero.teaser: Early voting for Florida's August primary election begins Saturday across the Treasure Coast, with locations opening in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.
hero.body:
Early voting for Florida's August primary election begins Saturday, August 9, and runs through Sunday, August 17, across the Treasure Coast region and surrounding counties. Voters in multiple counties will have the opportunity to cast their ballots ahead of the primary election day.

In Indian River County, early voting runs Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Voters can find a complete list of early voting locations and additional information at voteindianriver.com.

In Martin County, early voting runs Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Voters can find locations and additional information at martinvotes.gov. In St. Lucie County, early voting runs Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Voters can find locations and additional information at stlucievotes.gov.

Early voting is also available in Palm Beach County and Okeechobee County during the same period, running Saturday, August 9 through Sunday, August 17. Palm Beach County voters can visit votepalmbeach.gov for a full list of early voting locations. Okeechobee County voters can find more information at voteokeechobee.gov, though hours were not immediately available at the time of publication.

hero.headline: Fourth arrest made in death of 3-month-old in Fort Pierce, father charged
hero.teaser: The biological father of a 3-month-old who died from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce was arrested in Virginia on Tuesday, becoming the fourth person charged in the case.
hero.body: Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested by the U.S. Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia on Tuesday on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter, the biological father of the infant, was charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child's death. He is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County. The arrest marks the fourth made in the case. The child's mother, Nicole Marie Maxwell, 27, the child's grandfather, Robert Arthur Maxwell, 61, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, Vikki Nicole Koon, 38, are each charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. All three are being held in the St. Lucie County Jail on $1.5 million bond each. The investigation began on August 20, 2025, when deputies responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce after the 3-month-old child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandfather. The infant was pronounced dead on arrival. The boy died of dehydration and malnutrition in a mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce. Four other children in the home, ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old, were placed in foster care through the state Department of Children and Families.

cards.headline: Infant's father was warned baby was starving, records show in Fort Pierce malnutrition death
cards.teaser: Text messages recovered in the investigation showed family members repeatedly warned both parents of the 3-month-old that something was wrong with the child before his death in Fort Pierce.
cards.body: Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested Tuesday in Virginia on charges of felony child neglect causing great harm in connection with the death of his 3-month-old son in Fort Pierce. According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong with the infant. On August 12, 2025, messages sent to the child's mother, Nicole Maxwell, stated the baby had nothing to eat. Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Gunter was arrested at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia by the U.S. Marshals Service. An autopsy revealed the infant weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The Medical Examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide.
cards.article_text: A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old baby who allegedly died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Detectives had obtained an arrest warrant for Gunter in connection with the ongoing investigation into the child's death. He has been charged with felony child neglect causing great harm and is awaiting extradition to St. The arrest comes after three others were previously charged in the case: the child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell; the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell; and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon. See also: Body found in ocean off Boca Raton coast, investigation underway All three were charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. Investigation Began After Baby Was Brought to Hospital The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when Koon and Robert Maxwell brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs that the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed. Detectives assigned to the case conducted interviews with family members at the hospital before serving search warrants and beginning what would become a months-long investigation. Caregivers Allegedly Noticed Warning Signs According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, the infant had been primarily living with Koon and Robert Maxwell after Gunter moved to Virginia. During interviews, detectives learned caregivers had noticed numerous warning signs in the days leading up to the child's death. Investigators say Koon admitted the baby was often fed only a few times a day and claimed he sometimes drank as little as two bottles daily. She told detectives she noticed the child was becoming increasingly thin, pale and lethargic. She also described frequent vomiting, excessive sleeping and a decrease in wet diapers. Despite those concerns, detectives say no one sought emergency medical treatment. Text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong. 12, 2025, messages sent to Nicole Maxwell stated, "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Search Warrant Revealed Conditions Inside Home When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an "extreme environmental hazard." The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Autopsy Findings Led to Homicide Ruling An autopsy later revealed the extent of the infant's condition. According to the Medical Examiner's Office, Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The autopsy found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Examiners also documented numerous lesions and insect bites across the infant's body. The Medical Examiner ultimately determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide, writing that the infant was dependent on caregivers for nutrition and hydration and that the failure to provide those necessities directly caused his death. Father's Role Under Scrutiny Investigators say Gunter was aware of concerns about the child's condition. The criminal complaint states that messages sent to Gunter warned that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. Detectives also recovered messages discussing food shortages and concerns the infant was not being properly cared for. Despite those warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services. A separate text message recovered from his phone stated: "The baby is starving." Detectives included that message among evidence supporting criminal charges. Sheriff's officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the court system. Meanwhile, two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

cards.headline: Martin County residents lose over $1,200 buying fake Pokémon cards
cards.teaser: Two Martin County residents lost more than $1,200 combined after purchasing counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic, prompting a warning from the sheriff's office.
cards.body: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning residents after two people lost more than $1,200 combined while buying counterfeit Pokémon trading cards they believed were authentic. Deputies said the reports were made within the past few weeks. While Pokémon cards are often seen as collectibles, some rare cards can be worth hundreds or even thousands of dollars, making them a target for scammers and counterfeiters. The sheriff's office said fake cards are being sold through online marketplaces, social media and other online sales platforms across the country. Officials encourage buyers to do their research before making a purchase and to be wary of deals that seem too good to be true. They also recommend checking a seller's reputation and having high-value cards authenticated by a reputable expert before handing over money. When buying cards in person, deputies advise taking time to inspect the items carefully and verify they are authentic. For added safety, the agency recommends meeting in one of its designated exchange parking spaces, which are monitored by cameras around the clock.

cards.headline: Search warrant reveals $8,500 cash, gun found in vehicle tied to Southern Truss fraud suspect
cards.teaser: Deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, jewelry, designer items and a loaded pistol during a search of a vehicle connected to Laura Grasso, according to court records.
cards.body: Deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box during a search of a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Laura Grasso, according to an inventory filed with the court. A judge signed the warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search the vehicle that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after Grasso's arrest on July 16. Grasso is charged with first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity and money laundering of $100,000 or more in connection with an alleged fraud scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. A forensic audit later recovered a secret ledger on Grasso's computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone.
cards.article_text: A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce home showed extreme infestation, mold in infant malnutrition death case
cards.teaser: When investigators searched the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the 3-month-old had been staying, they documented what they described as an extreme environmental hazard.
cards.body: When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce where the 3-month-old had been staying, they documented what they described as an extreme environmental hazard. The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Four other children in the home, ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old, were placed in foster care through the state Department of Children and Families. Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of the infant, was arrested Tuesday in Virginia on charges of felony child neglect causing great harm. The child's mother, Nicole Marie Maxwell, 27, the child's grandfather, Robert Arthur Maxwell, 61, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, Vikki Nicole Koon, 38, are each charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse.
cards.article_text: A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old baby who allegedly died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Detectives had obtained an arrest warrant for Gunter in connection with the ongoing investigation into the child's death. He has been charged with felony child neglect causing great harm and is awaiting extradition to St. The arrest comes after three others were previously charged in the case: the child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell; the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell; and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon. See also: Body found in ocean off Boca Raton coast, investigation underway All three were charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. Investigation Began After Baby Was Brought to Hospital The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when Koon and Robert Maxwell brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs that the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed. Detectives assigned to the case conducted interviews with family members at the hospital before serving search warrants and beginning what would become a months-long investigation. Caregivers Allegedly Noticed Warning Signs According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, the infant had been primarily living with Koon and Robert Maxwell after Gunter moved to Virginia. During interviews, detectives learned caregivers had noticed numerous warning signs in the days leading up to the child's death. Investigators say Koon admitted the baby was often fed only a few times a day and claimed he sometimes drank as little as two bottles daily. She told detectives she noticed the child was becoming increasingly thin, pale and lethargic. She also described frequent vomiting, excessive sleeping and a decrease in wet diapers. Despite those concerns, detectives say no one sought emergency medical treatment. Text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong. 12, 2025, messages sent to Nicole Maxwell stated, "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Search Warrant Revealed Conditions Inside Home When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an "extreme environmental hazard." The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Autopsy Findings Led to Homicide Ruling An autopsy later revealed the extent of the infant's condition. According to the Medical Examiner's Office, Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The autopsy found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Examiners also documented numerous lesions and insect bites across the infant's body. The Medical Examiner ultimately determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide, writing that the infant was dependent on caregivers for nutrition and hydration and that the failure to provide those necessities directly caused his death. Father's Role Under Scrutiny Investigators say Gunter was aware of concerns about the child's condition. The criminal complaint states that messages sent to Gunter warned that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. Detectives also recovered messages discussing food shortages and concerns the infant was not being properly cared for. Despite those warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services. A separate text message recovered from his phone stated: "The baby is starving." Detectives included that message among evidence supporting criminal charges. Sheriff's officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the court system. Meanwhile, two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

hero.headline: Vero Beach moves forward on $4.7 million Humiston Beach boardwalk reconstruction four years after Hurricane Nicole
hero.body:
Vero Beach has established a five-person committee to help rebuild the boardwalk at Humiston Beach, which Hurricane Nicole destroyed four years ago. The city currently has $3.1 million raised toward the $4.7 million project cost, leaving a $1.6 million funding gap that the new committee will work to close through donor outreach and fundraising.

Vero Beach Councilmember John Carroll said beach use has dropped significantly since the boardwalk's destruction. The committee will develop a fundraising plan and ensure appropriate recognition for donors who have already contributed to the project. The city plans to accept project bids next week.

Residents including Calista Littleton said they have been waiting to restore normal beach access at the site. Doris DeAngelis said her aunt, who uses a walker, now has only a small area to enjoy the beach due to limited access without the boardwalk.

If the timeline holds, the city hopes to begin construction in November and complete a new boardwalk by April. DeAngelis said her aunt Mina, who will turn 105 and a half years old, would love to see the boardwalk return.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police release 911 call from domestic shooting that killed PBSO communications officer
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police released the 911 call from Saturday night when Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office communications officer, was shot and killed outside her home on the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace. Ralph Varela Sr., 50, shot Ortega before taking his own life inside the residence.

In the 911 call, a neighbor reported hearing five or six gunshots loud enough to rattle her house. The neighbor told the dispatcher she and her children were in the backyard when they heard the shots and that her 4-year-old child spotted Ortega lying motionless in the front yard. The caller said she did not go outside because she was frightened, and told police that Ortega and her husband were frequently heard arguing. "Her and her husband are always fighting," the caller said. "They're always cursing at each other. They're always leaving, always yelling, always speeding off down the street."

Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she later died. Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.

The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Port St. Lucie police extended their condolences to Ortega's family and encouraged anyone experiencing domestic violence to ask for help.

cards.headline: State lawmaker challenges Causeway Cove development's Live Local Act compliance in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: State Rep. Dana Trabulsy is challenging whether the Causeway Cove development in Fort Pierce properly complies with Florida's Live Local Act, raising questions about the massive waterfront project that would bring nearly 1,000 residential units and a 17-story hotel to the city's marina district.
cards.body:
Trabulsy told Fort Pierce city commissioners Monday that the proposed development does not meet the zoning requirements of the Live Local Act. The Causeway Cove project would transform the existing Causeway Cove Marina into a mixed-use development featuring more than 900 apartments and condos, restaurants, and a hotel tower reaching nearly 200 feet in height. The development has relied on the Live Local Act to override local zoning restrictions.

Trabusy argues the project fails to comply with the law's specific zoning requirements. The Live Local Act permits developers to exceed local height and density limits only in commercial and mixed-use zones, provided they dedicate 40 percent of residential units to affordable housing for at least 30 years. According to Trabulsy, a mapping error incorrectly designated portions of the Causeway Cove site as commercial zoning when they should be classified as aquatic development. The aquatic development zoning classification would prevent the project from utilizing Live Local Act provisions, potentially forcing developers to comply with Fort Pierce's original height and density restrictions.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick questioned whether such a significant zoning issue would have escaped state oversight during the approval process. When Trabulsy urged commissioners to rescind the project's approval and pursue legal action, Broderick expressed skepticism about the city's chances of success in court.

Dana Trabulsy told Fort Pierce city commissioners Monday that the proposed development doesn't meet the zoning requirements of the Live Local Act — the same law she supported in 2023 that allows developers to bypass local height and density restrictions.The Causeway Cove project would transform the existing Causeway Cove Marina into a mixed-use development featuring more than 900 apartments and condos, restaurants, and a hotel tower reaching nearly 200 feet in height. The development has relied on the Live Local Act to override local zoning restrictions.Trabulsy argues the project fails to comply with the law's specific zoning requirements. The Live Local Act permits developers to exceed local height and density limits only in commercial and mixed-use zones, provided they dedicate 40% of residential units to affordable housing for at least 30 years."I feel upon review the City of Fort Pierce land development regulations comprehensive plan and applicability of SB-102 Live Local Act, the Causeway Cove is not in compliance," Trabulsy said during Monday's commission meeting.According to Trabulsy, a mapping error incorrectly designated portions of the Causeway Cove site as commercial zoning when they should be classified as aquatic development. This distinction could prove crucial for the project's legal standing."The aquatic area or submerged lands within the site are in the A2 Aquatic Development Zoning District and therefore, not covered by Live Local Act," Trabulsy explained to commissioners.The aquatic development zoning classification would prevent the project from utilizing Live Local Act provisions, potentially forcing developers to comply with Fort Pierce's original height and density restrictions.WATCH WPTV'S PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Massive redevelopment in Fort Pierce could change the skyline and coastlineFort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick questioned whether such a significant zoning issue would have escaped state oversight during the approval process."I believe that if the zoning wasn't compliant, that the state people that were handling this would have caught on to that," Broderick said.When Trabulsy urged commissioners to rescind the project's approval and pursue legal action, Broderick expressed skepticism about the city's chances of success in court."I do not see the angle of attack that's not going to cost the city hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions of dollars, to fight this fight with what chance of prevailing?" Broderick said.The development has drawn opposition from residents who frequent the marina area. Mike Macy, who works on his uncle's boat at the marina, said the area feels like family property after four years of regular visits."This whole area has always been a part of the family," Macy said. "Instead of coming over here and walking on the docks and going fishing, we got to stare at big buildings."WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Ground broken on King's Landing project after years of delaysMacy expressed concerns about how the high-rise development would change the character of the waterfront area where he brings his children for recreational activities.The controversy adds another layer of complexity to a project that has already faced community resistance over its scale and impact on Fort Pierce's historic marina district.WPTV has reached out to Trabulsy for additional comment and is awaiting a response.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.Read more of WPTV's coverage below:
cards.source_summary: A state lawmaker is challenging whether the controversial Causeway Cove development in Fort Pierce properly complies with Florida's Live Local Act, raising new questions about the massive waterfront project that would bring nearly 1,000 residential units and a 17-story hotel to the city's marina district. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: Causeway Cove development faces legal challenge in Fort Pierce Fort Pierce development dispute: Live Local Act challenge State Rep. Dana Trabulsy told Fort Pierce city commissioners Monday that the proposed development doesn't meet the zoning requirements of the Live Local Act the same law she supported in 2023 that allows developers to bypass local height and density restrictions. Zoning Dispute Centers on Aquatic Development Areas The Causeway Cove project would transform the existing Causeway Cove Marina into a mixed-use development featuring more than 900 apartments and condos, restaurants, and a hotel tower reaching nearly 200 feet in height. The development has relied on the Live Local Act to override local zoning restrictions. Trabulsy argues the project fails to comply with the law's specific zoning requirements. The Live Local Act permits developers to exceed local height and density limits only in commercial and mixed-use zones, provided they dedicate 40% of residential units to affordable housing for at least 30 years. 'I feel upon review the City of Fort Pierce land development regulations comprehensive plan and applicability of SB-102 Live Local Act, the Causeway Cove is not in compliance,' Trabulsy said during Monday's commission meeting. Mapping Error May Invalidate Project's Legal Foundation According to Trabulsy, a mapping error incorrectly designated portions of the Causeway Cove site as commercial zoning when they should be classified as aquatic development. This distinction could prove crucial for the project's legal standing. 'The aquatic area or submerged lands within the site are in the A2 Aquatic Development Zoning District and therefore, not covered by Live Local Act,' Trabulsy explained to commissioners. The aquatic development zoning classification would prevent the project from utilizing Live Local Act provisions, potentially forcing developers to comply with Fort Pierce's original height and density restrictions. hero.headline: Martin County investigators warn of counterfeit Pokémon card scams after collectors lose $1,200
hero.teaser: Two Martin County collectors lost a combined $1,200 in separate fraud cases involving fake Pokémon cards sold through Facebook Marketplace.
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is investigating two separate cases involving counterfeit Pokémon cards after victims reported losing a combined $1,200 in deals arranged through Facebook Marketplace. In the first case, a collector met a seller at a gas station in Hobe Sound to trade nine Pokémon cards and cash. Investigators said the seller rushed through the transaction and left before the cards could be inspected. Once home, the victim realized the cards were counterfeit, and the seller blocked him online.

Ten days later, another collector reported a similar experience in Stuart. That victim traded collectible Pokémon card boxes and sent money through Zelle in exchange for two cards that were later determined to be fake.

Patrick Sutherland, who organizes Peetry's Card Show from the Treasure Coast to South Florida, said authentic cards often have specific textures, coloring and holographic features that can be difficult to counterfeit. He urged buyers to slow down and inspect items before completing a deal, warning that rushed transactions can be costly. Sutherland said the safest place to buy, sell, or trade collectibles is at a card show, where experienced collectors and vendors can help spot counterfeits. Martin County deputies said they are still working to identify the suspects in both fraud cases.

cards.headline: North Carolina family tells deputies of road rage attack that forced them off Martin County road
cards.teaser: Body camera footage shows a North Carolina family describing how they were chased off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95 in Martin County.
cards.body:
Body camera footage shows a North Carolina family walking out of the bushes and explaining what happened after being chased off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95 in Martin County over the weekend. The couple, visiting Florida with their young son, appeared visibly shaken as they recounted the incident to a sheriff's deputy. The family said the suspect chased the man's sister for miles, prompting his wife to call 911. The man's wife told the dispatcher the driver was chasing the woman, who had a baby in her car, with his lasers on.

The man explained that he and his wife tried to intervene, but the unknown driver then turned his focus on them. The man said they pulled over to let the driver go ahead, but he got out and came back. The man's sister managed to escape, but the driver continued to follow him and his wife, eventually forcing them off the road. The deputy asked if the driver chased them in the car, and the man confirmed he performed an evasive maneuver just off the road, describing it as a pit maneuver.

The driver, identified as Michael Spires, was taken into custody at a nearby gas station. Sheriff John Budensiek said the family did not know what was coming next and are extremely grateful they did not get injured. Budensiek noted that the suspect did not have a gun and that it could have ended much worse.

cards.headline: Stuart man arrested after using PIT maneuver to force North Carolina family's SUV into barbed-wire fence
cards.teaser: Michael Jeffrey Spiers, 36, faces charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse after a road rage attack that began on I-95 and passed through Stuart.
cards.body:
A Florida man is behind bars after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and, at one point, passed through Stuart. The crash happened around 7:30 p.m. on Saturday near Kanner Highway and I-95. Investigators identified the suspect as 36-year-old Michael Jeffrey Spiers, who is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Deputies say the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted.

According to investigators, Spiers first went after a woman who was driving alone, chasing her through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Authorities say Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. The woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95.

The impact of the PIT maneuver sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Despite the violent crash, no one was injured, including a child who was inside the family's vehicle. Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has since been reunited with its owner.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office warns residents after two collectors lose over $1,200 in counterfeit Pokémon card purchases
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning collectors to watch for counterfeit Pokémon trading cards after two local residents reported losing more than $1,200 in recent purchases.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is warning collectors to watch for counterfeit Pokémon trading cards after two local residents reported losing more than $1,200 in recent purchases. The reports were filed within the past few weeks. In both cases, the buyers believed they were purchasing authentic Pokémon cards but later learned the cards were not legitimate.

Although Pokémon cards are often viewed as children's collectibles, rare cards can sell for hundreds or even thousands of dollars. Their potential value has made them a target for counterfeiters and online scammers. Fraudulent cards may be offered through online marketplaces, social media pages and other sales platforms.

The sheriff's office cautioned buyers not to assume an item is authentic simply because it appears legitimate or is listed on a well-known website. Before making a purchase, buyers should research the card's typical value and investigate the seller's reputation. For expensive cards, authorities recommend having the item examined by a reputable trading-card expert or professional authentication service before payment is made. Residents conducting in-person transactions may also use the designated exchange parking spaces at the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The spaces are monitored by cameras 24 hours a day.

Before making a purchase, buyers should research the card’s typical value and investigate the seller’s reputation. Deals priced far below market value should be treated with caution. For expensive cards, authorities recommend having the item examined by a reputable trading-card expert or professional authentication service before payment is made. Buyers meeting sellers in person should also take time to inspect the cards carefully. See also: Police release photo of toy kitchen involved in Boynton toddler's death; family IDs girl The sheriff’s office noted that recovering money can be difficult once a transaction is complete, particularly when the item is later found to be counterfeit. Residents conducting in-person transactions may also use the designated exchange parking spaces at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The spaces are monitored by cameras 24 hours a day.

hero.headline: Florida property tax amendment draws organized opposition while supporters remain quiet
hero.body:
A proposed constitutional amendment to cut property taxes in Florida is facing mounting organized opposition while support remains largely silent. Groups representing police, firefighters, sheriffs, hospitals, cities and counties have raised alarms about Amendment 3, warning the proposed tax cut could hollow out local budgets and jeopardize police, fire, emergency medical and other services. The Republican-controlled Legislature placed Amendment 3 on the November ballot during a June special session. Under the proposal, the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes would increase to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. The amendment would also reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. A state fiscal analysis estimates the amendments quantifiable provisions would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion during the 2027-28 fiscal year, eventually reaching approximately $11.83 billion annually.

Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd called the proposal a train wreck during a Tuesday news conference. The Florida Sheriffs Association said it is significantly concerned about the proposal. The Florida State Fraternal Order of Police has formally opposed it, while the Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association warned that it could undermine public-safety funding without providing a replacement revenue source. On Wednesday, the No On Three campaign announced endorsements from 31 Democratic state lawmakers, including House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell and Senate Democratic Leader Lori Berman.

Governor Ron DeSantis called the special session that produced the proposal and said he will vote for it, but made clear the Legislature's final product fell short of what he wanted. Attorney General James Uthmeier paired support for tax relief with concern about potential consequences. U.S. Senator Rick Scott initially appeared skeptical but later announced he would vote for Amendment 3. No comparable statewide Yes On Three campaign has publicly materialized.

A July University of North Florida poll found 61% support when likely voters were told the amendment would begin phasing out non-school homestead taxes, only one percentage point above the 60% constitutional threshold needed to pass. Support fell to 45% when respondents were also told that estimates suggested the proposal could create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over its first two years. Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank ruled this week that the title and summary written by lawmakers were biased, misleading and factually inaccurate, ordering Attorney General Uthmeier to submit a replacement within 10 days.
hero.article_text: The campaign against Florida’s sweeping property-tax amendment is expanding by the day. A comparable effort to pass it, so far, barely exists.Groups representing police, firefighters, sheriffs, hospitals, cities and counties have all raised alarms about Amendment 3, warning the proposed tax cut could hollow out local budgets and jeopardize police, fire, emergency medical and other services.WATCH FORREST SAUNDERS' COVERAGE BELOW:One of the most forceful warnings came from Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd, one of Florida’s highest-profile conservative sheriffs.“It’s a train wreck,” Judd said during a Tuesday news conference.“This is the most ludicrous piece of unresearched stuff I’ve seen,” he added.The Florida Sheriffs Association said it is “significantly concerned” about the proposal. The Florida State Fraternal Order of Police has formally opposed it, while the Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association have warned that it could undermine public-safety funding without providing a replacement revenue source.Judd said sheriffs support meaningful tax relief—but not through Amendment 3.“Make no mistake about it: The Florida sheriffs believe that we can have meaningful tax savings for the people of the state of Florida, but this instrument in November is not the instrument to do that,” he said.The organized opposition grew again Wednesday when the No On Three campaign announced endorsements from 31 Democratic state lawmakers, including House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell and Senate Democratic Leader Lori Berman.“It will be a tax increase, or we’ll all lose services that we rely on every day,” campaign spokesperson Jackson Peel said.What Amendment 3 would doThe Republican-controlled Legislature placed Amendment 3 on the November ballot during a June special session.Under the proposal approved by lawmakers, the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes would increase to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School-district property taxes would remain unaffected.The full increase would immediately apply only to homeowners who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. Newer residents would receive a smaller exemption for four years before qualifying for the larger benefit in their fifth year.Amendment 3 would also reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties, including rentals and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%. It would restrict how cities and counties may spend remaining property-tax revenue and require lawmakers to create a process through which local governments could further increase the exemption.A state fiscal analysis estimates that the amendment’s quantifiable provisions would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion during the 2027-28 fiscal year. The projected annual impact eventually reaches approximately $11.83 billion.The analysis does not estimate the additional effect of any future effort to fully exempt homesteaded properties from county or municipal taxes.Support—but little enthusiasmDespite the increasingly organized opposition, no comparable statewide “Yes On Three” campaign has publicly materialized. The amendment has Republican support, but few prominent GOP leaders appear eager to become its champion.Gov. Ron DeSantis called the special session that produced the proposal and has said he will vote for it. But he has also made clear that the Legislature’s final product fell short of what he wanted.“I don’t think you’re going to see me leading that on this particular proposal, because while I support it, I do think it’s not all that I was hoping to see,” DeSantis said in June.Attorney General James Uthmeier has similarly paired support for tax relief with concern about the potential consequences.“We need to get money back in the pockets, but let me be crystal clear,” Uthmeier said, Tuesday. “I in no way want to do anything to jeopardize funding to go towards public safety.”U.S. Rick Scott initially appeared skeptical as well.“I’d love to get rid of property taxes,” Scott told Fox Business in May. “Unfortunately, you’ve got to think about, OK, so what are you going to replace it with?”Scott later announced that he would vote for Amendment 3.That has created an unusual political dynamic: The amendment was placed on the ballot by a Republican Legislature and is supported on paper by several leading Republicans, but most of the organized energy surrounding it is coming from opponents.Poll shows a fragile path to passageThat imbalance could prove decisive because Amendment 3 needs support from at least 60% of voters to pass.A July University of North Florida poll found 61% support when likely voters were told the amendment would begin phasing out non-school homestead taxes and restrict local property-tax spending to core services.That is only one percentage point above the constitutional threshold—and within the poll’s 3.8-point margin of error.Support fell to 45%, with 47% opposed, when respondents were also told that estimates suggested the proposal could create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over its first two years.“These numbers show how important the final ballot language will be in determining the outcome of this amendment,” UNF pollster Sean Freeder said.Exactly what voters will read is now changing.Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank ruled this week that the title and summary written by lawmakers were biased, misleading and factually inaccurate. He declared the language “clearly and conclusively defective” and ordered Uthmeier to submit a replacement within 10 days.The ruling does not remove Amendment 3 from the ballot. It changes only how the proposal will be described to voters.But with the amendment hovering near the threshold required for passage—and its organized opponents adding new allies—that rewrite could help determine whether Florida voters see Amendment 3 as meaningful tax relief or, as Judd put it, a train wreck.

hero.headline: State lawmaker challenges Fort Pierce Causeway Cove development's compliance with Live Local Act
hero.body:
State Rep. Dana Trabulsy told Fort Pierce city commissioners Monday that the proposed Causeway Cove development does not meet the zoning requirements of the Live Local Act, the same law she supported in 2023 that allows developers to bypass local height and density restrictions. The development would transform the existing Causeway Cove Marina into a mixed-use project featuring more than 900 apartments and condos, restaurants, and a hotel tower reaching nearly 200 feet in height.

Trabulsy argues a mapping error incorrectly designated portions of the Causeway Cove site as commercial zoning when they should be classified as aquatic development. According to Trabulsy, the aquatic area or submerged lands within the site are in the A2 Aquatic Development Zoning District and therefore not covered by the Live Local Act. The Live Local Act permits developers to exceed local height and density limits only in commercial and mixed-use zones, provided they dedicate 40% of residential units to affordable housing for at least 30 years.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick questioned whether such a significant zoning issue would have escaped state oversight during the approval process. When Trabulsy urged commissioners to rescind the project's approval and pursue legal action, Broderick expressed skepticism about the city's chances of success in court, saying he did not see the angle of attack that would not cost the city hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions of dollars, to fight.

The development has drawn opposition from residents who frequent the marina area. Mike Macy, who works on his uncle's boat at the marina, said the area feels like family property after four years of regular visits. Macy expressed concerns about how the high-rise development would change the character of the waterfront area where he brings his children for recreational activities.
