hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police release 911 call in fatal domestic shooting of Palm Beach Sheriff's Office employee
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police released the 911 call made the night Elizabeth Ortega, 50, was shot and killed outside her home on the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace, where suspect Ralph Varela Sr., 50, was later found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. In the 911 call, a neighbor described hearing five or six gunshots loud enough to rattle her house before her 4-year-old child spotted Ortega lying motionless in the front yard. The caller told the dispatcher she did not go outside because she was frightened, and that Ortega and her husband were frequently heard arguing.

The caller said both vehicles belonging to the residents were still parked outside the home and that Ortega was not moving. Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Palm Beach Sheriff's Office said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, and asked the community to keep both agencies in their thoughts. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Funeral arrangements are pending.

Port St. Lucie police extended their condolences to Ortega's family and loved ones. The department encouraged anyone experiencing domestic violence to ask for help and seek help.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police seek driver in hit-and-run that injured two children in crosswalk
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are investigating a hit-and-run crash at North 25th Street and Avenue M where an early-2000s gold Mercedes-Benz struck two children in a marked crosswalk before the driver fled the scene.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police are investigating a hit-and-run crash that injured two children who were crossing a street in a marked crosswalk. The crash happened at North 25th Street and Avenue M, where an early-2000s gold Mercedes-Benz was turning from Avenue M onto North 25th Street when it struck the children. The driver initially stopped and checked on the children before fleeing the scene.

The driver is described as a Black male between 20 and 30 years old. The car is described as a gold Mercedes-Benz with a tan interior, no window tint and damage to the driver's side. Police said one child was transported to a local hospital and later flown to St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach, where they were treated for non-life-threatening injuries.

The investigation remains active. Anyone with information regarding the vehicle or driver is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce King's Landing developer asks city for six more months, reports $15 million funding shortfall
hero.body:
The developer behind Fort Pierce's King's Landing project told city commissioners Monday it needs roughly $15 million more to complete the development's hotel and is requesting another 180 days to secure the funding. Live Oak CEO Paul Bertozzi said the shortfall stems largely from rising construction costs since the project's budget was first set. Commissioners did not vote on the request but scheduled a special meeting for September 14 to decide whether to grant the extension or take other action.

King's Landing is planned for the site of the former H.D. King Power Plant on the Fort Pierce waterfront and would include a hotel, condominiums, restaurants, retail space and public waterfront access. The project has changed hands multiple times since the city first selected Audubon Development to build it in 2019, most recently passing to Live Oak in 2025. City officials say the development agreement has already been amended three times to adjust deadlines and financing terms. Bertozzi told commissioners he is already in talks with potential investors and expects at least one to be part of the September presentation.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he will not support further delay, noting the city's financial exposure has already grown with the property's value as a city incentive rising from about $2.5 million to $8.5 million over time. Commissioner Michael Broderick took the opposite view, saying that terminating the agreement and reclaiming the property could mean years of litigation and cost the city hundreds of thousands of dollars, on top of the time needed to find a new developer and restart construction. The city attorney confirmed Monday that Live Oak is currently in breach of its development agreement over missed deadlines.

Bertozzi explained that hotel financing typically requires a 65-35 split between bank loans and investor equity, and that rising interest and construction costs widened the amount Live Oak needs to raise privately as the project's overall budget increased. While the funding gap continues for the hotel portion of King's Landing, homes are currently under construction next door with a different developer. Commissioners will revisit the issue at the September 14 special meeting, followed by a Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency board meeting the next day, since both bodies must approve any changes to the three-party development agreement.

cards.headline: State lawmaker challenges Fort Pierce Causeway Cove development over zoning compliance
cards.teaser: State Rep. Dana Trabulsy told Fort Pierce city commissioners Monday that the proposed Causeway Cove development does not meet the zoning requirements of the Live Local Act, raising questions about the massive waterfront project.
cards.body:
State Rep. Dana Trabulsy told Fort Pierce city commissioners Monday that the proposed Causeway Cove development does not meet the zoning requirements of Florida's Live Local Act, the same law she supported in 2023 that allows developers to bypass local height and density restrictions. The Causeway Cove project would transform the existing Causeway Cove Marina into a mixed-use development featuring more than 900 apartments and condos, restaurants, and a hotel tower reaching nearly 200 feet in height.

Trabulsy said a mapping error incorrectly designated portions of the Causeway Cove site as commercial zoning when they should be classified as aquatic development. The Live Local Act permits developers to exceed local height and density limits only in commercial and mixed-use zones, provided they dedicate 40% of residential units to affordable housing for at least 30 years. The aquatic development zoning classification would prevent the project from utilizing Live Local Act provisions, potentially forcing developers to comply with Fort Pierce's original height and density restrictions.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick questioned whether such a significant zoning issue would have escaped state oversight during the approval process. When Trabulsy urged commissioners to rescind the project's approval and pursue legal action, Broderick expressed skepticism about the city's chances of success in court, saying he does not see an angle of attack that would not cost the city hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions of dollars, to fight.

The development has relied on the Live Local Act to override local zoning restrictions.Trabulsy argues the project fails to comply with the law's specific zoning requirements. The Live Local Act permits developers to exceed local height and density limits only in commercial and mixed-use zones, provided they dedicate 40% of residential units to affordable housing for at least 30 years."I feel upon review the City of Fort Pierce land development regulations comprehensive plan and applicability of SB-102 Live Local Act, the Causeway Cove is not in compliance," Trabulsy said during Monday's commission meeting.According to Trabulsy, a mapping error incorrectly designated portions of the Causeway Cove site as commercial zoning when they should be classified as aquatic development. This distinction could prove crucial for the project's legal standing."The aquatic area or submerged lands within the site are in the A2 Aquatic Development Zoning District and therefore, not covered by Live Local Act," Trabulsy explained to commissioners.The aquatic development zoning classification would prevent the project from utilizing Live Local Act provisions, potentially forcing developers to comply with Fort Pierce's original height and density restrictions.WATCH WPTV'S PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Massive redevelopment in Fort Pierce could change the skyline and coastlineFort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick questioned whether such a significant zoning issue would have escaped state oversight during the approval process."I believe that if the zoning wasn't compliant, that the state people that were handling this would have caught on to that," Broderick said.When Trabulsy urged commissioners to rescind the project's approval and pursue legal action, Broderick expressed skepticism about the city's chances of success in court."I do not see the angle of attack that's not going to cost the city hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions of dollars, to fight this fight with what chance of prevailing?" hero.headline: Tradition Lakes K-8 to open Aug. 10 in St. Lucie County
hero.teaser: The new campus in the Tradition area will open its doors Aug. 10 with as many as 1,600 students expected on opening day, providing relief for one of the county's fastest-growing communities.
hero.body:
Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to open its doors on Aug. 10, offering classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities. Crews have worked throughout the summer to prepare the campus for its first group of students. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto, 'Traditions begin here,' reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments.

The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location. 'We are busting at the seams in the south and the west. And this school is so conveniently located to families that we're going to have a tremendous number of students that are walking or even other parents dropping the kids off in a golf cart,' said John R. Prince, superintendent of St. Lucie County Public Schools.

Greene emphasized that months of planning have gone into creating an environment where students can grow academically and socially. 'It's about being in an environment that you can grow and continue with great levels. But bigger than that, you begin to set the tone of creating those strong academics that move with you from year to year to year. You develop friendships,' Greene said.

cards.headline: Sheriff's office searches Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud case
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office executed a search warrant Tuesday at the Fort Pierce home of Laura Beth Grasso, who was arrested in July in connection with an alleged fraud scheme that cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million.
cards.body:
A large law enforcement presence descended on the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard in Fort Pierce Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso.

Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses.

Neighbor Greg Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. 'Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up,' he said. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box.
cards.article_text: A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Driver sought after hitting two children and fleeing scene in Fort Pierce
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department is searching for a driver who struck two children with a car on Saturday and left the scene before authorities arrived. The crash happened on 25th Street near the Elks Lodge in Fort Pierce.

Investigators said the driver, believed to be between 20 and 30 years old, stopped briefly to check on the children after the crash but then drove away. Police are looking for a gold Mercedes-Benz that may have damage to the driver's side.

One of the children was taken to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening. The condition of the second child has not been released.

Anyone with information about the driver or the vehicle is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed Saturday night in a murder-suicide at her home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
The victim in a weekend murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie has been identified as a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace.

Police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. 'One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive,' Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. Police said the shooter was Ortega's longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself.

McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. 'Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements,' McNally said. The couple's son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine.

Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. hero.headline: Stuart man arrested after using PIT maneuver on North Carolina family near I-95
hero.body:
A Stuart man faces charges after deputies say he used a law enforcement tactic to force a North Carolina family off the road near Kanner Highway and I-95 in Martin County on Saturday evening. Michael Jeffrey Spiers, 36, is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse, and reckless driving following the road rage attack that occurred around 7:30 p.m.

The incident began when Spiers chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before pursuing her onto the highway. The woman called 911 and told dispatchers Spiers repeatedly tried to force her off the road. Her brother was following behind in a separate vehicle with his wife and young son. The woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95.

Spiers then turned his attention to the family's SUV, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run the vehicle off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. Spiers intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's SUV, sending it spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran from the car into the brush to hide until deputies arrived.

Deputies arrested Spiers at the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street. Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers did not know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. No one was injured in the crash.
hero.article_text: Body camera footage shows a North Carolina family walking out of the bushes and explaining what happened after being chased off the road near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95 in Martin County over the weekend. The couple, visiting Florida with their young son, appeared visibly shaken as they recounted the incident to a sheriff's deputy, explaining what happened to them and the man's sister, who was driving ahead of them. "He was trying to run her off the road," the man said, referring to his sister. Were you guys traveling together? Okay," the deputy responded. The family said the suspect, seen in the body camera footage, chased the man's sister for miles, prompting his wife to call 911. "The lady that he's chasing, she has a little baby in her car," the wife said. "He's literally chasing her with his lasers on. She's trying to get away from him. She said he's pressing brakes, trying to get away, and he said he's chasing her." The man explained that he and his wife tried to intervene, but the unknown driver then turned his focus on them. "You all pulled over?" the deputy asked. "Yeah, we all pulled over essentially because he stopped us again. So, I figured if we let him go far enough ahead, maybe we'll keep going. He got out, and he came back," the man said. The man's sister managed to escape, but the driver continued to follow him and his wife, eventually forcing them off the road. "And he's chasing you in the car?" the deputy asked. He evasive maneuver just off the road. He pit you," the man said. The driver, identified as Michael Spires, was taken into custody at a nearby gas station. "They did not know what was coming next, so they are extremely grateful that they didn't get injured and that it wasn't worse," Sheriff John Budensiek said. "Thank goodness our suspect didn't have a gun. It could have ended so much worse." hero.headline: South Florida communities weigh data center moratoriums as residents report constant noise from cooling fans
hero.teaser: Multiple municipalities in the Treasure Coast region are exploring or enacting moratoriums on data center construction ahead of the August primary elections.
hero.body:
The debate over constructing massive artificial intelligence data centers is intensifying across South Florida ahead of the August primary elections, as proposals like Project Tango in Palm Beach County draw both interest and opposition. Multiple municipalities in the region are exploring or enacting moratoriums on data center construction. While Florida currently has no hyperscale AI centers, residents living near large-scale data centers in other parts of the country report a constant, industrial hum from cooling fans that operate 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

Mehran Basiratmand, the Director of Innovations and Programs at Florida Atlantic University and former policy board chairperson for the state's largest data center, said the noise level, the water consumption and electricity impact to surrounding neighborhoods are creating concerns. Basiratmand said these concerns have a legitimate basis, noting the demand is growing and AI is front and center, but officials need to also be equally responsible for the limited resources that are currently available.

Several cities and counties in the region are either discussing or have already passed temporary bans, or moratoriums, on the approval of new data centers. These measures are designed to give officials time to study the potential impacts and develop zoning and regulatory frameworks that could mitigate issues like noise and resource consumption before developers break ground.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detectives execute search warrant at Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud case
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at a Fort Pierce home in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard as part of an ongoing investigation into an alleged fraud scheme that cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso, who was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia. Grasso worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller and is accused of using her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business for luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and money laundering of $100,000 or more.

Neighbor Greg Longhway told CBS12 News he watched deputies arrive in SWAT gear Tuesday morning. He said the family got four or five brand new trucks and food delivery every day from four different services. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret shadow ledger on her computer tracking where the missing money had actually gone.

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more.

Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. cards.teaser: Jason Gunter, the biological father of a 3-month-old who died in Fort Pierce, was arrested Tuesday in Virginia and charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of a 3-month-old child who died, was arrested by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death. He is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County. The arrest marks the fourth made as part of the sheriff's office investigation into the child's death.

Three others were previously charged in the case. The child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell, the child's grandfather Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon, were all charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said it remains committed to conducting thorough investigations, holding those responsible accountable under the law, and seeking justice for victims and their families.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office searches for missing 24-year-old man last seen Tuesday afternoon
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is attempting to locate Kaden Joseph Simon, a 24-year-old man who was last seen leaving his residence around 2:30 p.m. on Tuesday. Simon was wearing black pants, a black shirt and flip-flop sandals when he left. His direction of travel was unknown.

Simon has brown hair and brown eyes, stands at 5-foot-7, and weighs 160 pounds. The sheriff's office announced the search for Simon on Tuesday.

Anyone with information regarding his whereabouts is asked to contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-8477. The sheriff's office did not release additional information about the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is located in Indian River County, which includes Vero Beach, Sebastian, and Fellsmere.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
hero.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed Saturday night in Port St. Lucie by her longtime boyfriend, who then killed himself.
hero.body:
Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. 'One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive,' McNally said.

Police said the shooter was Ortega's longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. 'Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements,' McNally said. The couple's son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. In February 2016, the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. 'She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room,' the sheriff's office said in a statement.
hero.article_text: The victim in a weekend murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie has been identified as a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. cards.headline: U.S. Marshals arrest baby's father in Fort Pierce malnutrition death case
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the biological father of a 3-month-old who died from severe dehydration and malnutrition has been arrested by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Jason Gunter, 45, faces felony child neglect causing great harm and awaits extradition to St. Lucie County. The investigation began Aug. 20, 2025, when Robert Maxwell and his girlfriend Vikki Koon brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed.

According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, text messages recovered during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong with the child. Messages sent to Nicole Maxwell, the child's mother, stated, 'The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him.' Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. A separate text message recovered from Gunter's phone stated, 'The baby is starving.' Investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services despite those warnings.

An autopsy revealed Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The Medical Examiner's Office found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. The manner of death was classified as homicide.

Three others were previously charged in the case. Nicole Maxwell, 27, Robert Maxwell and Vikki Koon, 38, each face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an extreme environmental hazard filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.
cards.article_text: A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old baby who allegedly died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Detectives had obtained an arrest warrant for Gunter in connection with the ongoing investigation into the child's death. He has been charged with felony child neglect causing great harm and is awaiting extradition to St. The arrest comes after three others were previously charged in the case: the child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell; the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell; and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon. See also: Body found in ocean off Boca Raton coast, investigation underway All three were charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. Investigation Began After Baby Was Brought to Hospital The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when Koon and Robert Maxwell brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs that the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed. Detectives assigned to the case conducted interviews with family members at the hospital before serving search warrants and beginning what would become a months-long investigation. Caregivers Allegedly Noticed Warning Signs According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, the infant had been primarily living with Koon and Robert Maxwell after Gunter moved to Virginia. During interviews, detectives learned caregivers had noticed numerous warning signs in the days leading up to the child's death. Investigators say Koon admitted the baby was often fed only a few times a day and claimed he sometimes drank as little as two bottles daily. She told detectives she noticed the child was becoming increasingly thin, pale and lethargic. She also described frequent vomiting, excessive sleeping and a decrease in wet diapers. Despite those concerns, detectives say no one sought emergency medical treatment. Text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong. 12, 2025, messages sent to Nicole Maxwell stated, "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Search Warrant Revealed Conditions Inside Home When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an "extreme environmental hazard." The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Autopsy Findings Led to Homicide Ruling An autopsy later revealed the extent of the infant's condition. According to the Medical Examiner's Office, Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The autopsy found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Examiners also documented numerous lesions and insect bites across the infant's body. The Medical Examiner ultimately determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide, writing that the infant was dependent on caregivers for nutrition and hydration and that the failure to provide those necessities directly caused his death. Father's Role Under Scrutiny Investigators say Gunter was aware of concerns about the child's condition. The criminal complaint states that messages sent to Gunter warned that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. Detectives also recovered messages discussing food shortages and concerns the infant was not being properly cared for. Despite those warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services. A separate text message recovered from his phone stated: "The baby is starving." Detectives included that message among evidence supporting criminal charges. Sheriff's officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the court system. Meanwhile, two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

hero.headline: Deputies execute search warrant at Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud investigation
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning to execute a search warrant at the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. The warrant is part of an ongoing investigation into an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the business.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbor Greg Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Her bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret shadow ledger on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone.

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions.

The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. cards.teaser: Kaden Joseph Simon was last seen leaving his residence around 2:30 p.m. Tuesday wearing black pants, a black shirt and flip-flop sandals.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is attempting to locate a missing 24-year-old male. On Tuesday, the IRCSO announced that they are trying to find Kaden Joseph Simon.

According to IRCSO, Simon was last seen leaving his residence around 2:30 p.m. on Tuesday, wearing black pants, a black shirt and flip-flop sandals. His direction of travel was unknown. Simon has brown hair and brown eyes, stands at 5-foot-7, weighing 160 pounds. The IRCSO says that if anyone has information regarding his whereabouts they are asked to contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-8477.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office makes fourth arrest in death of 3-month-old child
cards.teaser: Jason Gunter, 45, the child's biological father, was arrested Tuesday by U.S. Marshals at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia, and charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of a 3-month-old child who died, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death.

Gunter is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. The arrest marks the fourth made as part of the sheriff's office's investigation into the child's death. The investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.

cards.headline: Deputies find $8,500 in cash, loaded pistol in vehicle tied to Southern Truss fraud suspect
cards.teaser: A judge signed a warrant July 24 authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Laura Beth Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest.
cards.body:
A search warrant executed on a vehicle connected to Laura Beth Grasso, who was arrested July 16 in connection with an alleged $7 million fraud scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies, yielded cash, jewelry and a firearm. A judge signed the warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office evidence compound the day after her arrest.

According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. The search followed Tuesday's execution of a search warrant at Grasso's home in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard in Fort Pierce. Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft, organized fraud, racketeering and money laundering.
cards.article_text: A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

hero.headline: Tradition Lakes K-8 prepares to open in St. Lucie County with 1,600 students expected
hero.teaser: The new campus will open Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities.
hero.body:
Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to open its doors on Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto, 'Traditions begin here,' reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. 'Throughout this process, we have talked a lot about traditions and accomplishments and the achievements that we want to build and grow at this school. Hence, our motto for the school year is that tradition leads K through eight. Traditions begin here,' Greene said.

The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location. 'We are busting at the seams in the south and the west. And this school is so conveniently located to families that we're going to have a tremendous number of students that are walking or even other parents dropping the kids off in a golf cart,' said John R. Prince, superintendent of St. Lucie County Public Schools.

Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school's inaugural year. 'The academics component is going to be there, but it is going to be walking through this inaugural year and looking back on all the traditions that we have created as a team, as a family, and the strength of our culture, and how we just grow throughout the first year will be beyond the definition of success for us,' Greene said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County detectives search Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud case
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at the Fort Pierce home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard, part of an ongoing investigation into an alleged fraud scheme that cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home where Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the local business. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

Neighbor Greg Longhway told CBS12 News he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. 'Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up,' he said. Longhway said he and other neighbors on Sunset Boulevard had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. 'They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there,' he said. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. 'They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care. We figured something was up over there, though.'

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret 'shadow ledger' on her computer tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with 10 years at PBSO, was killed by her longtime boyfriend Saturday night at their home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace.
cards.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed in a murder-suicide Saturday night at her home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace in Port St. Lucie. Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. Port St. Lucie police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. 'One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive,' Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said.

Police said the shooter was Ortega's longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. 'Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements,' McNally said. The couple's son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. 'There's no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting,' McNally said.

On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, 'She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room.' The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega's co-workers cope with the loss. Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. In February 2016, the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.

In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. hero.headline: Florida man used police maneuver to run North Carolina family off road near Stuart
hero.body:
A Florida man used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and passed through Stuart on Saturday evening. Michael Jeffrey Spiers, 36, is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse after the crash near Kanner Highway and I-95 around 7:30 p.m.

Spiers first chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The woman called 911 and told dispatchers he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. She lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son.

Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. Spiers intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's SUV, a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence.

The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Deputies arrested Spiers at the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street. Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers did not know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Deputies found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

According to the arrest report, the woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. Deputies say the suspect continued chasing the family's SUV. hero.headline: Palm Beach County cities push for more trees and shade as extreme heat bakes neighborhoods
hero.body:
Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation says the number one need they hear from people, aside from beach access, is shade. Community Greening, a South Florida nonprofit, says adequate tree canopy coverage is around the 30 to 40 percent range and virtually every city in Palm Beach County is at least in the 20 percent range and most are lower. The nonprofit has helped plant and give away nearly 30,000 trees across Palm Beach, Broward and parts of Martin County over the past decade.

Neighborhoods that have adequate tree canopy coverage are on average 7 to 10 degrees cooler than the neighborhoods right next to them that don't have that adequate tree canopy coverage, including at nighttime once the sun is out of the way, according to Josh Weiner, director of communications and engagement for Community Greening. Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation recently partnered with Community Greening to plant 1,000 trees at Dyer Park in West Palm Beach. The county has also started installing additional shade structures, including new coverings over bleachers at Sandalfoot Cove Park in Boca Raton.

The Resilient Glades Tree Campaign aimed to revitalize tree canopy coverage in South Bay, Belle Glade, Pahokee and Canal Point by planting 2,000 trees at county parks and hosting eight giveaway events. The project was expected to receive roughly $1 million before funding was cut by the Environmental Protection Agency. Community Greening next tree giveaway is scheduled for September at Halpatiokee Regional Park in Martin County. The nonprofit is also partnering with the city of Boca Raton to plant 100 native shade trees along El Rio Trail in September.

over bleachers at Sandalfoot Cove Park in Boca Raton.For many residents, those improvements can’t come fast enough.“People should have an enjoyable space to at least go and sit in the hot summer days its awful,” said Denise Andrews during a Let’s Hear It community event where she told us about exposed bus stops in Boynton Beach.But city leaders told WPTV's Vannia Joseph the challenge is that most The need is off the charts. It's just trying to find the funders to make all these projects happen.”Even so, Weiner says the organization plans to continue expanding efforts in the Glades later this fall.In Lake Worth Beach, Mayor Betty Resch says her city is also prioritizing shade improvements downtown and along the waterfront.“We do have a lot of people walking and biking downtown, and we’re trying to see where can we put more trees,” Resch said.She credited the group Neighbors Encouraging Shade Trees for helping plant additional trees at Bryant Park, especially near playground areas where natural shade was limited.Resch also said the city continues to deal with residents illegally removing trees without permits — violations that can carry fines.“Trees are very important to the city. We’re doing our best and not just for shade, listen to the birds listen to the habitat for nature,” Resch said. “You plant a tree not for you for the next generation, If I could have the entire city of Lake Worth under a tree canopy I'd be the happiest girl in the world.”Community Greening’s next tree giveaway is scheduled for Sept. at Halpatiokee Regional Park in Martin County.The nonprofit is also partnering with the city of Boca Raton to plant 100 native shade trees along El Rio Trail on Sept.

hero.headline: Fourth arrest made in St. Lucie County infant death investigation
hero.teaser: U.S. Marshals arrested the biological father of a 3-month-old child in Virginia on a felony child neglect charge. He is the fourth person charged in connection with the infant's death.
hero.body:
Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of a 3-month-old child who died, was taken into custody Tuesday by the U.S. Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death and is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County.

The arrest marks the fourth made as part of the sheriff's office investigation into the child's death. The investigation began when the baby's grandparents brought the child to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Medical personnel told deputies the child had been pronounced dead and showed signs of injuries consistent with possible neglect. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.
