cards.headline: Deputies search Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud investigation
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at a Fort Pierce home in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard as part of an ongoing investigation into an alleged fraud scheme that cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso, who was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the local business. Grasso worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller and has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Investigators allege Grasso used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of Southern Truss Companies. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbor Greg Longhway told CBS12 News he had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. "They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," Longhway said. He watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said.

Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Her bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release.

The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret shadow ledger on her computer tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions.
cards.article_text: A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

Fort Pierce Police Department officers were called to N. 10th Street before 5 a.m. on July 31 regarding a suspicious vehicle parked in an empty field. When officers arrived, they found Leslie Howard, 70, and Rakeya Jackson, 28, and observed drug paraphernalia in plain view. Jackson refused several lawful commands to exit the vehicle and actively resisted the officers' attempts to detain her.

Howard was taken into custody without incident. Both suspects were transported to the St. Lucie County Jail and charged with possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia. Jackson was also charged with resisting an officer without violence and tampering with physical evidence.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools open Aug. 10 with new Tradition Lakes K-8 campus and AI courses
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Public Schools will open for students on Aug. 10 with enrollment expected to hold steady at 42,505 students, though the district is adding new facilities and programs. Tradition Lakes K-8 will welcome students in western St. Lucie County as the district's newest campus, serving the Tradition area where population growth has been expanding. Superintendent Jon Prince said enrollment is projected to remain flat this year after the district lost 150 students last year instead of gaining the 350 projected by the state, costing around $14 million in state and federal funding.

The district's tentative budget is $1.07 billion, nearly $60 million less than last year's final budget. Prince said the district made significant cuts, most at the district level rather than directly impacting schools, and no staff were laid off but were instead moved to other positions. Despite the budget reduction, the district is adding two new artificial intelligence courses at Legacy High School this year.

Over the past seven years, enrollment in St. Lucie County Public Schools has increased by 7 percent, but Prince attributes this year's plateau to more families choosing homeschooling or private schools. Families are already preparing for the first day. Parent Jovani Taylor said he has been purchasing school supplies, books and clothing for his daughter Jayla, who will be starting fourth grade. Another parent, Julia Lopez, said her daughter will be starting VPK and noted the district's growth, saying she sees schools like almost every corner.

Prince said the district expects as many as 1,600 students at Tradition Lakes K-8 on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location in an area of very expansive growth. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto is 'Traditions begin here,' reflecting the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school's inaugural year.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office for 10 years, was killed Saturday night by her longtime boyfriend at their Port St. Lucie home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace.
cards.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed Saturday night in a murder-suicide at her Port St. Lucie home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. Police said her longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr., began shooting at her inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. One of the neighbors located Ortega lying in the front yard unresponsive, according to Port St. Lucie Police Department Officer Brittany McNally.

McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Varela could find other living arrangements. The couple's son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. McNally said there is no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, disturbance or argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. In February 2016, the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said in a statement that Ortega was a respected and cherished part of the PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega's co-workers cope with the loss.

In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. cards.headline: Tradition Lakes K-8 prepares to open Aug. 10 in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County will open its doors on Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities.
cards.body:
Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County will open on Aug. 10, offering classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities. Crews have worked throughout the summer to prepare the campus for its first group of students. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto, 'Traditions begin here,' reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments.

The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location. Superintendent John R. Prince said the district is busting at the seams in the south and the west, and this school is so conveniently located to families that a tremendous number of students will be walking or even having parents drop the kids off in a golf cart. Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school's inaugural year, looking back on all the traditions created as a team and as a family and the strength of the school's culture.

Hence, our motto for the school year is that tradition leads K through eight. Traditions begin here," Greene said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Greene emphasized that months of planning have gone into creating an environment where students can grow academically and socially. "It's about being in an environment that you can grow and continue with great levels. But bigger than that, you begin to set the tone of creating those strong academics that move with you from year to year to year. You develop friendships," Greene said. hero.headline: Martin County REACH Center launches workforce training programs in aviation, healthcare, and manufacturing
hero.body:
Martin County's REACH Center has opened its doors and begun offering workforce training programs designed to prepare residents for jobs in high-demand industries. The roughly $4.5 million facility completed construction earlier this year and is now hosting courses ranging from medical administrative assistant certification to technical aviation training for Daher Aerospace.

Evelyn Lopez was among the first 10 students to complete a medical administrative assistant cohort this summer. She passed the certification exam and is now exploring job opportunities. The program included mock interviews with professionals to prepare students for the hiring process. Lopez said her parents were proud of her achievement because it opened more career opportunities.

George Stokus, assistant county administrator, said the center serves students uncertain about college, those without financial means to pursue higher education immediately, and adults seeking career changes or skill improvements. The facility aims to create a local pipeline for jobs in aviation, marine, medicine, manufacturing, and environmental studies.

Ted Astolfi, CEO and president of the Economic Council of Martin County, said the center's mission focuses on creating upward economic mobility for the community. The center aims to help residents grow into better jobs rather than remain at a single economic level. Additional programs are planned to expand the range of training opportunities available to Martin County residents.

cards.headline: Florida man used PIT maneuver to run North Carolina family off road near Stuart during I-95 road rage attack
cards.teaser: Michael Jeffrey Spiers faces aggravated battery and child abuse charges after deputies say he chased a family on I-95 and intentionally spun their SUV into a barbed-wire fence near Kanner Highway.
cards.body:
A 36-year-old Florida man is in custody after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and passed through Stuart. Michael Jeffrey Spiers faces charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse, and reckless driving following the Saturday evening incident near Kanner Highway and I-95. The Martin County Sheriff's Office said the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted.

Deputies said Spiers first chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway, repeatedly trying to force her off the road. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking, and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. The woman escaped by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95.

Spiers performed an intentional PIT maneuver on the family's SUV, sending it spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran from the car and hid in the brush until deputies arrived. Deputies arrested Spiers at the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street. Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers did not know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Budensiek said Spiers acted as if he was high on a stimulant or having a mental episode. No one was injured in the crash, including the child inside the vehicle. Deputies also found a dog in Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone he used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner.
cards.article_text: A Florida man is behind bars after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and, at one point, passed through Stuart. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the crash happened around 7:30 p.m. on Saturday near Kanner Highway and I-95. Investigators identified the suspect as 36-year-old Michael Jeffrey Spiers, who is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Deputies say the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted. See also: 100-car Florida street takeover sparks 140-mph pursuit ending in 4 arrests According to investigators, Spiers first went after a woman who was driving alone, chasing her through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman frantically called 911 and told dispatchers he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Authorities say Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Investigators say witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. According to the arrest report, the woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. Deputies say the suspect continued chasing the family's SUV. Eventually, the suspect intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car; a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact of the PIT-maneuver sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence, deputies said. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Deputies say Spiers didn't know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. [I] don't know what was in his mind," said Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. He acted as if he was high on some type of of drug, some kind of a stimulant, or he was having some kind of mental episode. We don't really know." Despite the violent crash, no one was injured, including a child who was inside the family's vehicle. "They did all the things that we would recommend they do. They called 911," said Sheriff Budensiek. "Thankfully, our suspect didn't have a gun; it could have ended so much worse." See also: 1 4-year-old killed in three car collision in PBC leaving two dead and four injured Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle. During the investigation, detectives learned the dog had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers use to dated. The dog has since been reunited with its owner, according to the sheriff's office. Spiers was taken into custody and remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

cards.headline: Body camera footage captures North Carolina family describing road rage chase near I-95 in Martin County
cards.teaser: Sheriff's deputies recorded a visibly shaken family emerging from the bushes near Kanner Highway after a driver chased them for miles and forced them off the road Saturday.
cards.body:
Body camera footage shows a North Carolina family walking out of the bushes near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95 in Martin County, after being chased off the road over the weekend. The couple, visiting Florida with their young son, appeared visibly shaken as they recounted the incident to a sheriff's deputy. The family said the suspect chased the man's sister for miles, prompting the wife to call 911. The wife told the dispatcher the driver was chasing the sister with his lasers on while she had a baby in her car.

The man explained that he and his wife tried to intervene but the driver then focused on them instead. The family pulled over, hoping the driver would move ahead, but he got out of his vehicle and came back. The man's sister managed to escape, but the driver continued to follow the couple and eventually forced them off the road. The man told the deputy the driver performed an evasive maneuver that sent their car off the road in what he described as a pit maneuver.

Deputies identified the driver as Michael Spiers and arrested him at a nearby gas station. Sheriff John Budensiek said the family did not know what was coming next and were extremely grateful they were not injured. Budensiek said the suspect did not have a gun and the situation could have ended much worse.

hero.teaser: The statewide association says a November ballot measure to increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners could create longer law enforcement response times.
hero.body:
The Florida Sheriffs Association has entered the tax reform debate, raising concerns about a November ballot measure that would increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners. The association states it has significant concerns with the referendum, warning it could potentially create longer law enforcement response times. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said the association's position carries weight, noting that Florida sheriffs are always moderate in their responses and tend to be very supportive of the governor, making their opposition to the governor in this case a clear signal.

Snyder said he understands the frustration driving the push for tax relief but warned the savings may come with hidden costs. He explained that instead of paying for services out of their left pocket, taxpayers will pay for it out of their right pocket, as sheriffs' offices and fire departments would look to other taxes and fees to make up the difference. Snyder served as Martin County sheriff for 12 years and managed the department's budgets throughout that time.

Snyder said his department looked at every single nickel and could shave a little off the edges, but when 80 percent of the budget is personnel services, unless deputies or firefighters are let go, there is not much that can be done with the budget. The debate over cutting taxes and its impact on public safety is central to the amendment question facing voters in November. County and city leaders are grappling with how they would manage significant cuts in revenue as homeowners look to Tallahassee for relief from high tax bills.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools open Aug. 10 with flat enrollment at 42,505 students
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County Public Schools will open Aug. 10 with enrollment expected to remain flat at 42,505 students, despite the district opening a new school to accommodate growth in western St. Lucie County.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Public Schools will open for students on Aug. 10 with enrollment expected to remain flat at 42,505 students, despite seven years of growth that increased enrollment by 7 percent. Superintendent Jon Prince attributes this year's plateau to more families choosing homeschooling or private schools. Last year, the state projected an increase of 350 students, but the district instead lost 150, costing it around $14 million in state and federal funding.

The district opened Tradition Lakes K-8, its newest school, to serve students in western St. Lucie County where the Tradition area is experiencing expansive growth. This year's tentative district budget is $1.07 billion, nearly $60 million less than last year's final budget. Prince said the district made significant cuts, mostly at the district level rather than at schools, and no staff were laid off but instead moved to other positions.

Despite budget reductions, the district is adding new programs. Two new courses focused on artificial intelligence will be available to students this year at Legacy High School. Prince said the district needs to provide avenues for students interested in AI-related careers based on future legislation.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detectives execute search warrant at Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud case
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at a Fort Pierce home connected to an alleged fraud scheme that cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the local truss manufacturing business.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Her bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

Neighbor Greg Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. Deputies came in with SWAT gear and guns pulled, hollering about the search warrant and ordering people to come out with their hands up, he said. Longhway said he and other neighbors had long been suspicious of the lifestyle at the Grasso residence, noting they had four or five brand new trucks and received four different food deliveries every day. The family largely kept to themselves and never spoke to neighbors during the year and a half to two years they lived there, he said.

The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records, according to the criminal complaint. A forensic audit later recovered a secret shadow ledger on her computer tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail.
hero.article_text: A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Fourth arrest made in death of 3-month-old child in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Jason Gunter, the biological father of a 3-month-old child who died from dehydration and malnutrition, was arrested Tuesday in Virginia and awaits extradition to St. Lucie County.
cards.body:
Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of a 3-month-old child, was taken into custody Tuesday morning by the United States Marshals Service at his residence in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter has been charged with felony child neglect resulting in great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child's death. He is currently awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge.

This arrest marks the fourth individual charged as a result of the investigation. Three people were arrested July 24 in relation to this case. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center in 2025 after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

cards.headline: Two accused of drug possession in Fort Pierce after officers find them parked in empty field
cards.teaser: Leslie Howard, 70, and Rakeya Jackson, 28, were arrested July 31 after Fort Pierce police found them in a vehicle parked in an empty field on North 10th Street with drug paraphernalia in plain view.
cards.body:
Leslie Howard, 70, and Rakeya Jackson, 28, were arrested after Fort Pierce Police Department officers responded to a call before 5 a.m. on July 31 regarding a suspicious vehicle parked in an empty field on North 10th Street. When officers arrived, they found Howard and Jackson and observed drug paraphernalia in plain view, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.

The department says Jackson refused several lawful commands to exit the vehicle and actively resisted the officers' attempts to detain her. Howard was taken into custody without incident. Both suspects were transported to the St. Lucie County Jail and charged with possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia. Jackson was also charged with resisting an officer without violence and tampering with physical evidence.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast homeowners say door-to-door solar sales left them with decades of debt and malfunctioning systems
cards.teaser: Several Treasure Coast homeowners told WPTV they were sold solar systems through door-to-door sales with the expectation of significantly reduced electric bills, but were left with financial obligations ranging from $40,000 to $60,000 lasting as long as 25 years.
cards.body:
Several Treasure Coast homeowners said door-to-door solar pitches left them with decades of debt, malfunctioning systems and power bills that never disappeared. What began with a knock at the door ended for homeowners with financial obligations ranging from $40,000 to $60,000 and lasting as long as 25 years. The homeowners told WPTV they were sold on the expectation that solar panels would significantly reduce or eliminate their electric bills. Instead, some said they were left with malfunctioning systems, continued utility costs and solar companies that later dissolved or filed for bankruptcy.

Documents Ana Perez shared with WPTV show she leased a roughly $40,000 solar system in November 2021. She said her monthly Florida Power & Light bill initially dropped from about $100 to approximately $30. That changed in the spring of 2026, when her bill climbed up to $131. When Perez called FPL, they told her the system had been down since the end of February. By July, bills reviewed by WPTV showed Perez was paying nearly $300 a month, about $150 to FPL and another $150 for the solar lease. That was roughly three times what she said she had paid before installing the panels. When Perez tried to have the system repaired under its 10-year warranty, she learned the installer had gone out of business. Records obtained from the Florida attorney general's office show nearly 750 consumer complaints have been filed against just three solar companies featured in WPTV's investigation.
cards.article_text: Florida homeowners say door-to-door solar pitches left them with decades of debt, malfunctioning systems and power bills that never disappeared. WATCH WPTV'S REPORT BELOW: Now, a WPTV investigation found some salespeople may not have held licenses required under state law — and some contracts were missing a key consumer disclosure.What began with a knock at the door ended, for several Treasure Coast homeowners, with financial obligations ranging from $40,000 to $60,000 and lasting as long as 25 years.The homeowners told WPTV they were sold on the expectation that solar panels would significantly reduce or eliminate their electric bills.Instead, some said they were left with malfunctioning systems, continued utility costs and solar companies that later dissolved or filed for bankruptcy.“What a waste of money,” homeowner Paula Wass said.“We got taken,” added her husband, David McCauley.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey reviewed the experiences of Wass and McCauley, Mike and Judy Schopp, Jane Bibee and Ana Perez as part of an ongoing investigation into Florida’s residential solar industry.Since WPTV’s first report, Marty Jacobson, an investigator with the Florida attorney general’s Seniors vs. Crime program, said additional homeowners have filed complaints against solar companies after seeing the investigation.Documents Perez shared with WPTV show she leased a roughly $40,000 solar system in November 2021. She said her monthly Florida Power & Light bill initially dropped from about $100 to approximately $30.That changed in the spring of 2026, when her bill climbed up to $131. “When I called FPL, they told me my system had been down since the end of February,” Perez said.By July, bills reviewed by WPTV showed Perez was paying nearly $300 a month — about $150 to FPL and another $150 for the solar lease. That was roughly three times what she said she had paid before installing the panels.When Perez tried to have the system repaired under its 10-year warranty, she learned the installer had gone out of business."So no phone that you called you got through," said Perez. "We've had systems that were just complete removals," said Justin Hoysradt, president of solar installation company Vinyasan Corp. Hoysradt said he has received a growing number of calls from homeowners facing similar problems, prompting him to launch a separate company, Fix My Solar, to repair or replace systems for homeowners whose original installers are no longer operating.“The calls were coming in so frequently,” Hoysradt said, "and the reality was, a lot of the competitors on the list weren't actually licensed solar contractors." Florida law requires solar installation companies to hold active contractor licenses. The statute also states that "even the attempted sale of contracting services" "constitutes contracting" and "requires the corresponding license." WPTV searched state licensing records for each installation company identified by the homeowners. Nearly all appeared to hold active contractor licenses.But when WPTV searched for four individual salespeople listed in the contracts, only one appeared in the state’s contractor licensing database.WATCH PREVIOUS REPORT: Florida seniors say solar companies left them in debt and in the darkHoysradt said a person or company selling solar contracting services without the proper construction industry license could be operating as an unlicensed contractor.Jacobson also told WPTV that people selling solar installation contracts door-to-door are required to be properly licensed.“It is more frequent than anyone would like to admit," said Hoysradt, "and there are penalties for that." The salesperson listed in the Schopps’ contract was cited in 2023 for solicitation.According to a notice to appear reviewed by WPTV, an officer wrote that the salesperson admitted 'he knew he was wrong for soliciting solar without a permit' and 'knew it was past the city’s permitted solicitation hours.' Court records show he later pleaded no contest, received six months of probation, was fined nearly $350 and was ordered to complete community service.“I answered the door, and then he was telling me, ‘We’re not like all these other solar companies. This is going to be for you, the people,’” Mike Schopp recalled. Lucie County court records show the salesperson listed on Bibee’s third-party-financed solar lease also pleaded no contest to an unlicensed solicitation misdemeanor in 2023 and was fined nearly $350.Bibee signed her solar lease two years after that case.WPTV attempted to contact every salesperson listed in the contracts by phone, email and social media. None responded.Several telephone numbers were disconnected, and some emails bounced back."There are types of enforcement that are starting to pop up," said Hoysradt, "but the harm that can be caused is significant." The contracts reviewed by WPTV contained language disclaiming guarantees about savings, electric bill reductions or system output.The agreements stated that if the panels failed to produce enough electricity, the homeowner would remain responsible for paying the difference to the utility company.WATCH BELOW: Families say solar panel promises left them trapped in costly 25-year loans“Everybody’s supposed to read the agreement, but a lot of the agreements are 20 pages long, and a lot of them are signed on an iPad,” Hoysradt said.Some homeowners said the written terms did not match the expectations created during the sales pitches.“You feel like a sap, and you feel like, ‘I should have known better,’” Wass said. Of the four sets of contract documents reviewed by WPTV, only the agreements involving Bibee and Perez included the required disclosure.The documents reviewed for Wass, McCauley and the Schopps did not include it."If you do not have this disclosure in your agreement, there are substantial penalties to the contracting organizations that did not give it to you," said Hoysradt. Florida law says a seller who willfully violates the disclosure requirements may face a penalty of up to the total cost of the solar system.The law also says a homeowner may be able to file a lawsuit seeking certain finance charges, fees and attorney’s fees.However, the statute does not explicitly state whether an entire solar contract becomes unenforceable when the required disclosure is missing."And I would love to hear directly from our regulators that that statute does govern the sale of solar energy," said Hoysradt. WPTV repeatedly asked the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation whether missing disclosures could affect the enforceability of a contract and whether the individual salespeople identified in the investigation were required to hold contractor licenses.WPTV first contacted the agency in June, followed up several times and sent an additional request July 27. The agency acknowledged the inquiry but had not provided substantive answers as of publication.Records obtained from the Florida attorney general’s office show nearly 750 consumer complaints have been filed against just three solar companies featured in WPTV’s investigation.That total does not include complaints involving other solar businesses that WPTV has not yet examined.The complaints vary in nature and are not limited to allegations involving unlicensed solar sales or missing disclosure forms.Jacobson said homeowners experiencing similar problems should preserve their contracts, financing documents, sales materials, utility bills and communications with the companies involved. They may also file complaints with Seniors vs. Crime or the Florida attorney general’s office.WPTV has connected the featured homeowners with consumer assistance resources.Bibee said Fix My Solar helped her better understand her options for attempting to cancel her contract.Perez said a contractor was ultimately able to repair her system and get the panels producing power again.Still, Perez said the experience left her regretting the agreement.“I never should have gotten it,” she said, “because it’s owning me.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

hero.headline: Detectives execute search warrant at Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud investigation
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at a Fort Pierce home connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Crime scene investigators gathered evidence outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard.

Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the company. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Investigators allege Grasso worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller and used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses.

Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO), and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Her bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release.

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2019 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's communications officer killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer with nearly 25 years of emergency communications experience, was shot and killed Saturday night at her Port St. Lucie home by her longtime partner.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office identified the victim Monday as Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years. Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.

Investigators identified the suspect as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. and confirmed Ortega was also 50 years old. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating. Police believe Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Investigators said Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting, according to detectives.

Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. PBSO said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.

hero.headline: Road rage attack ends with driver using police tactic to crash family's SUV into fence near Stuart
hero.body:
A Florida man faces aggravated battery and child abuse charges after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on Interstate 95 and passed through Stuart. The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested 36-year-old Michael Jeffrey Spiers following the crash around 7:30 p.m. Saturday near Kanner Highway and Interstate 95. Deputies say the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted.

According to investigators, Spiers first chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman frantically called 911 and told dispatchers he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Authorities say Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. The woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on Interstate 95. Deputies say the suspect continued chasing the family's SUV.

The suspect intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car, a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Deputies say Spiers didn't know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers acted as if he was high on some type of drug, some kind of a stimulant, or he was having some kind of mental episode. No one was injured, including a child who was inside the family's vehicle.

Sheriff Budensiek said the family did all the things the sheriff's office would recommend by calling 911. Thankfully, our suspect didn't have a gun; it could have ended so much worse, Budensiek said. Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle. During the investigation, detectives learned the dog had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has since been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

hero.headline: Fourth arrest made in St. Lucie County infant death investigation
hero.body:
A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old child in St. Lucie County. Jason Gunter, 45, the child's biological father, was taken into custody Tuesday morning by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death.

The investigation began in 2025 when deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. Medical personnel notified the sheriff's office that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Gunter is currently awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. This arrest marks the fourth individual charged as a result of the investigation. Three people were arrested on July 24 in relation to this case. The child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell, the child's grandfather Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon, were each charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process. Working with the Florida Department of Children and Families, authorities ensured the safety of two other children living in the home by placing them in a safe environment. All suspects are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's communications officer killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years, was killed Saturday night in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office announced Monday that Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years, was killed in what investigators say was a murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie over the weekend. Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators identified the suspect as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. and confirmed Ortega was also 50 years old. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating.

Police believe Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Investigators said Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting. Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office.

cards.headline: Two arrested on drug charges after being found in empty field in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police arrested two people on drug possession charges after officers found them parked in an empty field on N. 10th Street early Thursday morning.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested Leslie Howard, 70, and Rakeya Jackson, 28, before 5 a.m. on July 31 after officers were called to N. 10th Street regarding a suspicious vehicle parked in an empty field. When officers arrived, they observed drug paraphernalia in plain view inside the vehicle. The Fort Pierce Police Department said Jackson refused several lawful commands to exit the vehicle and actively resisted the officers' attempts to detain her. Howard was taken into custody without incident.

Both suspects were transported to the St. Lucie County Jail and charged with possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia. Jackson was also charged with resisting an officer without violence and tampering with physical evidence.

hero.headline: Man arrested after road rage attack involving PIT maneuver sends family into fence in Stuart area
hero.body:
A 36-year-old Florida man is in jail after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and passed through Stuart. Michael Jeffrey Spiers was arrested and charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse following the Saturday evening crash near Kanner Highway and I-95, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

The attack began around 7:30 p.m. when Spiers chased a woman who was driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman called 911 and told dispatchers Spiers repeatedly tried to force her off the road. Her brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters.

The woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. Spiers continued chasing the family's SUV and eventually performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car, sending it spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody.

No one was injured, including the child inside the family's vehicle. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers didn't know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Spiers acted as if he was high on some type of drug or having some kind of mental episode, Budensiek said. Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

hero.headline: Fourth arrest made in death of 3-month-old in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office arrested a fourth person Tuesday in connection with the death of a 3-month-old child who died from dehydration and malnutrition. Jason Gunter, 45, the child's biological father, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. He faces a charge of felony child neglect causing great bodily harm.

The arrest stems from an investigation that began in August 2025 when the child's grandparents brought the baby to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center. Medical personnel pronounced the child dead and observed injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the manner of death to be homicide, with the cause attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Three other people were arrested on July 24 in the case. The child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell, the child's grandfather, 61-year-old Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon, were each charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond.

Gunter is currently awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County. The sheriff's office said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.

According to investigators, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, the child's biological father, was taken into custody Tuesday, Aug. Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death. Authorities said Gunter is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. The arrest marks the fourth made as part of the sheriff's office's investigation into the child's death. Lucie County Sheriff's Office remains committed to conducting thorough investigations, holding those responsible accountable under the law, and seeking justice for victims and their families," the agency said in a statement. Officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process. No additional information has been released.

hero.headline: Three candidates vie for Martin County Commission District 4 seat in August 18 primary
hero.body:
Three candidates are running for the District 4 Martin County Commission seat in the August 18 Primary Election. John Dial, Sarah Heard, and John Kaz Kazanjian qualified for the race.

Dial identified over-development as the most serious issue facing Martin County, citing Senate Bill 180, SB102, and new mandates from Tallahassee that remove power from local voters and leaders. He said he would go to Tallahassee as often as necessary to represent local control and push to restore the county's ability to make decisions. Dial also opposed using taxpayer money to fund Brightline, calling it a private company that is not U.S.-owned, carries roughly $2 billion in debt, and is reportedly losing more than $220 million a year. He said he would be open to a train station if a private rail company wanted to invest its own capital, or a fair market land lease at the fairgrounds provided the property would revert to the county if the company fails.

Heard said the legislature is taking decision-making out of the Board's hands and only essential services like the Sheriff and Fire Rescue can be funded with ad valorem taxes. She said even if funding only public safety, the county would not be able to fund it by the third year. Heard said she is in favor of a train station downtown but would consider the fairgrounds location if the majority of residents overwhelmingly favors it. She said she does not want to see data centers in unincorporated Martin County because they are not allowed uses on agricultural lands, and a comprehensive plan amendment would have to be approved to change the future land use, which she would oppose.

Both Dial and Heard addressed a potential referendum on raising the Homestead exemption and cutting ad valorem property tax income. Dial said he would protect essential services first including fire protection, law enforcement, waste management, and education while reviewing non-essential programs and discretionary spending for reductions. He also suggested exploring ways to turn costly county assets like Sailfish Splash, the golf course, and the cafe on the beach into revenue-producing opportunities by leasing them to private operators. On the Business Development Board's annual $450,000 funding, which District 1 Commissioner Eileen Vargas opposed on June 23, Dial said he supports the BDB in its current role but that every use of taxpayer dollars must be examined carefully if spending cuts are forced. Heard agreed that the BDB is too dependent on government funding.
hero.article_text: John Dial John ‘Kaz’ Kazanjian Sarah Heard The Hometown News sent the same list of questions below to each qualified candidate in the August 18 Primary Election for the District 4 Martin County Commission Seat. Question 1: What do you view as the most serious issue facing Martin County and how would you propose addressing that if elected? Question 2: There will be a referendum this year on raising the Homestead exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income significantly to municipalities. If you are elected and that passes, what areas of the county budget would you suggest trimming or cutting out altogether if need-be? Question 3: Where do you stand on Martin County’s current plan to fund the Brightline train station and potentially relocating that to the county fairgrounds site? Question 4: Do you think the County Commission should address the lack of affordable housing, and if so, in what way? Question 5: On June 23, the County Commission majority voted to approve the Business Development Board’s annual $450,000 funding as part of the Consent Agenda. District 1 Commissioner Eileen Vargas cast the lone opposing vote, insisting the BDB become self-sufficient like the Economic Development Council of Martin County and potentially merge with that entity. If elected, would you support the BDB’s current funding or side with Commissioner Vargas? Question 6: The possibility of data center applications, particularly in the Indiantown area, have been very divisive. Have you studied this issue yourself, and if so, how do you think it should be addressed if you’re elected? Question 7: If elected, how would you work to improve the quality of life for Martin County voters? The most serious issue facing our county right now is over-development, and that problem has only gotten worse with Senate Bill 180, as well as SB102 and the new mandates coming from Tallahassee. These state actions take power away from local voters and leaders and make it harder for Martin County residents to control the kind of growth in their own communities. If I am elected, I will fight to take that authority back. I will go to Tallahassee as often as necessary to represent local control and push to restore the county’s ability to make decisions for itself. Without a repeal or major reform of this law, we will remain trapped in a cycle of over-development no matter what the people of Martin County want. In my view, we should have been more vocal, more organized, and more aggressive in standing up against these state changes before they were passed. We cannot afford to make that mistake again. The consequences for local government budgets are significant, and we must be prepared to act responsibly if it is approved. Like the families and taxpayers we serve, government must learn to live within its means. Over the past several years, citizens have been forced to make tough choices as housing costs, rent, groceries, and electric bills have continued to rise. If this measure passes, I will work to protect essential services first – fire protection, law enforcement, waste management and education – while carefully reviewing non-essential programs and discretionary spending for reductions. We must make sure taxpayer dollars are directed to priorities that truly serve the public. I also believe new development should pay its fair share and not shift additional burdens onto existing taxpayers. In addition, we should explore ways to turn costly county assets – Sailfish Splash, the golf course and the café on the beach – into revenue-producing opportunities. Facilities such as these could potentially be leased to private operators, allowing the county to reduce losses and create income. Every budget should be scrutinized, including the discretionary spending available to the five commissioners. I support a “use it or lose it” policy so that unused funds are returned to the general fund and put toward real needs in the districts. We should closely evaluate every dollar going to 501(c)(3) organizations to ensure there is a measurable return for the community, and we should look for better public-private partnerships where appropriate. I do not support using taxpayer money to fund a private company, especially one that is not U.S.-owned, carries roughly $2 billion in debt and is reportedly losing more than $220 million a year. That said, I would be open to a train station or stop in our county if a private rail company or a qualified buyer emerging from bankruptcy proceedings wanted to invest their own capital here. I would also consider a fair market land-lease for a smaller-scale facility at the fairgrounds or another appropriate location, provided the arrangement protects the public interest. If the company fails or goes out of business, the property should immediately revert to the county, and taxpayers should face zero financial risk. Yes, I do support it, either with non-profits such as Love And Hope In Action or if a developer is seeking to market a project as affordable housing or workforce housing. They should be required to deliver real affordability for the community. That means negotiating firm standards so that a defined percentage of the total units must be reserved at an affordable or workforce price-point. Permits should be made contingent on compliance with those terms. Affordable housing should serve working families, young people, teachers, first responders, and seniors. This is about fairness, accountability, and making sure that growth actually helps the people who live and work here. I support the Business Development Board in its current role. It plays an important part in helping Martin County grow by attracting quality jobs, strengthening our economic base and recruiting the kind of industries that support long-term prosperity. At the same time, if we are forced to make spending cuts, every use of taxpayer dollars must be examined carefully. No public funding should be automatic or off limits. That said, the BDB has a real value to our county. It helps position Martin County to compete for manufacturing opportunities, workforce recruitment, marine industry expansion, aeronautical jobs and other businesses that bring good-paying employment and responsible growth to our community. I am continuing to study this issue and will keep reviewing new information as it becomes available. If elected to the County Commission, I will give this matter my full attention and direct county staff resources toward gathering the facts before taking a position in support of or opposition to it. This is ultimately a decision for the Village of Indiantown, and whatever course they choose, the county should be prepared to assist and support them appropriately. At this time, I do not believe there is enough reliable information for me to make a final judgment. Protecting our natural resources must remain a top priority. I will work to improve water quality in both our fresh and saltwater systems and address the pollution sources that threaten them. I will also work to preserve agricultural lands, defend our development boundaries and review every available option to strengthen our comprehensive plan and restore appropriate limits on urban service expansion. At the same time, I will keep traffic concerns front and center, because growth must never outpace infrastructure. Within the laws and regulations I inherit, I will do everything possible to protect the character of Martin County and make sure our growth policies reflect the interests of current residents and not just future development pressure. Avoid allowing urban development to occur outside the Urban Services Boundary. The legislature is taking that decision-making out of the Board’s hands. Only essential services are allowed to be funded with ad valorem taxes, which means public safety – the Sheriff and Fire Rescue. All other public services are deemed non-essential. Even if funding only public safety, we would not be able to fund public safety by the third year. I am in favor of a train station here. At present the site is downtown. If the majority of residents overwhelmingly favors a fairgrounds location, I would consider it. We do through partnerships with the state and federal agencies, and we partner with Habitat for Humanity. We should continue to evaluate land trusts. I agree that the BDB is far too dependent on government funding. I don’t want to see data centers in unincorporated Martin County. They are not allowed uses on agricultural lands, so a comprehensive plan amendment would have to be approved to change the future land use. I would oppose such an amendment. My priorities have always been to clean up our water, stop over-development and keep our taxes low. Those remain my priorities. hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office communications officer killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
hero.body:
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office announced Monday that Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years, was killed in a murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie Saturday night. Ortega, 50, was shot by her longtime partner, Ralph Varela Sr., 50, at their home in the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace.

Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators said Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting. A neighbor found Ortega lying in the front yard unresponsive suffering from gunshot wounds. Responding officers airlifted her to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating. Investigators said the couple's adult son had left the home around 7:30 p.m. to pick up dinner and detectives found no indication of an argument or disturbance before he left.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Funeral arrangements are pending.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman arrested for drug possession after Walmart theft investigation
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce woman accused of stealing from Walmart was arrested Sunday after officers found narcotics and drug paraphernalia in her vehicle at a gas station on Orange Avenue.
cards.body:
Marrissa Bailey, 29, was arrested Sunday for grand theft, possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia after Fort Pierce police located her vehicle at a MAX gas station on Orange Avenue. Officers were called to 1228 Orange Avenue in reference to an investigation involving a white GMC Acadia that was connected to a late-July theft at Walmart.

Bailey was identified as the suspect in the Walmart theft. The Fort Pierce Police Department said narcotics and drug paraphernalia were also found during the investigation. Bailey was brought to the St. Lucie County Jail without incident.
